## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name

Bias toward working without stopping for clarifying questions — when you'd normally pause to check, make the reasonable call and keep going; they'll redirect you if needed. 1	# Review: Supertraining Chapter 3, 3.4.3 to end (36 entries)
2	
3	Reviewer: Claude Opus (independent falsification pass), 2026-09-27.
4	Brief: `staging/review_book_prompt.md`. Standards: `docs/ATOMIZE_BRIEF.md` (including the Ch1 lessons).
5	Scope: the 36 files in `staging/_scope_supertraining_ch3b.txt`, folder `staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/`, plus the `_book.md` Ch3 rows from 3.4.3 on.
6	Source: `staging/books/supertraining-6th-expanded.pdf`, printed pp. 166-200. Page convention: entry "PDF p. N" is the 0-based index; PDF idx = printed + 11; viewer page = idx + 1. Every page reference below gives both ("PDF 192 / printed 181").
7	
8	## How the source was checked
9	
10	- Full text of PDF idx 174-212 (printed 163-201) was extracted with PyMuPDF and read in full. Every entry was compared line by line with it.
11	- Page images opened with the Read tool (viewer pages): 181 (Tables 3.10-3.12, printed 169), 191 (3.5.3 end, 3.5.4, 3.5.5 start, printed 179), 199 (Fig 3.35, printed 187), 202-203 (Figs 3.37-3.39, printed 190-191), 205 (printed 193), 208-209 (Figs 3.43-3.45, printed 196-197).
12	- What the images settled: Table 3.10 rows are labelled "I-III" and "MS"; at 67.5 kg MS is 13.1 vs I-III 13.0 (MS higher). Table 3.12 caption reads "kcalories"; front squat elite is 12.7. Johns & Wright figures print as 41 / 35 / 11 / 10% (sum 97%). Fig 3.35: relaxation time about 0.40 s at level 1 falling to about 0.22 s at level 5; contraction time about 0.30 s to about 0.22 s. Fig 3.37 (stretch matrix, shoulder): biceps stretched by shoulder **extension + lateral rotation**; triceps by shoulder **flexion + abduction**. Fig 3.38: biceps stretched by elbow extension + pronation. Fig 3.39: iliopsoas stretched by hip extension + medial rotation. Fig 3.44 (movement matrix): triceps acts in shoulder extension + adduction.
13	- External checks (fetched, not from recall): Herbert, de Noronha & Kamper, Cochrane 2011 (CD004577.pub3; PMID 21735398, dated July 2011; cochrane.org displays the same pub3 as "2022, Issue 4"), results via cochrane.org and the Authors' conclusions via the Europe PMC record; Herzog & Leonard 2000, J Biomech 33:531-542, abstract via full-text PDF. Everything else external below is marked "(verify)".
14	- Vault (`SecondBrain/Knowledge/library`): no Herbert/Cochrane, Valsalva, blindfold, irradiation, stretch-tolerance or Johns & Wright material. Relevant stretching items found: `research-papers/dupuy-2018-...` (stretching did not improve DOMS or fatigue, p. 11), `research-papers/carvalho-2012-...` and `research-papers/chatzopoulos-2014-...` (acute stretching mode effects), Moyer `heuristic--passive-vs-active-rom-decision-rule-sprint` and `heuristic--pails-rails-close-active-passive-gap-sprint` (active-passive gap), `research-papers/collings-2026-...` (non-contact ACL mechanism).
15	- All `[[links]]` in the 36 files resolve. No inline em dashes (headers only). Nobody uses "Eric's baseline:" (no misuse; see G6).
16	- Rule 3: one `proven` (stretch-reflex framework), one `contested` (stretching benefits), four `untested` (no-unsafe-stretch, Olympic lifters, dedicated-stretching, spinal ligaments), the other 30 `supported`.
17	
18	## Global findings (rows cite "G1" etc.)
19	
20	- **G1. Locator errors, 3.5.3-3.5.9.** Several entries are one PDF page off, or cite a page the text is not on. 3.5.4 and 3.5.5 start on PDF 190 / printed 179 (not 189/178); the Magnusson bullet is PDF 192 / printed 181 (not 191); 3.5.9 is PDF 198-199 / printed 187-188 (not 199-201). Rows mark these "locator only" so they can be batched.
21	- **G2. Voice.** "The authors" is used throughout, which the brief allows. But 3.5-3.7 is clearly Siff's text: printed 180 (PDF 191) calls the section "this article", and printed 198 (PDF 209) says "a myotensiometer, which we used ... (Siff, 1986)". Where an entry rests on Siff (1986) or Siff (1987), say it is the author citing his own work. This matters for confidence in the Olympic-lifters, six-parameters and flexibility-definition entries.
22	- **G3. Missing mandatory section.** `claim--irradiation-...` and `claim--hypnosis-...` have no **When to apply** section (the skill schema requires it).
23	- **G4. "The book's own example" used for mixed content.** In several rows the Example adds the writer's material under that label (ligament "acute exposure", spurious tension "same tissue flexibility", movement matrix calf raise and leg curl, no-unsafe-stretch "paired example"). Only the source's words may sit under that label; the rest needs "Inference:".
24	- **G5. Source contradictions not recorded** (each is in its row): Table 3.10 vs printed 168 text; breathing volumes vs the "exhalation always exceeded inhalation" statement (printed 172); Iashvili vs Tumanyan on static stretching and active flexibility (printed 175, 185 vs 186); stretch tolerance with tissue "unaltered" (printed 181) vs elastic/plastic tissue change (printed 176, 179, 180, 181); stretching benefits and warm-up injury claims (printed 163, 176, 185) vs "many athletes dispense entirely with special stretching or even warm-up ... without suffering injury" (printed 192); Fig 3.34 separating ballistic from PNF vs the text making gentle ballistic a PNF subtype (printed 183, 186); triceps stretch text (printed 189) vs its own Figs 3.37 and 3.44; "prior stretching decreases isometric force" (printed 184) vs the force enhancement after stretch in the paper it cites.
25	- **G6. Baseline unused.** No entry cites `docs/method-baseline.md`. Not a defect, and better than misuse. Optional: the baseline line "Injury risk can be reduced, not eliminated ... an explicit refusal to promise injury prevention" (Inferred, class-1 transcript p.4) fits When to apply in the stretching-benefits and dedicated-stretching entries.
26	- **G7. "contested" as a category tag.** `claim--multiarticular-...` (confidence `supported`) and `claim--olympic-lifters-...` (confidence `untested`) carry `contested` in `category`. The brief treats contested as a confidence value that needs a named reason. Either drop the tag or set `confidence: contested` with a reason.
27	- **Improvement over the Ch2-3a batch:** Examples are almost all labelled "Inference:", no inline em dashes, no misused baseline lines. The remaining problems are misreads, locators, unrecorded contradictions and a few unlabeled mechanisms.
28	
29	## The three uncited claims on printed 181 (PDF 192)
30	
31	The printed-181 bullet list has many uncited lines. Three became entries or parts of entries:
32	
33	1. **Steroids disrupt the three-material bone-tendon transition** (`claim--tendon-insertion-...`). No citation in the book. The graded enthesis itself is well described in anatomy (fibrocartilaginous entheses with uncalcified and calcified fibrocartilage zones; e.g. Benjamin et al. 2006, J Anat 208:471, verify). I found no source for the steroid-disrupts-gradient mechanism; the steroid-tendon-rupture association rests mainly on case reports and animal studies (verify). Recommendation: set `confidence: untested` for the steroid clause (or split: `supported` for the graded transition, `untested` for the steroid effect), and keep the "uncited" flag the entry already has.
34	2. **"There is generally no such thing as an unsafe stretch or exercise"** (`heuristic--no-unsafe-stretch-...`). Uncited aphorism. `untested` is right.
35	3. **Russian/Eastern European scientists discourage cycling, push-ups and sit-ups for ROM** (absorbed into `framework--six-parameters-...`). Uncited ("they have discovered"). Treat as `untested` inside that entry. Note the book elsewhere lists cycling as an indirect warm-up that "can often enhance performance" (Franks list, printed 164 / PDF 175).

# Review: Supertraining Chapter 3, 3.4.3 to end (36 entries)

Reviewer: Claude Opus (independent falsification pass), 2026-09-27.
Brief: `staging/review_book_prompt.md`. Standards: `docs/ATOMIZE_BRIEF.md` (including the Ch1 lessons).
Scope: the 36 files in `staging/_scope_supertraining_ch3b.txt`, folder `staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/`, plus the `_book.md` Ch3 rows from 3.4.3 on.
Source: `staging/books/supertraining-6th-expanded.pdf`, printed pp. 166-200. Page convention: entry "PDF p. N" is the 0-based index; PDF idx = printed + 11; viewer page = idx + 1. Every page reference below gives both ("PDF 192 / printed 181").

## How the source was checked

- Full text of PDF idx 174-212 (printed 163-201) was extracted with PyMuPDF and read in full. Every entry was compared line by line with it.
- Page images opened with the Read tool (viewer pages): 181 (Tables 3.10-3.12, printed 169), 191 (3.5.3 end, 3.5.4, 3.5.5 start, printed 179), 199 (Fig 3.35, printed 187), 202-203 (Figs 3.37-3.39, printed 190-191), 205 (printed 193), 208-209 (Figs 3.43-3.45, printed 196-197).
- What the images settled: Table 3.10 rows are labelled "I-III" and "MS"; at 67.5 kg MS is 13.1 vs I-III 13.0 (MS higher). Table 3.12 caption reads "kcalories"; front squat elite is 12.7. Johns & Wright figures print as 41 / 35 / 11 / 10% (sum 97%). Fig 3.35: relaxation time about 0.40 s at level 1 falling to about 0.22 s at level 5; contraction time about 0.30 s to about 0.22 s. Fig 3.37 (stretch matrix, shoulder): biceps stretched by shoulder **extension + lateral rotation**; triceps by shoulder **flexion + abduction**. Fig 3.38: biceps stretched by elbow extension + pronation. Fig 3.39: iliopsoas stretched by hip extension + medial rotation. Fig 3.44 (movement matrix): triceps acts in shoulder extension + adduction.
- External checks (fetched, not from recall): Herbert, de Noronha & Kamper, Cochrane 2011 (CD004577.pub3; PMID 21735398, dated July 2011; cochrane.org displays the same pub3 as "2022, Issue 4"), results via cochrane.org and the Authors' conclusions via the Europe PMC record; Herzog & Leonard 2000, J Biomech 33:531-542, abstract via full-text PDF. Everything else external below is marked "(verify)".
- Vault (`SecondBrain/Knowledge/library`): no Herbert/Cochrane, Valsalva, blindfold, irradiation, stretch-tolerance or Johns & Wright material. Relevant stretching items found: `research-papers/dupuy-2018-...` (stretching did not improve DOMS or fatigue, p. 11), `research-papers/carvalho-2012-...` and `research-papers/chatzopoulos-2014-...` (acute stretching mode effects), Moyer `heuristic--passive-vs-active-rom-decision-rule-sprint` and `heuristic--pails-rails-close-active-passive-gap-sprint` (active-passive gap), `research-papers/collings-2026-...` (non-contact ACL mechanism).
- All `[[links]]` in the 36 files resolve. No inline em dashes (headers only). Nobody uses "Eric's baseline:" (no misuse; see G6).
- Rule 3: one `proven` (stretch-reflex framework), one `contested` (stretching benefits), four `untested` (no-unsafe-stretch, Olympic lifters, dedicated-stretching, spinal ligaments), the other 30 `supported`.

## Global findings (rows cite "G1" etc.)

- **G1. Locator errors, 3.5.3-3.5.9.** Several entries are one PDF page off, or cite a page the text is not on. 3.5.4 and 3.5.5 start on PDF 190 / printed 179 (not 189/178); the Magnusson bullet is PDF 192 / printed 181 (not 191); 3.5.9 is PDF 198-199 / printed 187-188 (not 199-201). Rows mark these "locator only" so they can be batched.
- **G2. Voice.** "The authors" is used throughout, which the brief allows. But 3.5-3.7 is clearly Siff's text: printed 180 (PDF 191) calls the section "this article", and printed 198 (PDF 209) says "a myotensiometer, which we used ... (Siff, 1986)". Where an entry rests on Siff (1986) or Siff (1987), say it is the author citing his own work. This matters for confidence in the Olympic-lifters, six-parameters and flexibility-definition entries.
- **G3. Missing mandatory section.** `claim--irradiation-...` and `claim--hypnosis-...` have no **When to apply** section (the skill schema requires it).
- **G4. "The book's own example" used for mixed content.** In several rows the Example adds the writer's material under that label (ligament "acute exposure", spurious tension "same tissue flexibility", movement matrix calf raise and leg curl, no-unsafe-stretch "paired example"). Only the source's words may sit under that label; the rest needs "Inference:".
- **G5. Source contradictions not recorded** (each is in its row): Table 3.10 vs printed 168 text; breathing volumes vs the "exhalation always exceeded inhalation" statement (printed 172); Iashvili vs Tumanyan on static stretching and active flexibility (printed 175, 185 vs 186); stretch tolerance with tissue "unaltered" (printed 181) vs elastic/plastic tissue change (printed 176, 179, 180, 181); stretching benefits and warm-up injury claims (printed 163, 176, 185) vs "many athletes dispense entirely with special stretching or even warm-up ... without suffering injury" (printed 192); Fig 3.34 separating ballistic from PNF vs the text making gentle ballistic a PNF subtype (printed 183, 186); triceps stretch text (printed 189) vs its own Figs 3.37 and 3.44; "prior stretching decreases isometric force" (printed 184) vs the force enhancement after stretch in the paper it cites.
- **G6. Baseline unused.** No entry cites `docs/method-baseline.md`. Not a defect, and better than misuse. Optional: the baseline line "Injury risk can be reduced, not eliminated ... an explicit refusal to promise injury prevention" (Inferred, class-1 transcript p.4) fits When to apply in the stretching-benefits and dedicated-stretching entries.
- **G7. "contested" as a category tag.** `claim--multiarticular-...` (confidence `supported`) and `claim--olympic-lifters-...` (confidence `untested`) carry `contested` in `category`. The brief treats contested as a confidence value that needs a named reason. Either drop the tag or set `confidence: contested` with a reason.
- **Improvement over the Ch2-3a batch:** Examples are almost all labelled "Inference:", no inline em dashes, no misused baseline lines. The remaining problems are misreads, locators, unrecorded contradictions and a few unlabeled mechanisms.

## The three uncited claims on printed 181 (PDF 192)

The printed-181 bullet list has many uncited lines. Three became entries or parts of entries:

1. **Steroids disrupt the three-material bone-tendon transition** (`claim--tendon-insertion-...`). No citation in the book. The graded enthesis itself is well described in anatomy (fibrocartilaginous entheses with uncalcified and calcified fibrocartilage zones; e.g. Benjamin et al. 2006, J Anat 208:471, verify). I found no source for the steroid-disrupts-gradient mechanism; the steroid-tendon-rupture association rests mainly on case reports and animal studies (verify). Recommendation: set `confidence: untested` for the steroid clause (or split: `supported` for the graded transition, `untested` for the steroid effect), and keep the "uncited" flag the entry already has.
2. **"There is generally no such thing as an unsafe stretch or exercise"** (`heuristic--no-unsafe-stretch-...`). Uncited aphorism. `untested` is right.
3. **Russian/Eastern European scientists discourage cycling, push-ups and sit-ups for ROM** (absorbed into `framework--six-parameters-...`). Uncited ("they have discovered"). Treat as `untested` inside that entry. Note the book elsewhere lists cycling as an indirect warm-up that "can often enhance performance" (Franks list, printed 164 / PDF 175).

## Entry table

| File | Verdict | Problem (entry vs source, with page) | Exact correction |
|---|---|---|---|
| `claim--irradiation-effect-raises-prime-mover-force-and-endurance` | FIX (heavy) | Checked: jaw example, overflow/irradiation (Knott & Voss 1968), cross-training citations, dominance mechanism (Shatenstein & Yordanskaya 1955), Vinogradov 1966 factors, 25-33% (Mukhammedova), at PDF 177-178 / printed 166-167. Problems: (1) Misattribution: entry says "Concrete numbers (Mukhammedova, 1958)" for the 39-42% and 8-22% figures; the source gives them, and the fatigue result, as Popov 1938 (printed 167). Mukhammedova's finding is qualitative: a momentary contraction of the left elbow **extensors** raises right elbow-flexor strength and speed more than a left-flexor contraction (printed 166). (2) Reversed detail: entry says "tensing the left elbow's **flexors** after first fatiguing the right flexors increased the right's capacity"; source: "Tensing the **extensors** of the left arm after first fatiguing the flexors of the right, increases the capacity ... Tensing the flexors of the left arm has no effect in this case" (printed 167). (3) Entry says the 8-22% decrease happens "without prior right-arm fatigue"; source gives it "during rhythmic flexing of the right arm", no fatigue condition stated. (4) Omits the amortisation reactive-force figure ("by an average of 25% in the vertical jump", printed 167). (5) G3: no When to apply section. (6) Locator "PDF p. 177, printed p. 166"; content runs to PDF 178 / printed 167. Headline ("can raise or lower") still holds, so FIX not NO-GO. | Rewrite the numbers: "Popov (1938): during rhythmic right-arm flexion, momentarily tensing the left extensors raised right-arm work capacity 39-42%; tensing the left flexors lowered it 8-22%. After fatiguing the right flexors, tensing the left extensors raised work capacity; tensing the left flexors had no effect. Mukhammedova (1958): left-extensor contraction raised right-flexor strength and speed more than left-flexor contraction; the largest effect came when the additional effort was 25-33% of the right arm's." Fix When NOT accordingly ("two dated lab studies, Mukhammedova 1958 and Popov 1938"). Add the 25% vertical-jump figure. Add a When to apply (label any application "Inference:"). Locator "PDF pp. 177-178, printed pp. 166-167". |
| `claim--multijoint-coordination-compensates-for-disadvantageous-joint-angles` | GO | Checked: three forms of change (Averianov 1963; Moikin 1964), cyclic phase shifts, proximal-link shift (Ivanitsky, Lebedev, Moikin), differentiation within muscle (Averianov & Shibanov), non-additive force, Table 3.9 largest summed force and % utilisation at the beginning (34/31/32/33% vs 27-29% middle, 24-26% end), Egorov 1966, "in this instance, the back muscles", at PDF 178-179 / printed 167-168. Example labelled. Optional: add Related `[[framework--kinematic-pair-chain-system-movement-analysis-levels]]` (Ch2 gives the same "resulting force is less than the sum" point, printed 103-104). | None required. |
| `claim--exercise-economy-improves-with-skill-and-interval-style-costs-more` | FIX | Checked on image (viewer 181 / printed 169): all Table 3.10-3.12 values quoted; kcal is correct (caption "kcalories"); front squat 12.7 elite vs 11.8 ranked; 35% single-rep figure and the momentum/elastic-energy explanation (PDF 181 / printed 170). Problems: (1) "9.9 kJ/min for Class I-II lifters": the row is "I-III". (2) "lower at the same bodymass division for Masters of Sport": false at 67.5 kg (MS 13.1 vs I-III 13.0). (3) G5: the text (printed 168) says Class I-III expenditure runs "from under 8 kjoules/min in the 56 kg division to over 23 kJ/min in the +110kg division"; the table gives 9.9 for I-III at 56 kg (7.5 is MS) and a top class of "> 90kg". Why it works and Example labelled. Optional: add the printed-198 point that "isolation" depends on load, "the greater the load, the greater the overflow" (see Missing 1). | None required. |

### `_book.md` (not in the 36 count): FIX

Entry counts per row match the 36 files (8 for 3.4.3-3.4.10, 28 for 3.5-3.7; "60" for Ch3 is right). Page errors: 3.4.3 is printed 166-167 (PDF 177-178), not 166 only; 3.4.6 runs printed 168-170 (PDF 179-181); 3.5.3 runs printed 176-179 (PDF 187-190); **3.5.4 is printed 179 / PDF 190** (row says 178 / 189); **3.5.5 is printed 179-180 / PDF 190-191** (row says 178-180 / 189-191). The 3.4.4 "0 entries" dedup note is acceptable, but name the entries it defers to (Ch3a `claim--pre-working-muscle-state-ranks-performance`, Ch1 `principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy`).

## Missing (important ideas in printed 166-200 that no entry captures)

1. **"Isolation" is load-dependent (printed 198 / PDF 209).** "The greater the load, the greater the overflow and the greater the involvement of other muscle groups"; isolation by electrical stimulation, low load or loadless training "generally develops more muscle hypertrophy than functional strength"; palpation versus EMG or myotensiometer (Siff 1986). This ties the irradiation entry (3.4.3) to exercise selection (3.7).
2. **Overtraining is not an energy sum (printed 170 / PDF 181).** Overload vs overuse types; "a workout consisting of a few maximal attempts may elicit an overload type of overtraining far more readily than a much longer workout ... with moderate weights"; overload may come more from technique that raises stress (force per unit area); actual work is 5-12 min of a 1.5-2.5 h session.
3. **The other reflexes (printed 178-179 / PDF 189-190).** Crossed extensor reflex 0.2-0.5 s later, relevant to unilateral dumbbell work; reciprocal inhibition; rebound making repeated maximal acyclic efforts harder but cyclic ones easier; local muscle spasm as a "physiological splint", sometimes relieved by contracting the opposite muscle with the joint fixed.
4. **Multi-directional and rotational stretching (printed 181, 186 / PDF 192, 197).** Collagen fibre orientation differs by tissue, so stretching should be multi-directional; "very few rotational stretches about the longitudinal axes of the limbs are ever used"; PNF spiral-diagonal patterns give "superior three-dimensional functional ROM". Plus printed 175 (PDF 186): ROM in one direction depends on concurrent movement in another, so single-plane lab ROM measures are equivocal.
5. **Hormonal state and stretching (printed 183 / PDF 194).** Pregnancy, menstruation and exogenous hormones (anabolic steroids, cortisone) change collagen mechanics, "so that stretching techniques should be adjusted accordingly (Viidik, 1973)". The book's only cited steroid-collagen statement; relevant to the steroid entry and to Athletic Medicine.

## Overall verdict

**GO AFTER FIXES.** Counts over the 36 scoped entries: **GO 5, FIX 31, NO-GO 0.** Plus `_book.md` FIX.

Verdict rule applied: NO-GO only where the title or headline reverses or misreports the source. Two entries have reversed or wrong physiology in the body (irradiation: flexors/extensors and the Popov/Mukhammedova attribution; history dependence: "prior stretching decreases isometric force" presented as well known); both headlines hold, so both are heavy FIXes.

Fix before promotion:

1. Heavy rewrites: `claim--irradiation-...` (Popov vs Mukhammedova numbers, extensors not flexors after fatigue, add When to apply) and `claim--stretch-shortening-history-dependence-...` (restate from the Herzog & Leonard abstract; force enhancement after stretch; "perhaps"; cat soleus; label the transfer to jumps).
2. Scope `proven` in `framework--stretch-reflex-types-...` to the replicated core, mark the Guyton-specific claims not proven, and rewrite When to apply so it no longer contradicts Basmajian's EMG silence (printed 177-178).
3. Correct factual misreads: Table 3.10 "I-III" and the 67.5 kg exception; biceps "abducted" and obliques "flexion" (stretching matrix); "which limb" (positive supportive reaction); flexibility-speed "static and dynamic"; "acute exposure" (ligament Example); "valuable" vs "invaluable"; "each from a single citation" (hypnosis); weightlifting vs depth-jump (instruction); cold "not as pre-exercise preparation"; Olympic-lifters context; coach guidance (blindfold); javelinists.
4. Record the source contradictions listed in G5, each with both pages.
5. Confidence: set the steroid clause `untested` (or split); keep the cycling/push-up/sit-up recommendation flagged uncited and `untested`; add Lauersen 2014 or Herbert & Gabriel 2002 (verify) and Dupuy 2018 (vault) to the stretching-benefits contested reason.
6. Locators (G1, batchable): soft-tissue, six-parameters, stretch-tolerance, reflex-techniques, spurious-tension, relaxation methods, irradiation, hypnosis, spinal ligaments, movement matrix, ligament adaptation; and the `_book.md` rows.
7. Labels (G4 and rows): "Inference:" on the unlabeled mechanisms and applications named in the rows (four-methods, ballistic, joint stabilization, spinal ligaments, soft-tissue, stretch-tolerance, Valsalva blood pressure, flexibility qualities, taxonomy Example, no-unsafe-stretch Example, movement-matrix Example, spurious-tension Example, six-parameters Example). Add When to apply to the irradiation and hypnosis entries (G3). Note Siff self-citations (G2).
8. Related links to add: Moyer active-passive entries (active-flexibility, eccentric quasi-isometrics), Ch1 S-factors (flexibility qualities), Ch1 SEC/PEC (stretch tolerance tension), Ch3a pelvic tilt (spinal ligaments), Myszka constraints entries (instruction, as tension), Dupuy 2018 (stretching benefits), Carvalho 2012 and Chatzopoulos 2014 (taxonomy), collings-2026 (joint stabilization).

1	# Eric's method baseline (draft for Eric's review)
2	
3	Purpose: this is the step-1 baseline for Flint. It pulls every position, practice, and decision rule out of Eric's own 23-document corpus (Baylor Applied Performance playbook, protocols, assessment manual, professional writing, and HHPR 5355 graduate-course material) so that every future synthesis note comparing an outside source (Landon Evans, TB's Training Info, Old Bull, Harries RTP, SCN/Moyer, etc.) has something of Eric's own to compare against. Date: 2026-09-26.
4	
5	## Provenance note (read this before the bullets)
6	
7	Not all 23 documents are Eric's own words, and the two richest sources (the class transcripts) have a diarization problem. Read this once, then use these tags:
8	
9	- **Eric-authored, high confidence**: the two SportSmith articles, the Performance Playbook Development Plan, the Force Plate Testing V3 and Iso Seated Calf protocols, the Applied Performance Playbook (departmental document under his unit), and the HD ODSF metrics note (adopted practice, though the framework itself is Hawkin Dynamics' own).
10	- **Course slide decks (Week 1, Week 3, Class 4)**: co-branded to Ruf/Rash/Wenger on every title slide. Per `spring-2026-teaching.md`, Eric was the assigned instructor for the Feb. 5 and Feb. 12 sessions (Week 3 Lecture and Class 4 2026 respectively), so bullets from those two decks are marked **Explicit**. Week 1 (Jan. 22, "All") and Class 8/Lesson 8 (Mar. 19, Wenger's session) are marked **Inferred** — shared team material, not confirmed as Eric's individual position.
11	- **Both class transcripts (Class 1, Class 3) are diarized entirely under one Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line, across 100+ minutes combined.** This is true even for Class 3 (Feb. 5), which the syllabus assigns solo to Rash. Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name rather than doing real per-speaker diarization. That means specific sentences in these transcripts cannot be confidently attributed to Rash vs. Ruf vs. Wenger. Bullets drawn from the transcripts are marked **Inferred**, with a citation note, even where the statement itself is a direct, confident, first-person claim in the text. Flint should treat these as "the HHPR 5355 teaching team's shared position, individual speaker unconfirmed" until Eric ratifies them.
12	  - **Confirmed by Eric, 2026-09-26:** HHPR 5355 is taught each spring by Chris Ruf, Eric and Mike Wenger. The lecture material is split among the three of them. This confirms the course is partly Eric's, but it cannot say who spoke a given transcript line. So transcript bullets stay tagged Inferred and read as **course team positions**. Each one becomes Eric's own only when he claims it, in review or in the interview.
13	- **Reference material, not Eric's position**: `intencurriculumn.md` is Jason Avedesian's (Clemson) authored curriculum end to end, used by the Development Plan as a benchmark, not as something Eric wrote or necessarily agrees with. The two Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are explicitly staff templates filled in (thinly) by Geyer and Skodinski, not Eric. The AP Assessment Manual V12 and the TechnologyTemplateSOP (TMG) have uncertain/likely-legacy authorship (see Tensions below) and are marked accordingly.
14	
15	Sections below use **Explicit** (the source states Eric holds this position, with confidence in authorship per the tiers above) and **Inferred** (implied by protocol design, shared course material, or transcript content with unconfirmed speaker attribution).
16	
17	---
18	
19	## Philosophy and decision principles
20	
21	- Applied Performance's stated mission is to "drive elite performance ... by leveraging science and technology through education and relationships," enabling the high-performance team to answer questions, ask better questions, and discover new ones — not to hand down answers unilaterally. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
22	- The department's four operating principles are Athlete Monitoring and Analysis, Athlete Evaluation and Return-to-Performance, Performance Team Collaboration, and Research and Development. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
23	- Institutional framing: "Prepare Champions for Life" across four pillars (academic, athletic, social, spiritual), operationalized through six "One Standard, One Accord" principles. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.3-4]
24	- Data collection is judged on cost versus insight: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
25	- A test can be scientifically valid and still be the wrong choice operationally: "The lesson wasn't about the test. It was about the infrastructure required to make a test useful ... even a valid test stops being valuable" without staff ownership and consistent collection. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
26	- "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" — a test's validity doesn't rescue it if it can't be collected consistently at scale. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
27	- Reject ownership language ("my team," "my athletes"): the athlete's development is shared across every department that touches them, not owned by any one coach. **Inferred (transcript, speaker unconfirmed)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5, "we got to get away from like the me and my"]
28	- Injury risk can be reduced, not eliminated, through sound programming, progression, and collaboration with Athletic Medicine — an explicit refusal to promise injury prevention. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.4]
29	- Be skeptical of social-media-driven training trends: a viral clip is "just a brief snapshot," stripped of the context that would tell you whether it's sound. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.3]
30	- Recovery has to be earned by training hard first; a culture of fear grew out of early GPS/load-monitoring work that pushed teams toward under-training in the name of "recovery." **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10]
31	- "Knowledge from experience" as a stated operating value: safety first, keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything advanced, treat strength as the base, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5; week1-lecture.md p.12]
32	
33	## Department model and roles
34	
35	- Applied Performance operates inside the Baylor Athletics Health & Wellness department, alongside (not above or below) Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.5-6]
36	- The athlete is described as the hub of a wheel, with every support function (academics, Athletic Medicine, nutrition, mental health, Applied Performance) as a spoke — no single discipline owns the athlete's development. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5]
37	- An Athletic Performance coach is framed in explicit contrast to a narrower "Strength Coach" identity: "we/our" and holistic mind-body-spirit development versus "me/my" and just lifting/running. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5; week1-lecture.md p.13]
38	- The current Baylor Applied Performance Operations Guide is judged, by Eric's own gap analysis, as missing: an intern/GA curriculum, sport-specific data dictionaries, daily operational checklists, Baylor-specific (not generic-template) technology workflows, and a guiding-principles/policy framework for staff and interns. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 1, 3.2]
39	- A three-phase roadmap (Foundation, weeks 1-4; Operational Depth, weeks 5-10; Education and Culture, weeks 11-16+) is the stated plan to close those gaps, ending with an annual Playbook review cycle each May. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]
40	- Some assessments coaches already run inside practice should not be duplicated; use that existing data to triangulate rather than re-testing, and set objective criteria for coach-mandated tests when none exist. **Inferred (author uncertain — see Testing tensions)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Team Cultures and Assessments"]
41	
42	## Testing and assessment
43	
44	- Assessment is continuous, not a single test day: start with movement quality, injury history, and training background, then observe daily via warm-ups and practice. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5]
45	- Testing protocol has to be exactly repeatable over time ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April") or the resulting data cannot be trusted for comparison. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6]
46	- Favor a small number of valid, reliable tests mapped to clear KPI categories over an exhaustive battery — illustrated with a simple baseball profile (bodyweight, 60-yard dash, vertical jump, broad jump, back squat, push-up max). **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6; week1-lecture.md p.16]
47	- Weekly tracking is preferred over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early enough to adjust programming. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]
48	- Preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness (day-to-day fluctuation) — both are tracked, but they answer different questions. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]
49	- Reassessment timing is governed by three factors: proximity to competition, the expected magnitude of change for that training phase and athlete level, and current recovery status — "do not reassess an athlete if there is known fatigue." **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Reassessment"]
50	- 1RM testing is reserved for intermediate/advanced athletes with real exposure to near-maximal loads; novices and most women's-sport testing default to repetition-max protocols, which are described as better tolerated neurologically, psychologically, and physically for smaller-framed lifters. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.18; week1-lecture.md p.39]
51	- Velocity-based 1RM estimation (linear-displacement transducer, ~10% load increments to 85-90% or a target mean velocity) is preferred over live 1RM attempts to avoid the fatigue and injury risk of true maxing, with published target mean velocities at 1RM (squat 0.3 m/s, bench 0.2 m/s, power hang snatch 1.0 m/s, power hang clean 0.8 m/s). **Inferred (author uncertain — legacy protocol, see Tensions)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
52	- The Baylor Sport Assessment Table (V4) assigns a specific battery per sport (movement screen, anthropometrics, CMJ, broad jump, weighted throw, upper/lower strength estimation, strength endurance, aerobic fitness, repeat sprint ability, linear sprint, change of direction) rather than testing every sport the same way. **Inferred** [update-baylor-sport-assessment-table-v4.md]
53	- The current data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar), not by sport, which Eric's own gap analysis flags as a real usability problem for staff and a priority to fix with sport-specific, threshold-contextualized dictionaries. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]
54	
55	## Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring
56	
57	- Force plates (CMJ testing) were already the department's longitudinal performance-tracking tool well before the 2022-23 wellness-survey experiment, and remained in place after that experiment ended. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]

177	## Tensions and contradictions
178	
179	1. **The task's own premise doesn't fully hold.** Both class transcripts (Class 1 and Class 3) are diarized entirely under a single Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line — including Class 3, which the Spring 2026 teaching schedule assigns solo to Rash (`spring-2026-teaching.md`: "Feb. 5 | Conditioning - Alactic-Aerobic | Rash"). Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name instead of doing real per-speaker diarization. This means roughly 30,000 words of the richest, most first-person material in this corpus cannot be confidently attributed to Rash specifically versus Ruf or Wenger. Every transcript-sourced bullet above is marked Inferred for this reason, even where the underlying statement is a confident, first-person claim.
180	
181	2. **Department reporting model is not internally consistent.** The Playbook (p.6) frames Applied Performance as a peer discipline inside Health & Wellness that "enables" Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Nutrition, and Mental Health to answer their own questions. But Week 1 course material lists "Applied Performance" as one of many training sub-categories nested under Athletic Performance itself (p.11), and the same transcript narration describes Rash's role as "helping program and plan the training" — a support-staff framing, not a peer-department framing. Which model actually governs day-to-day authority is not reconciled anywhere in these documents.
182	
183	3. **Coach's-eye-first versus objective-first is argued both ways.** The course material repeatedly argues that "you don't need a fancy test... you have to have a good coach's eye" and criticizes the GPS/load-monitoring era for breeding a fear-driven under-training culture. Eric's own SportSmith writing moves the opposite direction on daily monitoring specifically: he replaced subjective wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI because subjective self-report couldn't be trusted. Both share a skepticism of trendy or convenient data, but they land on opposite defaults (trust the trained eye vs. require an objective number) for the daily-monitoring question specifically.
184	
185	4. **The Assessment Manual (V12) reads as an older document than the current technology stack.** It builds its 1RM-estimation protocol around GymAware, and its CMJ description references a "contact mat" for jump height. The current Playbook technology stack and the Development Plan both center velocity-based training on Perch, not GymAware, and the current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol runs all CMJ variants exclusively on ForceDecks force plates, with no contact mat mentioned. This suggests the Assessment Manual predates the current VALD/Perch-centered stack and may be a legacy document rather than the currently operative protocol — worth confirming directly with Eric before treating any of its specifics as current practice.
186	
187	5. **Testing cueing instructions conflict across two protocol documents for the same test.** The Assessment Manual's CMJ instructions say explicitly: "Do not coach the strategy of jumping." The current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol gives testers specific verbal cues to give athletes during CMJ, squat-jump, and hop-test administration ("keep chest up," "land softly," "land stiff-legged on only the toes"). These may be reconcilable (safety/technique cues vs. jump-strategy cues are different things), but the two documents read differently on how much a tester should say out loud.
188	
189	6. **Two different anaerobic-threshold heart-rate methods appear back to back in the same slide deck without being reconciled.** One slide gives an age-based formula (max HR = 220-age for men, 226-age for women, threshold at ~85% of that), and the very next slides give a body-size-based table (big/medium/small athlete, ~165/170/175 bpm threshold) as the operational standard used elsewhere throughout the conditioning material. Which one is actually used day to day is not stated. [class-4-2026.md pp.27-29]
190	
191	7. **The Development Plan's own critique cuts against the corpus it's part of.** It states the current Baylor Playbook "has no educational component whatsoever" and reads "like a vendor product reference manual," even though Eric personally co-teaches a full graduate-level course covering much of the same material the Playbook is missing. The department's teaching capacity clearly exists; it just hasn't been captured back into the Playbook or a formal intern curriculum yet.
192	
193	8. **The Playbook's NordBord documentation has not caught up with practice.** The Playbook's Technology Overview and Workflows still document a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord data-collection SOP. The SportSmith piece describes explicitly retiring roster-wide NordBord testing for football starting after January 2023, keeping it only for small, targeted return-to-play groups. The written SOP has not been updated to reflect that decision.
194	
195	9. **A personally-stated periodization preference is stated inside an unreliable-speaker transcript.** "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use" (about undulating over linear periodization) is a strong, direct, first-person preference claim — but it comes from the same unreliably-diarized Class 1 transcript described in Tension 1, so it cannot be confirmed as Eric's own stated preference without his direct confirmation.
196	
197	10. **Older vs. current unit-goal templates show almost no adopted content.** The Geyer and Skodinski Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are staff-authored templates for individual sport programming philosophy; Geyer's is mostly filled in (periodization model, weekly split, KPI tests for softball), Skodinski's is nearly blank (just the section headers). Neither is attributed to Eric, and there's no equivalent document in this corpus showing Eric's own answers to the same template questions — a real gap if Flint wants Eric's own unit-goal-style programming philosophy in his own words.
