+canoe-kayak paddlers who took part in the USSR National team and earned medals in
+the Olympic Games and World Championships within eight years prior to the study"
+(PDF p. 163, printed p. 152, citing Sozin, 1986). Respondents were interviewed about
+their official performance results from ages 14-15, "the end of their first year of
+long-term preparation"; athletes who began preparation later were excluded from the
+analysis. **Verified against the page image (Figure 4.10, PDF p. 163, printed p. 152):**
+performance time on a 500-m course is plotted by two-year age band (14-15 through
+18-19) for three groups — kayak-males, kayak-females, canoeists — all three showing a
+steep improvement curve from roughly 140-152 seconds at 14-15 down to roughly
+102-120 seconds by 18-19, with kayak-males consistently fastest across every age band
+and kayak-females and canoeists tracking close together. The book frames the result as
+a usable historical benchmark rather than a fixed standard: "despite the substantial
+improvement of paddles and boats in the two decades since this study was conducted,
+the results achieved by outstanding athletes in the earlier stages of their preparation
+remain relevant to this day for evaluation of giftedness in today's young athletes" (PDF
+p. 163, printed p. 152).
+**Why it works** — **The author gives no mechanism** connecting age-14-15
+performance time to eventual elite status; the case is presented purely as a descriptive
+benchmark curve, not as a validated predictive model (no reported correlation,
+sensitivity, or false-positive/false-negative rate for using these times to screen
+today's youngsters). Issurin's own claim that equipment-era changes do not invalidate
+the benchmark is asserted, not tested against any comparison of era-adjusted times.
+**When to apply — Inference** — As a template, not as transferable numbers: the
+approach of interviewing an already-elite cohort about their own performance at a
+fixed early-career age point, to build a retrospective reference curve for evaluating
+today's youngsters, is a reusable talent-identification method independent of the
+specific canoe-kayak times. It illustrates the general "model characteristics" approach
+named earlier in the chapter (Bulgakova, 1986,
+[[framework--athletic-talent-four-factor-heredity-model]]) with a concrete worked
+example of how such a benchmark curve is actually built and reported.
+**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** This is a retrospective,
+survivorship-selected sample: all 35 respondents were already-successful medalists at
+the time of interview, so the study cannot say what fraction of 14-15-year-olds with
+similar performance times failed to reach the same level (no comparison group of
+similarly-fast 14-15-year-olds who did not become elite). It is also sport- and era-specific
+(1970s-80s Soviet canoe-kayak, single national federation, pre-modern boat and
+paddle equipment) with no cited data from any other sport or country, and the book's
+own claim that "the results... remain relevant to this day" is the author's assertion, not
+a re-tested comparison against a current cohort. Do not use the specific second-count
+benchmarks as a screening cutoff for any current sport without independent
+verification.

+sport Applied Performance evaluates by asking current or recent elite alumni for their

+looked like at this checkpoint" compares to a current prospect — while explicitly
+tracking that such a curve, built only from athletes who succeeded, cannot say how
+many similarly-scoring peers did not.

+# Four Features of the Adaptation Process: Overload, Accommodation, Specificity, Individualization
+**What it is** — The authors give a four-item checklist that "from a practical point of
+view" governs sport training adaptation: (1) stimulus magnitude (overload), (2)
+accommodation, (3) specificity, and (4) individualization (printed p. 4). **Overload**: a
+training adaptation happens only if the training load is above the athlete's habitual
+level, achieved either by raising intensity/volume on the same drill or by switching to a
+new, unaccustomed drill. Below-habitual load causes detraining. Training loads are
+classified as stimulating (above the neutral zone, drives adaptation), retaining (within
+the neutral zone, maintains fitness), or detraining (below it) (figure 1.1). Elite
+athletes' training load is roughly 10 times that of beginners with 6 months' experience:
+elite weightlifters lift around 5,000 tons/year versus 1/10th-1/12th of that for novices;
+elite cross-country skiers cover 8,000-12,000 km/year versus about 1,000 km for beginners
+(printed pp. 4-5). **Accommodation** and **specificity** are each large enough topics to
+carry their own entries in this library ([[principle--accommodation-and-the-diminishing-returns-law]],
+[[framework--transfer-of-training-coefficient-calculation]]). **Individualization**:
+"training programs must be adjusted individually to each athlete. Remember that all
+people are different" (printed p. 15) — stated here only as a checklist item, not
+developed further in this chapter. (PDF pp. 13-15, printed pp. 4-5, 15.)
+**Why it works** — Inference: the authors do not give a unified mechanism for why these
+four features specifically govern adaptation; each is instead grounded separately in its
+own subsection (overload in the dose-response and detraining discussion, accommodation in
+a biological-response-decay argument, specificity in the transfer-of-training data,
+individualization only asserted). Treat this entry's "why it works" as a summary of the
+book's own separate justifications, not a single mechanism.
+**When to apply** — As a four-point programming checklist when auditing whether a training
+block is actually driving adaptation: is the load above the athlete's habitual level
+(overload), is it varied enough to avoid accommodation, is it close enough to the target
+skill to transfer (specificity), and is it adjusted to this athlete rather than copied from
+a template (individualization). **Eric's baseline:** individualization matches Baylor's own
+department framing that stressors are additive and load must be adjusted per athlete
+(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power" and the vault's own
+[[periodization--bompa/principle--individualization]], which already treats
+individualization in full depth); this entry does not add a new angle on individualization
+beyond restating the checklist item, so readers wanting the developed treatment should use
+the Bompa entry.
+**When NOT to apply** — Inference: the elite-vs-beginner load ratios (10x, 5,000 tons/yr,
+8,000-12,000 km/yr) are illustrative benchmarks from weightlifting and cross-country
+skiing, not a football-specific dosing rule; do not transfer them directly to a
+position-group's off-season volume without adjustment. The individualization item is
+asserted, not developed with a mechanism or example in this chapter; do not treat it as
+carrying independent evidentiary weight here.
+**Example** — The training-load classification is illustrated with identical triplets: all
+three could lift a 57.5-kg barbell once; they began training with a 50-kg barbell to
+failure at 5 reps; once adapted, they could lift 60 kg once but stopped improving further
+on the same routine. At that point Athlete A increased the load (stimulating load,
+improved further), Athlete B kept the same routine (retaining load, no change), and
+Athlete C decreased the load (detraining load, strength declined) (printed p. 5, the
+authors' own example, not invented).

SUPERTRAINING
One more feature should be noted. If the given means do not elicit an adequate training effect, then increase 
m  work capacity becomes more a factor of specialised exercise than training volume and then only if it is executed 
by training at or near personal maximum levels. It should be pointed out that the execution of specialised 
exercises in training at near maximal intensity (as advocated by Bulgarian experts) should be regarded as an 
advanced strategy, a method which cannot be acknowledged as being universally appropriate. This would imply 
not only rejecting the principles of the rational structuring of training based on research into training methods, but 
also a return to the original concepts from which these began.
Thus, the problem of establishing scientifically the means of sport training is far from being solved and the 
current tendency to increase the volume of the training load should not detract from its significance and turn the 
attention of specialists away from its in-depth study.
If a logical sequence is to be recommended as a practical solution to the problem of improving the 
effectiveness of special strength training methods, then it should be laid down as follows:
1. Regime — 2. Means — ► 3. Methods —► 4. System —► 5. Volume
From this scheme it follows that the means of special strength training should be selected on the basis of 
quantitative descriptions of the motor specificity of the given sport and thereby provide an adequate regime of 
work for the body. The basic criterion for this is a guarantee of a definite training effect for the given level of 
special fitness.
The next step is to determine a suitable method of using the means based not only on the specific motor 
regimes of the given sport, but also on factors such as one’s level of fitness and the tasks of the current stage of 
training. Of great potential for perfecting the methods of special strength training, is the principle o f systematic 
application of means to produce the necessary cumulative training effect.
Finally, attaining the necessary level of special strength training depends on the volume of the special work, 
the optimal magnitude of which should be determined by the stage and current tasks of the athlete's preparation, 
the competition calendar and the intensity of the load.
This scheme emphasizes that, to rely on any one parameter of the load for achieving any given potential is 
appropriate only after the potential of the previous parameter has been completely exploited. For example, it is 
unwise to increase training volume without having fully elicited the maximum training effect of the individual 
strength training means at a particular intensity. This requires dedication and persistence from the specialists, 
because it requires in-depth investigative effort Since increasing the training volume is easier than finding a really 
effective means of special preparation, such a course tends to be a much simpler choice.
4.2 Different Means of Strength Development
The external force generated by muscles is a result of voluntary effort. However, under normal everyday 
conditions, muscular tension produced by voluntary effort has certain limitations. To increase the external 
muscular force it is necessary to stimulate them from the outside, for example, by means of mechanical 
stimulation. Afferent impulses elicited by mechanical stimulation inform the central nervous system about the 
strength of the external influence evoking the muscular tension. The greater the intensity of the external stimulus, 
the greater the muscle effector discharge, and the larger the external work produced.
Thus, afferent signals to the neuromuscular system play an important role in determining the qualitative and 
quantitative characteristics of muscular strength. Therefore, the stimulation of muscular tension for the 
development of strength is of great significance. So, in all cases the magnitude of working muscular tension is 
determined by voluntary effort and external mechanical action. The stimulation of working force can be divided 
into the following basic types:
• Stimulation when muscular tension is produced by voluntary effort against external resistance, and the
resistance of the moving load accelerates and regulates the effector impulses to the muscles
• Stimulation by the kinetic energy of a falling object or the body, when the effort is primarily reflexive
• Stimulation caused primarily by voluntary effort, under conditions where additional external mechanical
stimulation is absent or limited
• Stimulation of muscle elicited or intensified involuntarily by means of external electrical current.
207


=== page 219 viewer 220 ===
SUPERTRAINING
The first two cases are associated with dynamic work and the third with isometric work. An increase in 
stimulation is realised in the first case by increasing the velocity of the preliminary fall of the body or load, and by 
mobilising the athlete's voluntary resources in the third. It should also be pointed out that voluntary effort plays 
an important role in the magnitude of the effector response of the muscles in the first instance, whereas its 
influence in the second is insignificant.
The mechanism chiefly responsible for the braking or amortisation work of the muscles causes a protective 
effector response more rapidly than a voluntary sequence of actions. Therefore, such a reflex stimulus is able to 
provoke an extraordinary mobilisation of the neuromuscular apparatus, which is impossible where there is reliance 
on voluntary effort alone. This mechanism forms the foundation of plyometric training (5.2.4).
4.2.1 Electrostimulation
As has already been stated, there is always an ongoing search for novel, highly effective means of special strength 
training. For example, Russian studies have established that clcctrostimulation of muscle furnishes an adequate 
training stimulus for effective development of muscular strength (Kots, 1971; Kots & Khvilon, 1971; Khvilon, 
1974). Electrostimulation can be effective for certain purposes in the preparation of highly qualified athletes 
(mainly in speed-strength sports) and there are a number of advantages associated with this method of developing 
strength, in particular the reduction of joint loading. It can occupy a specific place in the yearly training cycle, be 
used in combination with other methods of developing muscular strength and be applied chiefly in the preparation 
of highly qualified athletes.
Ratov has found that functional electrical stimulation (FENS) can be particularly useful in improving sporting 
performance. His techniques, developed decades ago from his PhD programme on the interrelation between 
electrical stimulation and electromyography, has used EMG signals from agonist and antagonist muscles to act as 
triggers or control mechanisms for electrical stimulation of musclcs directly involved in producing functional 
movements in sport. In his laboratory at the State Central Institute for Sports Science in Moscow he has 
successfully implemented these neuromuscular stimulation methods in training athletes such as fencers, boxers, 
rowers, shotputtcrs and weightlifters.
However, it is inappropriate to consider the training applications of electrostimulation in detail here because 
its methodological fundamentals have still not been determined, especially as it should be applied preferably under 
suitable conditions by qualified personnel. The next section summarises the effects and applications of 
electrostimulation as a form of supplementary sports preparation.
4.2.1.1 The Physiological Effects of Electrostimulation
The concept of elcctrostimulation is not new, and for years has been used by physical therapists in clinical 
applications such as muscle rehabilitation, relief of muscular spasm, reduction of swelling and pain control. Its 
possible value in sports training is still considered controversial. In strength conditioning, the applications of 
electrostimulation fall into the following broad categories:
• Imposition of local physical stress to provoke supercompensation
• Local restoration after exercise or injury
• General central nervous and endocrine restoration after exercise or injury
• Neuromuscular stimulation for pain control or movement patterning
Electrostimulation usually involves feeding the muscles low current electrical impulses via moistened electrode 
pads placed firmly on the skin. The effectiveness, comfort and depth of excitation depends on factors such as 
pulse shape, frequency, duration, intensity and modulation pattern. The resulting number of possible stimulation 
combinations immediately emphasizes how difficult it is to determine the optimum balance of variables and 
compare the results of different researchers.
The typical clinical machine supplies pulsating direct (galvanic) and/or alternating (faradic) current in the form 
of brief pulses. The frequency of faradic current is most commonly chosen in the range of about 50-100 Hz, while 
pulse duration (width) ranges from about 100 microseconds to several hundred milliseconds. This brevity of pulse 
duration is important to minimise skin irritation and tissue damage. However, the duration at any particular 
intensity of faradic stimulation should not be too brief Although they may be suitable for decreasing pain, pulses 
that are too brief will supply insufficient energy to cause full, tetanic muscle contraction.
208


=== page 220 viewer 221 ===
SUPERTRAINING
Machines are designed to apply alternating currents directly at a preset or selected frequency (conventional 
faradism), or in the form of low frequency currents superimposed on a medium frequency (2000 to 5000 Hz) 
earner wave. A variation of the latter method, using two pairs of electrodes each supplying medium frequency 
waves carrying low frequency waves differing slightly in frequency, forms the basis of what is called interferential 
stimulation. A major advantage of using a higher frequency carrier wave is that impedance between the electrodes 
and skin is lowered, enhancing comfort and effectiveness.
American interest in electrostimuiation as a training adjunct was aroused in 1971, when Kots in Russia 
reported increases of more than 20% in muscle strength, speed and power produced by several weeks of 
dectrotraining. Unable to produce comparable results, the Canadians invited him to lecture at Concordia 
University in 1977. Armed with the new information that Kots employed a sinusoidally modulated 2500 Hz 
cunent source applied in a sequence of 10 seconds of contraction followed by 50 seconds of relaxation, they again 
tried to duplicate Russian claims.
It is noteworthy that this procedure differed significantly from that of top Belgian superheavy weightlifter. 
Serge Reding, who had close training contact with one of the authors (Siff) while he stayed with him In South 
Africa in the early 1970s. After training sessions he used 0.5 to 2 second, very high intensity contractions with 
10 to 15 second rest periods, for a total of 5 minutes per major muscic group, with agonists and antagonists of 
each limb alternately stimulated in ipsilateral and contralateral sequences (Siff, 1973). Reding always concluded 
his sessions with a few repetitions (1-3) of a long duration (10-15 seconds) fairly intense tetanic contraction to 
serve as a type of deep massage, followed by about 10-15 minutes of microcurrent stimulation (less than 200 
microamps) applied across the head and spinal cord with another electrostimulator.
Despite the subsequent success reported by various track coaches in integrating conventional faradic 
electrostimulation into a carefully periodised training programme (Francis, 1982), researchers continue to disagree 
on increase in muscle strength.
4.2.1.2 Reasons for Conflicting Research
There are several main reasons for the contradictory research findings:
1. Many studies focus largely on isometric or isokinetic strength changes, which complicates research 
comparisons. Such research often neglects possible effects of other vital factors such as power, speed, muscular 
endurance, residual muscic tension, muscle growth and rate of neuromuscular recovery.
2. Much of the research examines injured patients in the process of rehabilitation, untrained individuals, or trained 
subjects from differing fitness and training backgrounds. It is well known that an increase in strength is 
proportionately greater in the early stages of a training programme or among untrained subjects. Moreover, 
increases in strength for novices during the first few weeks of training mainly are due to neuromuscular adaptation 
and learning, rather than muscle hypertrophy.
3. The effectiveness of electrostimuiation is determined by the intensity of the current used and individual 
tolerance of discomfort caused by stimulation. In addition, no specific waveform has been found to be universally 
most comfortable. There also can be considerable variation among subjects in their response to different 
waveforms and stimulation impedances (Delitto & Rose, 1986; Mannheimcr & Carlsson, 1979; Moreno-Aranda 
&  Seirig, 1981).
4. The effects of electrostimuiation depend on the types and frequency of waveforms used, particularly since 
there is a distinct difference in the recruitment patterns and functional characteristics of slow-twitch and fast- 
twitch muscle fibres (Lloyd ct al, 1986; Mannheimer & Carlsson, 1979; Pette & Vrbova, 1985). Moreover, the 
higher the frequency, particularly if a carrier wave is used, the lower the impedance between electrodes and skin, 
and the greater the degree of comfort.
5. The type, size, number and location of electrodes, as well as the electrode gel, affect the amount of electrical 
energy transmitted to the muscles, the resultant force of contraction and patient comfort. Many studies do not 
discuss these details, and therefore, valid comparisons largely are meaningless.
6. Most studies have used commercial electrostimulators which arc able to vary only a few of all the possible 
stimulation parameters. Some of the more extensive studies have varied several of these parameters, as 
summarised in the thorough review by Lloyd et al (1986). However, because of the enormous number of
209


=== page 221 viewer 222 ===
SUPERTRAINING
stimulation combinations theoretically possible, no single extensive study has been able to examine the effects of 
varying all the stimulation parameters. This includes frequency, waveform, pulse-width, type of modulation 
(Frequency Modulation, Amplitude Modulation or pulse-width modulation), impulse interval and electrical 
energy delivered.
7. The effects of electrostimulation, like plyometric training, may be enhanced by optimal integration into an 
overall strength and sport specific training programme (e.g. Francis, 1982)
8. Many of the training regimes have been deficiently designed. Usually, the electrostimulator is selected according 
to the maximum tolerated by subjects, or to a certain percentage of a maximal voluntary isometric or isokinetic 
contraction as measured on isokinetic or other dynamometers. It should be noted that adaptation to any stimulus 
occurs, and subjects can withstand greater intensities of electric current from the start to end of any session, and 
from week to week.
Similarly, studies examining the combined effects of electrostimulation and normal strength training often 
prescribe weight training with a fixed number of sets and loads at a fixed percentage of single repetition maximum, 
despite the fact that the latter maximum gradually increases. The accompanying electrical stimulation also is set at 
a fixed value, which fails to consider that the basic principle of strength and power enhancement is gradual 
overload. Such a training regime in normal weight training is known to be highly limited in improving physical 
performance. It would be surprising if it were any different with electrostimulation training.
9. The design and effects of the electrostimulator depend on the choice of physiological model. Most stimulators 
are designed on the basis of the action-potential model of nerve cell discharge, which considers that cellular 
communication in the body is mediated by bursts of electrical discharge transmitted along nerve axons. The cell is 
assumed to be W  (discharging electricity) or 'off (resting), depending on whether the build-up of electrical charge 
in the cell is large enough to exceed a certain threshold, rendering the cell membrane temporarily more permeable to 
certain chemical ions. Intermediate subthreshold states arc presumed unimportant, although they are central to an 
understanding of the EEG (brain waves) and other electrical potentials of the central nervous system (Siff, 1981).
Similarly, the numerous glial cells which surround all nerve cells are assumed to play little more than a 
nutritional or supportive role for the nerves, despite the fact that they display a steady or quasi-steady electric 
field (Galambos, 1961; Siff, 1981). Some scientists believe that glial cell potentials may have a profound effect on 
nerve cells by modulating their activity similar to semiconductors such as transistors in electronic circuits (Becker. 
1974; Galambos, 1961). In addition, the DC injury potentials measurable on the skin surface after tissue damage 
are not associated with the action potential system (Becker, 1982).
Moreover, little is known about electrical fields at the subcellular level. The sensitivity of the body to 
external electric, magnetic and electromagnetic fields cannot satisfactorily be explained in terms of action 
potentials, which are not directly affected by these fields (Becker, 1965; Cope, 1974). The classical theories also 
do not explain the mechanisms whereby electric and other fields stimulate processes such as the repair of 
fractures, the healing of wounds and reduction of thrombosis.
On discovering evidence for semiconduction and the possible existence of superconductivity at room 
temperature in biological systems, scientists now have postulated that tissue healing, pain mechanisms, cell 
growth and disease processes may involve biological semiconduction and superconductivity (Becker, 1965; Cope, 
1971; Cope, 1974). In addition, Nordenstrom claims to have shown the presence of closed electric circuits in the 
body, whereby ionic flow concerned with growth and regulatory processes takes place via blood vessels and 
through or along the capillaries (Nordenstrom, 1983).
All faradic, medium frequency and interferential stimulators (including sports-oriented machines) are designed 
on the action-potential model for cell operation, which, therefore, do not permit applications relying on the other 
types of models described above. Such applications involve cell growth, tissue repair and general recuperation, all 
of which are essential features of physical conditioning. In recent years a few innovative micro-current machines 
based on these models have been applied clinically with significant success in neuromuscular rehabilitation (Chee 
& Walton, 1986; Matteson, 1984; Matteson & Eberhardt, 185; Meyer & Nebrensky, 1983; Noto & Grant, 1985).
4.2.1.3 Clinical Applications of Electrostimulation
At this point it is relevant to survey the clinical and research evidence supporting the value of elcctrostimulation 
in medical situations. Its major applications or effects are the following:
210


=== page 222 viewer 223 ===
SUPERTRAINING
1. Increase in Muscle Strength
A  wide range of low and medium frequencies has been shown to strengthen muscle tissue in the case of subjects 
who have been incapacitated by injury, illness or childbirth ( Eriksson, 1981; Johnson et al, 1977; Laughman et al, 
1983; Lloyd et al, 1986; Raitsin, 1974; Romero et al, 1982; Turk et al, 1980). Some studies on the effect of 
clectrostimulation (ES) alone on normal subjects also have revealed strength increases (Currier & Mann, 1983; 
Laughman et al, 1983: McMiken et al, 1983; Romero et al, 1982; Sekowitz, 1985), although some of these studies 
showed that ES was not superior to voluntary exercise (Currier & Mann, 1983; Laughmen et al, 1983; McMiken 
et al, 1983; Sckowitz, 1985). Further studies found minimal or insignificant changes in strength (Massey et al, 
1965; Mohr ct al, 1985; Singer etal, 1983).
In general, most of these studies indicate that ES unaccompanied by physical training at best produces long­
term  strength gains which are similar to or smaller than those of voluntary exercise. The greatest strength increases 
are invariably found in the weakest or most unfit subjects (Fahey et al, 1985; Johnson et al, 1977; Romero et al, 
1982). However, in conjunction with periodised exercise programmes, ES appears to increase the strength of 
competitive athletes in some instances (Francis, 1982; Kots & Chwilon, 1971; Matteson, 1984; Reding, 1973), 
although these changes may have been the indirect result of some of the other effects of ES discussed below.
2. Re-education of Muscle Action
Some medical disorders or kinesiological habits may produce weak or faulty patterns of muscle action. ES may 
facilitate more efficient use of the affected muscles. It can be particularly effective in treating chondromalacia 
patellae, tennis elbow and 'frozen shoulder* (Eriksson, 1981; Godfrey et al, 1979; Johnson et al, 1977; Nirchl & 
Sobel, 1981).
3. Facilitation of Muscle Contraction
If one is unable to produce a voluntary muscle contraction because of disuse, pain or injury, ES can promote 
muscle activity and reduce the likelihood of extensive tissue wasting (Eriksson, 1981; Johnson ct al, 1977; Turk et
il, 1980; Vodovnik et al, 1982).
4. Increase of Muscular and Systemic Endurance
Prolonged application of sub-maximal ES can stimulate the fatiguing conditions encountered in strenuous physical 
work thereby increasing endurance of the muscles involved (Ikai & Yabe, 1969; Johnson et al, 1977). Russian 
research reported improvement in cardiovascular efficiency, muscle contractility and rate of general recovery 
(Dombrovskaya, 1982). Moreover, low frequency (under 15 Hz) ES of long duration (24-hour) continuous 
stimulation experiments or cross-innervation experiments in animals have been shown to alter fast twitch fibres to 
bccome predominantly aerobic and more resistant to fatigue (Jolesz & Sreter, 1981; Pette, 1984; Pette & Vrbova, 
1985; Salmons & Vrbova, 1969; Salmons & Henriksson, 1981).
5. Increase of Speed of Muscle Contraction
Long-term higher frequency (more than 40 Hz) ES can improve reaction time and decrease the time to peak 
tension of fast twitch muscles (Fluery & Lagasse, 1979; Salmons & Vrbova, 1967, 1969).
6. Increase in Local Blood Supply
ES stimulates muscles to contract rhythmically, producing dilatation of the blood vessels, facilitating the transport 
of nutrients to the tissues, and possibly accelerating healing in tissues which are not extensively injured 
(Dombrovskaya, 1982; Salmons & Vrbova, 1967 Wadsworth & Chanmugam, 1980). Experiments using different 
stimulation regimes have measured increases in blood flow ranging from about 20% to more than 200%, both 
during and after ES, particularly if the frequencies used are below approximately 30 Hz (Currier et al, 1986; 
Richardson, 1981; Wakim ct al, 1948; Wakim, 1953). In general, the higher the frequency of ES, the lower the 
percentage increase in blood flow (Currier ct al, 1986; Wakim, 1953).
7. Provision of Effective Massage
ES increases the pumping action of muscle on the venous and lymphatic systems, which help injured, tense or 
fatigued areas dissipate fluid and toxin accumulation (Dombrovskaya, 1982; Wadsworth & Chanmugam, 1980). 
Russian studies using radioactive Xenon (Xei33) injected as a tracer confirm that massage accelerates local blood
211


=== page 223 viewer 224 ===
SUPERTRAINING
flow and reduces muscle tension, resulting in improved oxygen and nutrient supply to the tissues and faster 
removal of metabolic waste products (Dubrovsky, 1982).
8. Relief of Pain
ES applied by TENS (Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation) devices can relieve painful muscle spasm or 
tension, as well as diminish acute or chronic pain caused by a wide range of musculoskeletal conditions (Gersh &  
Wolf, 1985; Jeans, 1979; Lloyd et al, 1986; Mannheim & Carlsson, 1979; Sjolund & Eriksson, 1979; Strauss, 
1987; Wadsworth & Chanmugam, 1980). Conventional TENS employs low frequency (50 to 100 Hz) stimulation 
with no muscle contraction. TENS modes for management of deeper pain may use short, high intensity bursts at 
frequencies between 1  and 150 Hz with definite muscle contraction.
9. Reduction of Muscle Spasm
Protective spasm can occur in any overloaded, injured, inflamed or painful muscle. The effectiveness of ES in 
reducing spasm and spasticity has been attributed to one or more of the following mechanisms: promotion of 
muscular fatigue, disruption of the pain-spasm cycle or restoration of the normal contraction-relaxation process 
(Alfieri, 1982; Mills et al, 1984; Wadsworth & Chanmugam, 1980).
10. Promotion of Relaxation and Recuperation
Short-term, intense, muscle-contracting ES and mild, non-contracting TENS-type stimulation both can promote 
local and general relaxation. This effect has been ascribed, in animal and human subjects, to the release in the 
central nervous system of endorphins and enkephalins, classes of analgesic and tranquiliser which occur naturally 
in the body (Gersh & Wolf, 1985; Sjolund & Eriksson, 1979). This application is used by Russian athletes in 
recuperating after strenuous training sessions and in facilitating the onset of sleep, even by applying mild stimu­
lation to the thighs alone (Dombrovskaya, 1982; Kopisov & Nagorniy, 1982).
11. Increase in Range of Movement
In physical therapy, PNF (Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation) techniques often arc used to improve joint 
mobility caused by inactivity or injury. ES may be used in conjunction with such mobilisation techniques to 
enhance their effectiveness. In the case of injury, the ES may aid relaxation and mobility by diminishing pain, 
reducing swelling and improving microcirculation within the tissues (Wadsworth & Chanmugam, 1980).
12. Reduction of Swelling
Swelling (oedema) is the accumulation of excessive extracellular fluid in the region of a joint, arising from leakage of 
protein and plasma through the capillary walls of soft tissues. It may be caused by inflammation, sprains, strains, 
tendinitis, rheumatoid arthritis, surgery or disease. Low intensity ES can rapidly reduce swelling of non-infectious 
origin (Wadsworth & Chanmugam, 1980). Its effectiveness may be due to the pumping action of muscle and/or 
the creation of an electric gradient across the cell membranes, which triggers the lymphatic system to absorb 
excess fluid.
13. Reduction of Musculoskeletal Abnormalities
Abnormal spinal curvaturc has been halted or the progress has slowed in mild to moderate scoliosis, by ES 
appropriately applied to specific back muscles (Axelgaard et al, 1983; Friedman et al, 1982; Kots & Chwilon, 
1971; Schultz etal, 1981).
14. Preferential Recruitment of Different Muscle Fibres
ES tends to recruit the largest diameter axons first (Enoka, 1988), which is the reverse of the natural order of 
recruitment (see 1.12, especially Fig 1.24). These largest axons are difficult to activate under normal training 
conditions, so ES may play a useful supplementary role in this respect.
15. Acute Increase in Strength
Several researchers have shown that ES can have a profound effect on strength after a single session (Howard & 
Enoka, 1987; Alon, 1985). In particular, Alon, in studying a group of 14 subjects, found that one experimental 
session of ES produced a mean increase in quadriceps strength of about 13%.
212


=== page 224 viewer 225 ===
SUPERTRAINING
16. Improvement in Metabolic Efficiency
Application of ES during exercise can improve the metabolic economy of the movement. Studies carried out by 
Ratov & Kryazhev (1986) which examined the effect of electrically stimulating the quadriceps during cycling and 
speed skating showed that oxygen consumption decreased by 10-17% and the time taken to fatigue was extended 
by 15-20%. Similar research which analysed the effect of ES applied to an athlete running on a treadmill revealed 
a reduction of some 10% in oxygen consumption. In addition, if work was performed by the muscles which were 
electrically stimulated shortly before, energy consumption decreased by about 5%.
17. Increase in Muscle Speed
Phasic type of electrical stimulation increases the contractile speed of skeletal muscle. Electrical stimulation, wher 
employed as a technique for subjecting selected muscles to altered use, facilitates precise entrainment of the patten 
of functional activity (Karba et al, 1990).

Recent research and clinical experience have revealed that electric currents as much as 1000 times smaller than that 
of all the traditional physical therapy modalities can be far more successful than the latter in achieving many of

Currents as low as 10 microamps (millionths of an amp) pulsating at between 0.1 to 400Hz are too weak to

1	=== page 218 viewer 219 ===
2	SUPERTRAINING
3	One more feature should be noted. If the given means do not elicit an adequate training effect, then increase 
4	m  work capacity becomes more a factor of specialised exercise than training volume and then only if it is executed 
5	by training at or near personal maximum levels. It should be pointed out that the execution of specialised 
6	exercises in training at near maximal intensity (as advocated by Bulgarian experts) should be regarded as an 
7	advanced strategy, a method which cannot be acknowledged as being universally appropriate. This would imply 
8	not only rejecting the principles of the rational structuring of training based on research into training methods, but 
9	also a return to the original concepts from which these began.
10	Thus, the problem of establishing scientifically the means of sport training is far from being solved and the 
11	current tendency to increase the volume of the training load should not detract from its significance and turn the 
12	attention of specialists away from its in-depth study.
13	If a logical sequence is to be recommended as a practical solution to the problem of improving the 
14	effectiveness of special strength training methods, then it should be laid down as follows:
15	1. Regime — 2. Means — ► 3. Methods —► 4. System —► 5. Volume
16	From this scheme it follows that the means of special strength training should be selected on the basis of 
17	quantitative descriptions of the motor specificity of the given sport and thereby provide an adequate regime of 
18	work for the body. The basic criterion for this is a guarantee of a definite training effect for the given level of 
19	special fitness.
20	The next step is to determine a suitable method of using the means based not only on the specific motor 
21	regimes of the given sport, but also on factors such as one’s level of fitness and the tasks of the current stage of 
22	training. Of great potential for perfecting the methods of special strength training, is the principle o f systematic 
23	application of means to produce the necessary cumulative training effect.
24	Finally, attaining the necessary level of special strength training depends on the volume of the special work, 
25	the optimal magnitude of which should be determined by the stage and current tasks of the athlete's preparation, 
26	the competition calendar and the intensity of the load.
27	This scheme emphasizes that, to rely on any one parameter of the load for achieving any given potential is 
28	appropriate only after the potential of the previous parameter has been completely exploited. For example, it is 
29	unwise to increase training volume without having fully elicited the maximum training effect of the individual 
30	strength training means at a particular intensity. This requires dedication and persistence from the specialists, 
31	because it requires in-depth investigative effort Since increasing the training volume is easier than finding a really 
32	effective means of special preparation, such a course tends to be a much simpler choice.
33	4.2 Different Means of Strength Development
34	The external force generated by muscles is a result of voluntary effort. However, under normal everyday 
35	conditions, muscular tension produced by voluntary effort has certain limitations. To increase the external 
36	muscular force it is necessary to stimulate them from the outside, for example, by means of mechanical 
37	stimulation. Afferent impulses elicited by mechanical stimulation inform the central nervous system about the 
38	strength of the external influence evoking the muscular tension. The greater the intensity of the external stimulus, 
39	the greater the muscle effector discharge, and the larger the external work produced.
40	Thus, afferent signals to the neuromuscular system play an important role in determining the qualitative and 
41	quantitative characteristics of muscular strength. Therefore, the stimulation of muscular tension for the 
42	development of strength is of great significance. So, in all cases the magnitude of working muscular tension is 
43	determined by voluntary effort and external mechanical action. The stimulation of working force can be divided 
44	into the following basic types:
45	• Stimulation when muscular tension is produced by voluntary effort against external resistance, and the
46	resistance of the moving load accelerates and regulates the effector impulses to the muscles
47	• Stimulation by the kinetic energy of a falling object or the body, when the effort is primarily reflexive
48	• Stimulation caused primarily by voluntary effort, under conditions where additional external mechanical
49	stimulation is absent or limited
50	• Stimulation of muscle elicited or intensified involuntarily by means of external electrical current.
51	207
52	
53	
54	=== page 219 viewer 220 ===
55	SUPERTRAINING
56	The first two cases are associated with dynamic work and the third with isometric work. An increase in 
57	stimulation is realised in the first case by increasing the velocity of the preliminary fall of the body or load, and by 
58	mobilising the athlete's voluntary resources in the third. It should also be pointed out that voluntary effort plays 
59	an important role in the magnitude of the effector response of the muscles in the first instance, whereas its 
60	influence in the second is insignificant.
61	The mechanism chiefly responsible for the braking or amortisation work of the muscles causes a protective 
62	effector response more rapidly than a voluntary sequence of actions. Therefore, such a reflex stimulus is able to 
63	provoke an extraordinary mobilisation of the neuromuscular apparatus, which is impossible where there is reliance 
64	on voluntary effort alone. This mechanism forms the foundation of plyometric training (5.2.4).
65	4.2.1 Electrostimulation
66	As has already been stated, there is always an ongoing search for novel, highly effective means of special strength 
67	training. For example, Russian studies have established that clcctrostimulation of muscle furnishes an adequate 
68	training stimulus for effective development of muscular strength (Kots, 1971; Kots & Khvilon, 1971; Khvilon, 
69	1974). Electrostimulation can be effective for certain purposes in the preparation of highly qualified athletes 
70	(mainly in speed-strength sports) and there are a number of advantages associated with this method of developing 
71	strength, in particular the reduction of joint loading. It can occupy a specific place in the yearly training cycle, be 
72	used in combination with other methods of developing muscular strength and be applied chiefly in the preparation 
73	of highly qualified athletes.
74	Ratov has found that functional electrical stimulation (FENS) can be particularly useful in improving sporting 
75	performance. His techniques, developed decades ago from his PhD programme on the interrelation between 
76	electrical stimulation and electromyography, has used EMG signals from agonist and antagonist muscles to act as 
77	triggers or control mechanisms for electrical stimulation of musclcs directly involved in producing functional 
78	movements in sport. In his laboratory at the State Central Institute for Sports Science in Moscow he has 
79	successfully implemented these neuromuscular stimulation methods in training athletes such as fencers, boxers, 
80	rowers, shotputtcrs and weightlifters.
81	However, it is inappropriate to consider the training applications of electrostimulation in detail here because 
82	its methodological fundamentals have still not been determined, especially as it should be applied preferably under 
83	suitable conditions by qualified personnel. The next section summarises the effects and applications of 
84	electrostimulation as a form of supplementary sports preparation.
85	4.2.1.1 The Physiological Effects of Electrostimulation
86	The concept of elcctrostimulation is not new, and for years has been used by physical therapists in clinical 
87	applications such as muscle rehabilitation, relief of muscular spasm, reduction of swelling and pain control. Its 
88	possible value in sports training is still considered controversial. In strength conditioning, the applications of 
89	electrostimulation fall into the following broad categories:
90	• Imposition of local physical stress to provoke supercompensation
91	• Local restoration after exercise or injury
92	• General central nervous and endocrine restoration after exercise or injury
93	• Neuromuscular stimulation for pain control or movement patterning
94	Electrostimulation usually involves feeding the muscles low current electrical impulses via moistened electrode 
95	pads placed firmly on the skin. The effectiveness, comfort and depth of excitation depends on factors such as 
96	pulse shape, frequency, duration, intensity and modulation pattern. The resulting number of possible stimulation 
97	combinations immediately emphasizes how difficult it is to determine the optimum balance of variables and 
98	compare the results of different researchers.
99	The typical clinical machine supplies pulsating direct (galvanic) and/or alternating (faradic) current in the form 
100	of brief pulses. The frequency of faradic current is most commonly chosen in the range of about 50-100 Hz, while 
101	pulse duration (width) ranges from about 100 microseconds to several hundred milliseconds. This brevity of pulse 
102	duration is important to minimise skin irritation and tissue damage. However, the duration at any particular 
103	intensity of faradic stimulation should not be too brief Although they may be suitable for decreasing pain, pulses 
104	that are too brief will supply insufficient energy to cause full, tetanic muscle contraction.
105	208
106	
107	
108	=== page 220 viewer 221 ===
109	SUPERTRAINING
110	Machines are designed to apply alternating currents directly at a preset or selected frequency (conventional 
111	faradism), or in the form of low frequency currents superimposed on a medium frequency (2000 to 5000 Hz) 
112	earner wave. A variation of the latter method, using two pairs of electrodes each supplying medium frequency 
113	waves carrying low frequency waves differing slightly in frequency, forms the basis of what is called interferential 
114	stimulation. A major advantage of using a higher frequency carrier wave is that impedance between the electrodes 
115	and skin is lowered, enhancing comfort and effectiveness.
116	American interest in electrostimuiation as a training adjunct was aroused in 1971, when Kots in Russia 
117	reported increases of more than 20% in muscle strength, speed and power produced by several weeks of 
118	dectrotraining. Unable to produce comparable results, the Canadians invited him to lecture at Concordia 
119	University in 1977. Armed with the new information that Kots employed a sinusoidally modulated 2500 Hz 
120	cunent source applied in a sequence of 10 seconds of contraction followed by 50 seconds of relaxation, they again 
121	tried to duplicate Russian claims.
122	It is noteworthy that this procedure differed significantly from that of top Belgian superheavy weightlifter. 
123	Serge Reding, who had close training contact with one of the authors (Siff) while he stayed with him In South 
124	Africa in the early 1970s. After training sessions he used 0.5 to 2 second, very high intensity contractions with 
125	10 to 15 second rest periods, for a total of 5 minutes per major muscic group, with agonists and antagonists of 
126	each limb alternately stimulated in ipsilateral and contralateral sequences (Siff, 1973). Reding always concluded 
127	his sessions with a few repetitions (1-3) of a long duration (10-15 seconds) fairly intense tetanic contraction to 
128	serve as a type of deep massage, followed by about 10-15 minutes of microcurrent stimulation (less than 200 
129	microamps) applied across the head and spinal cord with another electrostimulator.
130	Despite the subsequent success reported by various track coaches in integrating conventional faradic 
131	electrostimulation into a carefully periodised training programme (Francis, 1982), researchers continue to disagree 
132	on increase in muscle strength.
133	4.2.1.2 Reasons for Conflicting Research
134	There are several main reasons for the contradictory research findings:
135	1. Many studies focus largely on isometric or isokinetic strength changes, which complicates research 
136	comparisons. Such research often neglects possible effects of other vital factors such as power, speed, muscular 
137	endurance, residual muscic tension, muscle growth and rate of neuromuscular recovery.
138	2. Much of the research examines injured patients in the process of rehabilitation, untrained individuals, or trained 
139	subjects from differing fitness and training backgrounds. It is well known that an increase in strength is 
140	proportionately greater in the early stages of a training programme or among untrained subjects. Moreover, 
141	increases in strength for novices during the first few weeks of training mainly are due to neuromuscular adaptation 
142	and learning, rather than muscle hypertrophy.
143	3. The effectiveness of electrostimuiation is determined by the intensity of the current used and individual 
144	tolerance of discomfort caused by stimulation. In addition, no specific waveform has been found to be universally 
145	most comfortable. There also can be considerable variation among subjects in their response to different 
146	waveforms and stimulation impedances (Delitto & Rose, 1986; Mannheimcr & Carlsson, 1979; Moreno-Aranda 
147	&  Seirig, 1981).
148	4. The effects of electrostimuiation depend on the types and frequency of waveforms used, particularly since 
149	there is a distinct difference in the recruitment patterns and functional characteristics of slow-twitch and fast- 
150	twitch muscle fibres (Lloyd ct al, 1986; Mannheimer & Carlsson, 1979; Pette & Vrbova, 1985). Moreover, the 
151	higher the frequency, particularly if a carrier wave is used, the lower the impedance between electrodes and skin, 
152	and the greater the degree of comfort.
153	5. The type, size, number and location of electrodes, as well as the electrode gel, affect the amount of electrical 
154	energy transmitted to the muscles, the resultant force of contraction and patient comfort. Many studies do not 
155	discuss these details, and therefore, valid comparisons largely are meaningless.
156	6. Most studies have used commercial electrostimulators which arc able to vary only a few of all the possible 
157	stimulation parameters. Some of the more extensive studies have varied several of these parameters, as 
158	summarised in the thorough review by Lloyd et al (1986). However, because of the enormous number of
159	209
160	
161	
162	=== page 221 viewer 222 ===
163	SUPERTRAINING
164	stimulation combinations theoretically possible, no single extensive study has been able to examine the effects of 
165	varying all the stimulation parameters. This includes frequency, waveform, pulse-width, type of modulation 
166	(Frequency Modulation, Amplitude Modulation or pulse-width modulation), impulse interval and electrical 
167	energy delivered.
168	7. The effects of electrostimulation, like plyometric training, may be enhanced by optimal integration into an 
169	overall strength and sport specific training programme (e.g. Francis, 1982)
170	8. Many of the training regimes have been deficiently designed. Usually, the electrostimulator is selected according 
171	to the maximum tolerated by subjects, or to a certain percentage of a maximal voluntary isometric or isokinetic 
172	contraction as measured on isokinetic or other dynamometers. It should be noted that adaptation to any stimulus 
173	occurs, and subjects can withstand greater intensities of electric current from the start to end of any session, and 
174	from week to week.
175	Similarly, studies examining the combined effects of electrostimulation and normal strength training often 
176	prescribe weight training with a fixed number of sets and loads at a fixed percentage of single repetition maximum, 
177	despite the fact that the latter maximum gradually increases. The accompanying electrical stimulation also is set at 
178	a fixed value, which fails to consider that the basic principle of strength and power enhancement is gradual 
179	overload. Such a training regime in normal weight training is known to be highly limited in improving physical 
180	performance. It would be surprising if it were any different with electrostimulation training.
181	9. The design and effects of the electrostimulator depend on the choice of physiological model. Most stimulators 
182	are designed on the basis of the action-potential model of nerve cell discharge, which considers that cellular 
183	communication in the body is mediated by bursts of electrical discharge transmitted along nerve axons. The cell is 
184	assumed to be W  (discharging electricity) or 'off (resting), depending on whether the build-up of electrical charge 
185	in the cell is large enough to exceed a certain threshold, rendering the cell membrane temporarily more permeable to 
186	certain chemical ions. Intermediate subthreshold states arc presumed unimportant, although they are central to an 
187	understanding of the EEG (brain waves) and other electrical potentials of the central nervous system (Siff, 1981).
188	Similarly, the numerous glial cells which surround all nerve cells are assumed to play little more than a 
189	nutritional or supportive role for the nerves, despite the fact that they display a steady or quasi-steady electric 
190	field (Galambos, 1961; Siff, 1981). Some scientists believe that glial cell potentials may have a profound effect on 
191	nerve cells by modulating their activity similar to semiconductors such as transistors in electronic circuits (Becker. 
192	1974; Galambos, 1961). In addition, the DC injury potentials measurable on the skin surface after tissue damage 
193	are not associated with the action potential system (Becker, 1982).
194	Moreover, little is known about electrical fields at the subcellular level. The sensitivity of the body to 
195	external electric, magnetic and electromagnetic fields cannot satisfactorily be explained in terms of action 
196	potentials, which are not directly affected by these fields (Becker, 1965; Cope, 1974). The classical theories also 
197	do not explain the mechanisms whereby electric and other fields stimulate processes such as the repair of 
198	fractures, the healing of wounds and reduction of thrombosis.
199	On discovering evidence for semiconduction and the possible existence of superconductivity at room 
200	temperature in biological systems, scientists now have postulated that tissue healing, pain mechanisms, cell 
201	growth and disease processes may involve biological semiconduction and superconductivity (Becker, 1965; Cope, 
202	1971; Cope, 1974). In addition, Nordenstrom claims to have shown the presence of closed electric circuits in the 
203	body, whereby ionic flow concerned with growth and regulatory processes takes place via blood vessels and 
204	through or along the capillaries (Nordenstrom, 1983).
205	All faradic, medium frequency and interferential stimulators (including sports-oriented machines) are designed 
206	on the action-potential model for cell operation, which, therefore, do not permit applications relying on the other 
207	types of models described above. Such applications involve cell growth, tissue repair and general recuperation, all 
208	of which are essential features of physical conditioning. In recent years a few innovative micro-current machines 
209	based on these models have been applied clinically with significant success in neuromuscular rehabilitation (Chee 
210	& Walton, 1986; Matteson, 1984; Matteson & Eberhardt, 185; Meyer & Nebrensky, 1983; Noto & Grant, 1985).
211	4.2.1.3 Clinical Applications of Electrostimulation
212	At this point it is relevant to survey the clinical and research evidence supporting the value of elcctrostimulation 
213	in medical situations. Its major applications or effects are the following:
214	210
215	
216	
217	=== page 222 viewer 223 ===
218	SUPERTRAINING
219	1. Increase in Muscle Strength
220	A  wide range of low and medium frequencies has been shown to strengthen muscle tissue in the case of subjects 
221	who have been incapacitated by injury, illness or childbirth ( Eriksson, 1981; Johnson et al, 1977; Laughman et al, 
222	1983; Lloyd et al, 1986; Raitsin, 1974; Romero et al, 1982; Turk et al, 1980). Some studies on the effect of 
223	clectrostimulation (ES) alone on normal subjects also have revealed strength increases (Currier & Mann, 1983; 
224	Laughman et al, 1983: McMiken et al, 1983; Romero et al, 1982; Sekowitz, 1985), although some of these studies 
225	showed that ES was not superior to voluntary exercise (Currier & Mann, 1983; Laughmen et al, 1983; McMiken 
226	et al, 1983; Sckowitz, 1985). Further studies found minimal or insignificant changes in strength (Massey et al, 
227	1965; Mohr ct al, 1985; Singer etal, 1983).
228	In general, most of these studies indicate that ES unaccompanied by physical training at best produces long­
229	term  strength gains which are similar to or smaller than those of voluntary exercise. The greatest strength increases 
230	are invariably found in the weakest or most unfit subjects (Fahey et al, 1985; Johnson et al, 1977; Romero et al, 
231	1982). However, in conjunction with periodised exercise programmes, ES appears to increase the strength of 
232	competitive athletes in some instances (Francis, 1982; Kots & Chwilon, 1971; Matteson, 1984; Reding, 1973), 
233	although these changes may have been the indirect result of some of the other effects of ES discussed below.
234	2. Re-education of Muscle Action
235	Some medical disorders or kinesiological habits may produce weak or faulty patterns of muscle action. ES may 
236	facilitate more efficient use of the affected muscles. It can be particularly effective in treating chondromalacia 
237	patellae, tennis elbow and 'frozen shoulder* (Eriksson, 1981; Godfrey et al, 1979; Johnson et al, 1977; Nirchl & 
238	Sobel, 1981).
239	3. Facilitation of Muscle Contraction
240	If one is unable to produce a voluntary muscle contraction because of disuse, pain or injury, ES can promote 
241	muscle activity and reduce the likelihood of extensive tissue wasting (Eriksson, 1981; Johnson ct al, 1977; Turk et
242	il, 1980; Vodovnik et al, 1982).
243	4. Increase of Muscular and Systemic Endurance
244	Prolonged application of sub-maximal ES can stimulate the fatiguing conditions encountered in strenuous physical 
245	work thereby increasing endurance of the muscles involved (Ikai & Yabe, 1969; Johnson et al, 1977). Russian 
246	research reported improvement in cardiovascular efficiency, muscle contractility and rate of general recovery 
247	(Dombrovskaya, 1982). Moreover, low frequency (under 15 Hz) ES of long duration (24-hour) continuous 
248	stimulation experiments or cross-innervation experiments in animals have been shown to alter fast twitch fibres to 
249	bccome predominantly aerobic and more resistant to fatigue (Jolesz & Sreter, 1981; Pette, 1984; Pette & Vrbova, 
250	1985; Salmons & Vrbova, 1969; Salmons & Henriksson, 1981).
251	5. Increase of Speed of Muscle Contraction
252	Long-term higher frequency (more than 40 Hz) ES can improve reaction time and decrease the time to peak 
253	tension of fast twitch muscles (Fluery & Lagasse, 1979; Salmons & Vrbova, 1967, 1969).
254	6. Increase in Local Blood Supply
255	ES stimulates muscles to contract rhythmically, producing dilatation of the blood vessels, facilitating the transport 
256	of nutrients to the tissues, and possibly accelerating healing in tissues which are not extensively injured 
257	(Dombrovskaya, 1982; Salmons & Vrbova, 1967 Wadsworth & Chanmugam, 1980). Experiments using different 
258	stimulation regimes have measured increases in blood flow ranging from about 20% to more than 200%, both 
259	during and after ES, particularly if the frequencies used are below approximately 30 Hz (Currier et al, 1986; 
260	Richardson, 1981; Wakim ct al, 1948; Wakim, 1953). In general, the higher the frequency of ES, the lower the 
261	percentage increase in blood flow (Currier ct al, 1986; Wakim, 1953).
262	7. Provision of Effective Massage
263	ES increases the pumping action of muscle on the venous and lymphatic systems, which help injured, tense or 
264	fatigued areas dissipate fluid and toxin accumulation (Dombrovskaya, 1982; Wadsworth & Chanmugam, 1980). 
265	Russian studies using radioactive Xenon (Xei33) injected as a tracer confirm that massage accelerates local blood
266	211
267	
268	
269	=== page 223 viewer 224 ===
270	SUPERTRAINING
271	flow and reduces muscle tension, resulting in improved oxygen and nutrient supply to the tissues and faster 
272	removal of metabolic waste products (Dubrovsky, 1982).
273	8. Relief of Pain
274	ES applied by TENS (Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation) devices can relieve painful muscle spasm or 
275	tension, as well as diminish acute or chronic pain caused by a wide range of musculoskeletal conditions (Gersh &  
276	Wolf, 1985; Jeans, 1979; Lloyd et al, 1986; Mannheim & Carlsson, 1979; Sjolund & Eriksson, 1979; Strauss, 
277	1987; Wadsworth & Chanmugam, 1980). Conventional TENS employs low frequency (50 to 100 Hz) stimulation 
278	with no muscle contraction. TENS modes for management of deeper pain may use short, high intensity bursts at 
279	frequencies between 1  and 150 Hz with definite muscle contraction.
280	9. Reduction of Muscle Spasm
281	Protective spasm can occur in any overloaded, injured, inflamed or painful muscle. The effectiveness of ES in 
282	reducing spasm and spasticity has been attributed to one or more of the following mechanisms: promotion of 
283	muscular fatigue, disruption of the pain-spasm cycle or restoration of the normal contraction-relaxation process 
284	(Alfieri, 1982; Mills et al, 1984; Wadsworth & Chanmugam, 1980).
285	10. Promotion of Relaxation and Recuperation
286	Short-term, intense, muscle-contracting ES and mild, non-contracting TENS-type stimulation both can promote 
287	local and general relaxation. This effect has been ascribed, in animal and human subjects, to the release in the 
288	central nervous system of endorphins and enkephalins, classes of analgesic and tranquiliser which occur naturally 
289	in the body (Gersh & Wolf, 1985; Sjolund & Eriksson, 1979). This application is used by Russian athletes in 
290	recuperating after strenuous training sessions and in facilitating the onset of sleep, even by applying mild stimu­
291	lation to the thighs alone (Dombrovskaya, 1982; Kopisov & Nagorniy, 1982).
292	11. Increase in Range of Movement
293	In physical therapy, PNF (Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation) techniques often arc used to improve joint 
294	mobility caused by inactivity or injury. ES may be used in conjunction with such mobilisation techniques to 
295	enhance their effectiveness. In the case of injury, the ES may aid relaxation and mobility by diminishing pain, 
296	reducing swelling and improving microcirculation within the tissues (Wadsworth & Chanmugam, 1980).
297	12. Reduction of Swelling
298	Swelling (oedema) is the accumulation of excessive extracellular fluid in the region of a joint, arising from leakage of 
299	protein and plasma through the capillary walls of soft tissues. It may be caused by inflammation, sprains, strains, 
300	tendinitis, rheumatoid arthritis, surgery or disease. Low intensity ES can rapidly reduce swelling of non-infectious 
301	origin (Wadsworth & Chanmugam, 1980). Its effectiveness may be due to the pumping action of muscle and/or 
302	the creation of an electric gradient across the cell membranes, which triggers the lymphatic system to absorb 
303	excess fluid.
304	13. Reduction of Musculoskeletal Abnormalities
305	Abnormal spinal curvaturc has been halted or the progress has slowed in mild to moderate scoliosis, by ES 
306	appropriately applied to specific back muscles (Axelgaard et al, 1983; Friedman et al, 1982; Kots & Chwilon, 
307	1971; Schultz etal, 1981).
308	14. Preferential Recruitment of Different Muscle Fibres
309	ES tends to recruit the largest diameter axons first (Enoka, 1988), which is the reverse of the natural order of 
310	recruitment (see 1.12, especially Fig 1.24). These largest axons are difficult to activate under normal training 
311	conditions, so ES may play a useful supplementary role in this respect.
312	15. Acute Increase in Strength
313	Several researchers have shown that ES can have a profound effect on strength after a single session (Howard & 
314	Enoka, 1987; Alon, 1985). In particular, Alon, in studying a group of 14 subjects, found that one experimental 
315	session of ES produced a mean increase in quadriceps strength of about 13%.
316	212
317	
318	
319	=== page 224 viewer 225 ===
320	SUPERTRAINING
321	16. Improvement in Metabolic Efficiency
322	Application of ES during exercise can improve the metabolic economy of the movement. Studies carried out by 
323	Ratov & Kryazhev (1986) which examined the effect of electrically stimulating the quadriceps during cycling and 
324	speed skating showed that oxygen consumption decreased by 10-17% and the time taken to fatigue was extended 
325	by 15-20%. Similar research which analysed the effect of ES applied to an athlete running on a treadmill revealed 
326	a reduction of some 10% in oxygen consumption. In addition, if work was performed by the muscles which were 
327	electrically stimulated shortly before, energy consumption decreased by about 5%.
328	17. Increase in Muscle Speed
329	Phasic type of electrical stimulation increases the contractile speed of skeletal muscle. Electrical stimulation, wher 
330	employed as a technique for subjecting selected muscles to altered use, facilitates precise entrainment of the patten 
331	of functional activity (Karba et al, 1990).
332	4.2.1.4 Further Research Findings
333	Recent research and clinical experience have revealed that electric currents as much as 1000 times smaller than that 
334	of all the traditional physical therapy modalities can be far more successful than the latter in achieving many of 
335	the benefits outlined in the previous section.
336	Currents as low as 10 microamps (millionths of an amp) pulsating at between 0.1 to 400Hz are too weak to 
337	cause muscle contraction, block pain signals or cause local heating, yet their effectiveness and safety is often 
338	superior in many applications to that of faradism, interfercntialism and conventional TENS (Matteson & 
339	Eberhardt, 1985).
340	The steps to satisfactorily modify the existing paradigm for ES may be sought in the research findings quoted 
341	earlier in the section: 'Reasons for conflicting research'. There, it was learned that cellular and subcellular 
342	processes not involving cell discharge, propagated electrical impulses, or muscle contraction, appear to be 
343	involved with cellular growth and repair.
344	Some studies have produced findings which offer partial answers to the questions posed by 
345	microstimulation. For instance, work by Becker and others suggests that small, steady or slowly varying currents 
346	can cause sub-threshold modulation of the electric fields across nerve and glial cells, thereby directly regulating cell 
347	growth and communication (Becker, 1974; Becker & Marino, 1982). In this respect, some of Becker's applications 
348	included the acceleration of wound healing, partial regeneration of amphibian and rat limbs, and induction of 
349	narcosis with transcranial currents. Nordenstrom maintains that these electric currents can stimulate the flow of 
350	ions along the blood vessels and through the cell membranes which constitute the body's closed electric circuits 
351	postulated by his theory (Nordenstrom, 1983).
352	Pilla (1974) has paid particular attention to electrochemical information transfer across cell membranes. The 
353	model in this case hypothesizes that the molecular structure of the cell membrane reflects its current genetic

501	4.2.2 Resistance and Strength Training
502	In principle, the heavier the weight which muscles lift, the greater the tension they develop. The latter is achieved 
503	by the effective stimulation and recruitment into the work of a large proportion of the involved musclcs. Strength 
504	development through the use of resistance activity was demonstrated around 500 BC by the legendary Milo of 
505	Crotona. According to legend, he increased his strength enormously by lifting a young bull daily onto his 
506	shoulders. As the bull grew in mass, so did Milo's strength.
507	In our own era Milo's approach is exemplified by the DeLorme method of progressive resistance exercise 
508	(DeLorme, 1945; DeLorme & Watkins, 1948, 1951). Essentially, this method consists of developing strength 
509	through repetitively lifting a weight which is gradually increased in the workout, as well from workout to 
510	workout, as strength increases.
511	However, when the display of great force was required, the imposition of resistance was a natural means of 
512	training, but where speed of movement plays a decisive role, resistance was used initially with great care. At the 
513	same time, some researchers noted that strength training makes it possible to improve results in speed type 
514	exercises (Dupperon, 1926; Lubimov, 1927; Curie, 1937; Markov, 1938, Ozolin, 1939; Chui, 1950; Gullwer, 
515	1955; Pennybaker, 1961). However, a long period of experimental and practical verification was required before 
516	this hypothesis gained acceptance. However, it is correct only relative to the amount of weight, the coordination 
517	pattern of the movement, the tempo and the number of repetitions.
518	When resistance is used for stimulating muscular tension, it is necessary to consider the fact that strength 
519	may be displayed in resistance exercises in the form of maximal tension or maximal speed of muscle contraction. 
520	One can then refer to strength exercises in which force is displayed primarily by increasing the amount of weight, 
521	and speed-strength exercises in which the display of force is associated with increasing the speed of movement 
522	(Farfel, 1940). In the first case, one tries to work with the largest resistance possible and in the second with a 
523	resistance whose optimal magnitude is determined by the required speed of movement.
524	It should be pointed out that the work regimes of strength with primarily slow movements and speed- 
525	strength exercises (using inherently fast movements) are essentially different with respect to the physiological 
526	mechanisms and the manner in which energy resources are used. Execution of explosive movements invariably 
527	requires a high level of excitation of the basic neural processes. In the case of slow movements, the basic role of 
528	the nervous system is to produce sufficient excitation and maintain it for a relatively long period (Federov, 1957).
529	It is useful to examine more closely the dynamics of movements with maximal effort in terms of the 
530	magnitude of the resistance displaced and the regime of muscular work. The amount of work obviously increases 
531	as the load raised by a weightlifter is increased. However, the changes in the power output of the work arc not 
532	unidirectional. Initially, power output increases, but after the weight of the barbell exceeds 66% of maximum, it 
533	begins to decrease (Chikvadze, 1961). A similar result is observed in the jump with a barbell on the shoulders (Fig 
534	4.2). Maximal dynamic force increases as the weight of the apparatus increases during the rapid increase in the 
535	movement time, mainly during the active thrust phase. Maximum power output is achieved with weights of 30- 
536	40% of the IRM and a maximal coefficient of reactivity at 30-33% of the 1RM.

724	force to be developed from rest.
725	Several studies suggest that such exercises can have a place if, for example, muscular tension is achieved by 
726	means of an abrupt stretch at the instant when a falling body or object is stopped (Ramsey, 1944; Hill, 1955; 
727	Tweit et al, 1963). It should be emphasized that significant and almost instantaneous development of muscular 
728	tension in this case is due to the mechanical stimulation of proprioceptors in the neuromuscular system, which 
729	creates the conditions for developing starting strength and explosiveness of muscular action.
730	Thus, we have a specific work regime which no heavy resistance exercise can imitate, because stimulation of 
731	muscular activity with significant extra resistance slows down the transition from eccentric to concentric work. 
732	The utilisation of energy of a falling body or object for mechanical stimulation requires the muscles to initially 
733	develop significant clastic tension, use it in overcoming the inertia of a relatively small weight then quickly switch 
734	to concentric work and produce a high speed of muscle contraction.
735	The role of kinetic energy in stimulating explosive muscle action warrants detailed analysis. To do this in the 
736	laboratory a special experimental stand was constructed to measure the height attained by a load when a subject 
737	threw it upward after it had first fallen from some height (from 0.5 to 3.0 metres). The kinetic energy used for
738	221
739

742	SUPERTRAINING
743	muscle stimulation changcd according to the weight (3.3, 6.6, 9.9 and 13.3% of the maximum isometric strength! | 
744	and the height of the fall (Vcrkhoshansky, 1977). The experiment showed that an increase in kinetic energy caused 
745	by an increase in the mass of the load decreases the height to which a load is thrown, but an increase in the 
746	distance through which a load falls increases the height to which it is thrown (Fig 4.8a).
747	A similar picture emerges from research on reactive ability (Fig 4.8b). This tendency, in general, is displayed 
748	by movements executed under other conditions, although these have their own peculiarities (Figs 4.9, 4.10). ]  
749	These examples show clearly that it is not beneficial to increase kinetic energy by use of heavier loads. It is 
750	therefore necessary to examine a better means of increasing the thrust height. The depth jump which has 
751	immediate practical significance for developing jumping ability is given in the example illustrated in Figure 4.10. 
752	Here maximal force (Fmax) increases up to a height of 1.15 metres, then diminishes sharply, while movement time 
753	begins by changing insignificantly, then increasing sharply. Maximum power and reactivity are achieved using a 
754	drop height of approximately 0.75 metres.
755	Figure 4.8 (a) Changes in height (h2) of thrown loads of different mass (in terms of maximum isometric strength Po), after having 
756	fallen from different heights (hi) (b) Changes in reactivity coefficient (RC) with respect to the kinetic energy of the falling load. 
757	(Verkhoshansky, 1977).
758	Thus, the optimal range of depth jumping for the stimulation of muscular activity is 0.75-1.15 metres, because at 
759	the lower end of this range the muscles are working at maximal power and at the upper end they are working at 
760	maximal dynamic force. This finding forms the basis for the recommendations for using depth jumps in the 
761	training of advanced jumpers (Vcrkhoshansky 1963, 1964, 1966), though it is preferable to err on the 
762	conservative side of using considerably lower jump heights with anyone who is unused to this type of training 
763	and to strictly limit the volume of this type of‘shock’ training.
764	Further increases in the height of the depth jump significantly decrease the magnitude of the dynamic 
765	parameters of the take-off. The support time increases quickly, primarily because the phase of switching from 
766	eccentric to concentric work is lengthened. In addition, the maximum dynamic force of take-off and the speed of 
767	muscular contraction stabilise and do not increase any further.
768	The take-off comprises two distinct actions: amortisation (where the kinetic energy of the fall is absorbed), 
769	and the thrust proper. The amortisation is characterised by the increasing depth of the resulting knee flexion, and 
770	the thrust proper by a fairly constant speed of muscle contraction. Thus, the positive effect of muscle 
771	stimulation by absorption of kinetic energy from a fall can be used successfully only under certain conditions by 
772	taking into consideration the optimal height of the fall, bodymass, additional load, and any other factors which 
773	may facilitate a quick take-off.
774	However, the state of the neuromuscular system during the amortisation phase of the falling body also can 
775	play an independent training role. Tension developed reflexively during this phase enhances the ability of the 
776	muscles to switch quickly to the active state. Experience indicates that this is not detrimental to speed-strength
