2	SUPFRTRA1NING
3	A  great deal of muscle testing and rehabilitation after injury is based on the use of isokinetic dynamometers such 
4	is Cybex™ and Orthotron™. Inadequate performance and injuries are attributed to differences in strength 
5	between interacting muscle groups as determined isokinetically. Athletes are claimed to be training scientifically 
6	if they are tested regularly under isokinetic conditions. Research evaluating the effectiveness of training regimes is 
7	limost invariably based on isokinetic measurement and often the reputation of their authors means that the 
8	validity of this work is rarely doubted. This section examines if this extensive reliance on isokinetic measurement 
9	and rehabilitation is warranted.
10	Fundamental Biomechanics of Isokinetic Devices
11	The faulty basic assumption is that isokinetic dynamometers are accurately constant angular velocity devices. 
12	T he laws of physics deem it impossible to construct any machine which offers purely isokinetic resistance from 
13	beginning to end of motion. When a body is at rest, it has to be accelerated to reach a certain terminal velocity 
14	that can be maintained for a given period of time before it has to be decelerated to return to rest once more. This 
15	m eans that there is always a period of positive or negative acceleration associated with all movement, isokinetic or 
16	otherwise. The best that manufacturers of isokinetic devices can do is to minimise the duration of these phases, 
17	although they can never entirely eliminate them. To produce entirely isokinetic conditions from beginning to end 
18	of motion would necessitate the production of infinite acceleration, which contradicts the laws of science.
19	Justifiably, it might be asked if the existence of non-isokinetic measuring phases on these machines is 
20	important. This fact is vitally important, because most injuries occur during these transition phases when a limb 
21	is changing its velocity or tension is changing in the musculotendinous system and isokinetic testing can reveal no 
22	useful information about what is happening to the muscles then. A most serious problem is that isokinetic testing 
23	can give no information on the major contribution played by the storage and release of elastic energy in the soft 
24	tissues during dynamic, natural actions such as walking, running, jumping or throwing. Stated simply, isokinetic 
25	testing or training is non-functional, except possibly for swimmers whose movements are approximately 
26	isokinetic over part of their range.
27	Biomechanical analysis of the force-time and rate of force development (RFD) curves for resisted free 
28	movement confirm the existence of vital muscular performance qualities such as maximal strength, starting 
29	strength (at the beginning of a movement), acceleration strength (while the movement is speeding up to maximum 
30	velocity) and explosive strength (see Fig 2.13). The curves obtained isokinetically are so radically different from 
31	tbeir free movement equivalents that they are of minimal value either for functional analysis or specific 
32	neuromuscular conditioning.
33	Recommended Strength Ratios
34	It is often claimed that the optimal ratio of quadriceps to hamstring strength is 60:40, but Russian scientists have 
35	found that this ratio depends on the specific type of sport (Vorobyev, 1978). For example, they have determined 
36	that this ratio (measured when knee extension torque is greatest) should be nearer 80:20 for weightlifters and 
37	lumpers. Moreover, if the ratio is measured during movement on a treadmill, the ratio for runners is 
38	approximately 50:50. Despite these findings, the traditional 60:40 recommendation is widely accepted and much 
39	rehabilitation is based on restoring this ratio. Another popular belief is that injuries are far more common if the 
40	difference in strength between left and right lower extremities is more than 10%.
41	Recent research, however, has shown that neither of these recommendations is supported by scientifically 
42	controlled experiments which correct torque outputs for the effect of gravity and avoid stretching the hamstrings 
43	(Stephens & Reid, 1988). In addition, the recommendation of a specific flexor/extensor ratio is vague, because this 
44	ratio varies throughout the range of joint motion, as may be seen in Figure 4.16.
45	For example, the ratio for the knee at 80° is about 75:25 at 36 degs/sec, whereas it is 68:32 at 180 degs/ sec. 
46	The only stage at which the ratio is 60:40 occurs at an angle of approximately 50°. Not only does the ratio change 
47	w ith joint angle, but it also changes with velocity of measurement, so it is meaningless to prescribe an optimal 
48	alio for any joint. It would be more relevant to refer to a characteristic curve over a full range of movement for a 
49	given angular velocity.
50	4.2.6.2 Limitations of the Isokinetic Method
51	233
52	
53	
54	=== page 245 viewer 246 ===
55	SUPERTRAINING
56	234
57	Functional Anatomy
58	Another confounding factor is the influence of the angle of nearby joints on the torque that is produced by given 
59	muscles about the joint in question. For instance, knee extension torque increases with hip angle, a phenomenon 
60	that is of immense practical importance to weightlifters, jumpers and sprinters, in particular. These athletes arc 
61	well aware of operating over optimal ranges of relative knee and hip angle. Measurement of the relative 
62	disposition of these angles forms the basis of the cyclogram used by biomechanists to study gait efficiency. 
63	Therapists attempt to solve this problem by immobilising the seated athlete’s hips by using strong inextensiblc 
64	straps across the upper thighs. This immediately creates non-functional conditions for evaluating the 
65	biomechanics of knee extension/flexion in free space. The seated posture produces highly constrained and 
66	accurate conditions for measuring torque that is specific to the seated posture and not to the posture exhibited 
67	during any actual sporting action.
68	Furthermore, seated isokinetic evaluation of knee motion is usually imprecisely controlled, since it is rarely 
69	combined with electromyography or myotonometry (muscle tension measurement) to ascertain the relative 
70	contributions made to joint torque by the different muscles comprising the quadriceps and hamstrings. 
71	Prescription of any exercise regime without knowing precisely which muscles are involved is just as haphazard 
72	with or without the aid of costly isokinetic devices. What complicates matters farther is that the degree of lateral 
73	or medial rotation of the lower extremity has a significant effect on the relative involvement of vastus medialis and 
74	lateralis, so that this variable also needs to be more accurately controlled if isokinetic testing is to become 
75	scientifically rigorous. Open-chain testing of the lower extremity with the sole of the foot not in contact with the 
76	ground alters the way in which poplitcus initiates knee flexion or gastrocnemius contributes to knee flexion, two 
77	actions that are of great importance in running, lifting or jumping.
78	In addition, seated testing does not take into consideration medial rotation of the knee by sartorius, gracilis, 
79	semimembranosus or semitendinosus, or lateral rotation by biceps femoris. The role of these muscles in 
80	performance may be largely ignored for the average client, but certainly not in the case of competitive athletes, 
81	who place maximal demands on their bodies.
82	The entire system of PNF is based on the importance of specific patterns of joint action and rnusclc 
83	recruitment in determining movement efficiency and safety, yet therapists with an extensive knowledge of PNF 
84	unquestioningly accept results produced under the highly unnatural conditions imposed by isokinetic machines. 
85	They are fully aware that training in a given way produces specific neural changes which become part of the 
86	central nervous programme that determines all movement efficiency; they meticulously apply the precise 
87	kinesiological patterns prescribed by Knott and Voss (1977), but they are compelled to ignore this knowledge 
88	when using isokinetic machines.
89	Muscle Physiology
90	Some of the implications of muscle physiology are also relevant to understanding the limitations of isokinetic 
91	testing:
92	
93	
94	=== page 246 viewer 247 ===
95	SUPERTRAINING
96	• The initial muscular state preceding many sporting actions is intense isometric contraction or explosive 
97	isomctric contraction accompanied by storage of elastic energy in the tendons (see 1.6.2). This state has a 
98	profound influence on explosive strength, metabolic efficiency and safety, yet all isokinetic testing or training 
99	involves insignificant initial levels of isometric contraction.
100	• The myotatic stretch reflex has great significance for increasing the working effect of concentric muscle action, 
101	with the greater the rate of stretch, the stronger this reflex. Most explosive movements in running, jumping, 
102	lifting and throwing rely on intense recruitment of this reflex, which is not possible under isokinetic 
103	conditions. In fact, the production of powerful, skillful movements in all sports relies on the establishment of 
104	precise neuromuscular patterns through integration of many different reflexes. The elimination of most of 
105	these reflex actions by isokinctic apparatus ensures that isokinetic testing and training is only of value during 
106	the early general conditioning or rehabilitation phase, but of no real significance during the specific 
107	preparation or competitive phases of sports training.
108	• Musclcs generally interact to produce two kinds of action: cocontraction or ballistic movement (see 1.8). In 
109	cocontraction, agonists and antagonists contract simultaneously, with dominance of the former producing the 
110	external motion. Ballistic movement comprises bursts of agonist activity followed by phases of relaxation 
111	during which the motion continues due to stored limb momentum. Skilled, rapid ballistic and fast continuous 
112	movements are preprogrammed in the central nervous system (CNS) and rarely involve feedback during the 
113	action, whereas slower, discontinuous movements involve cocontraction and ongoing feedback to the CNS 
114	from the muscles and joints. Isokinetic conditions do not permit the production of ballistic or discontinuous 
115	cocontractive actions, so that they address only a few of the needs of sports testing and preparation.
116	• Some authorities maintain that strength is best developed if muscle tension is kept at a maximum throughout 
117	the movement by the use of isokinetics (Thistle et al, 1967). This proposition is neither proved nor is it 
118	universally accepted with reference to all types of strength. Moreover, torque produced under isokinetic 
119	conditions is usually much lower than that produced isometrically at the same joint angle (Figs 2.8, 2.9).
120	• If contraction of the agonists is preceded immediately by maximal contraction of the antagonists, the force 
121	produced by the agonists is increased, a phenomenon often called reciprocal inhibition and regularly used in 
122	PNF. Most isokinetic devices do not permit this type of motion, which commonly occurs during plyometric 
123	rebounding activity.
124	• The patterns of force production are different for bilateral (simultaneous use of both limbs) and unilateral 
125	(alternate use of each limb) sports, so that isokinetic comparisons of relative limb strength can be very 
126	misleading. Furthermore, each person has a dominant limb, so that functional asymmetry is perfectly normal. 
127	This docs not imply that the dominant limb has superior strength; it often displays superiority in skill, 
128	especially in kicking, jumping and throwing sports. Yet, it is common to find therapists trying to strengthen 
129	the weaker kicking limb of a footballer isokinetically, although the support leg is meant to produce greater 
130	stabilising strength.
131	The Importance of Specificity
132	Indiscriminate use of isokinetics neglects the proven principle of specificity (discussed in detail in 1.3) with 
133	respect to:
134	• Type of Muscle Contraction • Musclc Fibre Recruitment
135	• Movement Pattern • Metabolism
136	• Region of Movement • Biochcmical Adaptation
137	• Velocity of Movement • Flexibility
138	• Force of Contraction • Fatigue
139	Therefore, it is vital to understand the limitations of using isokinetics to test or train the athlete and appreciate 
140	that sport specific conditioning has little to do with isokinetic performance. As has been stressed by Sale and 
141	McDougall (1981), increased strength is apparent only when measured during the same type of movement used in 
142	training. The importance of training specificity is underlined further by the considerable research of 
143	Verkhoshansky, which culminated in his formulating the principle of dynamic correspondence (see 4.3) This 
144	principle emphasizes that the means of strength training for all sports should enhance the required motor qualities
145	235
146	
147	
148	=== page 247 viewer 248 ===
149	SUPERTRAINING
150	in terms of factors such as amplitude and direction of movement, and the rate and time of maximal force 
151	production.
152	On this basis, as well, isokinetic training and measurement are seen to be so functionally different from 
153	normal sporting movement as to be relatively useless for giving any information that is accurately applicable to 
154	the competitive athlete.
155	Concluding Remarks
156	Although technological measurement is invaluable and highly desirable in sport and rehabilitation, 
157	oversimplification of any highly complex situation can lead to serious errors and hinder scientific progress. The 
158	simplistic central sun and planetary electron model of the atom was a valuable tool for early 20th century 
159	physicists, but its replacement by more sophisticated quantum models has advanced our understanding of the 
160	universe enormously. Unqualified reliance on a single isokinetic model to assess muscular strength and endurance 
161	is tantamount to permanently accepting the early model of the atom, just because it is easy to work with.
162	The fact is that human motion involving static and dynamic multiple link components is extremely 
163	complicated and isokinetic testing can offer only a very simplistic way of obtaining information on a limited 
164	number of variables. Isokinetic machines are useful for measuring isokinetic actions and changes in two 
165	dimensions, just as isometric dynamometry is useful for measuring isomctric strength at a given joint angle. 
166	Extrapolation of results obtained under these conditions to sporting actions involving other types of muscle 
167	contraction and patterns of movement is scientifically unacceptable and misleading. Human mobility and stability 
168	are the integrated result of the appropriate phases of isomctric and non-isokinetic muscle contraction occurring 
169	with a specific timing in three-dimensional space over specific ranges of joint angle. Multi-faceted human 
170	movement demands the use of far more versatile and complex technological means, a type of kincsiological 
171	polygraph which integrates information yielded by concurrent use of devices such as high speed video, EMG, 
172	myotensiometers, accelerometers and force plates.
173	The ultimate measure of successful testing and training is unequivocal improvement in the athlete's 
174	performance, so that sporting movements should still be regarded as the final test of any training or rehabilitation 
175	regime. In addition, an inexpensive and highly effective alternative to isokinetics is the APRE system based on the 
176	original work of DeLorme (sec 5.2.2). The convenience of isokinetic testing should be weighed against its high 
177	cost, limited application and the unsupported claims of manufacturers. The detailed review of the strengths and 
178	weaknesses of isokinetic methods given by Ostemig (1986) provides further useful information in this regard.
179	4.2.6.3 Static-Dynamic Methods
180	The static-dynamic method of developing muscular strength involves the sequential combination in one exercise of 
181	isometric and dynamic (auxotonic) muscular activity, each of which can provide its own distinct quantitative 
182	characteristics. For example, the following variations of static-dynamic exercise have been shown to be effective:
183	• a 2-3 second isometric contraction (at 80% of one's maximum) is held, followed by explosive concentric 
184	dynamic work with a load of 30% of maximum
185	• with both the isometric and dynamic components, a constant load of 75-80% of maximum is used.
186	In the latter case, for instance, the athlete sinks into the half-squat position with a barbell on his shoulders, holds 
187	this position for 2 seconds, then with maximal acceleration, jumps upward. After careful landing he repeats the 
188	exercise.
189	It has been established experimentally that the first variant of static-dynamic exercise is better than dynamic 
190	exercise alone for developing speed-strength. The second variant has an equivalent affect on the improvement of 
191	speed-strength and absolute strength (Dobrovolsky, 1972, 1973).
192	4.2.6.4 Choice of Muscle Training Regimes
193	One may now ask the question: Of all these regimes, which is the most effective? It is difficult to give a 
194	categorical answer for several reasons:
195	1. Comprehensive research to evaluate the effectiveness of all the regimes has not been conducted. An attempt, 
196	for example, to study the effectiveness of eccentric, concentric, isometric and combined regimes revealed
197	236
198	
199	
200	=== page 248 viewer 249 ===
201	SUPERTRAINING
202	some advantages of the concentric over the eccentric and isometric method, but the main method using 
203	combined regimes showed a clear advantage (Plctnev, 1975).
204	2. Similar comparative research is difficult with respect to controlling the training loads of the different regimes.
205	3, It is inappropriate to raise the question of the absolute effectiveness of any specific regime. Each of them 
206	can be the most effective, depending upon factors such as the situation, stage of the annual cycle, level of the 
207	athlete, the primary regime of muscular work in the special exercise, and the specificity of the strength ability 
208	acquired as a result of training.
209	Today it can be ascertained with reasonable certainty that the most rational means of enhancing the effectiveness 
210	of special strength preparation is to combine the various regimes of muscular work. This has been corroborated 
211	by several studies (Vorobyev, 1966; Andrianov & Vorobyev, 1969; Kuznetsov, 1970; Verkhoshansky, 1970, 
212	1972; Slobodyan, 1972; Tatyan, 1974; Pletnev 1975; Khodykin, 1975; Savin, 1974). Such a training combination 
213	ts selected by taking into consideration its cumulative effect and its correspondence to the specific conditions of 
214	the sport.
215	4.2.7 The Use of Training Machines
216	Recently, training machines for strength development have become very popular in most modem gymnasia. 
217	However, before machines are used in training, it is important to understand that there are essentially two distinct 
218	classes of machine:
219	• Functional resistance machines, whose purpose is to offer resistance in sport specific patterns
220	• Non-Junctional resistance machines, whose sole purpose is to offer general resistance in non-sport specific 
221	patterns
222	A n appreciation of this distinction is vital for many coaches and athletes in the West, because the impressive 
223	fitness centres in which they often train are usually entirely equipped with non-functional resistance (NFR) 
224	nuchincs. In fact, the machine training syndrome has become so popular among the average population that it is 
225	frequently difficult to find adequate free weights or functional resistance (FR) machines in these 'state-of-the-art' 
226	ccntres. While the use of NFR machines may be adequate for the casual fitness client, it can be profoundly 
227	counterproductive for sport specific trainees if used in place of FR machines or free weights. Current commer­
228	cialised emphasis on circuit and cross training has proliferated the use of NFR machines, so the serious athlete 
229	should become aware of their limitations in sport and rehabilitation, particularly regarding the detrimental effects 
230	they can have on the specificity of fitness, proprioceptive efficiency, central nervous programming and sporting 
231	skills. The remarks of Zatsiorsky (1995) on this issue are highly relevant:
232	The important limitation of many strength training machines is that they are designed to train muscles, not 
233	movement. Because of this, they are not the most important training tool for athletes.
234	4.2.7.1 Functional Resistance Machines
235	Functional strength (FR) machines are devised to provide resistance to various movements encountered in sport. 
236	Depending on the setting, sport-specific resistance devices are supposed to imitate or train certain elements of an 
237	athletic exercise in order to provide the necessary specific loads in the different regimes of muscular work (Ratov, 
238	1976). Research on the use of FR training devices in athletics has shown them to be very effective for aspects of 
239	special strength training of many types of athlete (Semenov, 1970; Petrova & Gorbunov, 1970; Vcrkhoshansky, 
240	1970; Deniskin & Kuznetsov, 1972; Dobrovolski, 1972, 1973; Kuznetsov & Aiunts, 1974; Savin, 1974).
241	This can be explained by the fact that they permit the strict regulation of the load and the spatial 
242	characteristics of the movement in order to use extensively the appropriate regimes of muscular work and to 
243	programme the characteristics of the force over time. They reproduce stereotypical training movements and are 
244	economical for the athlete in terms of time and energy.
245	One of the simplest, cheapest and most versatile of all FR devices is the pulley machine, which used to be 
246	widely used in gymnasia until supplanted by the more commercially persuasive chromium-plated ’modem' 
247	machines. The 'hi-Io* pulley machine permits one to use the pulleys in high or low positions for all varieties of 
248	movement in space and time. Since the handles are attached to ropes unlike the fixed bars and pivots of most 
249	N FR machines, they can be used to exercise in sport specific patterns of great complexity, if so desired.
250	237
251	
252	
253	=== page 249 viewer 250 ===
254	SUPERTRAINING
255	With appropriate choice and layout of hand grips, bars, pulleys and benches, it is possible to perform dozens 
256	of different exercises for every body part on a single pulley machine. A fixture of only 4 pulley machines can 
257	actually provide a circuit training facility which cannot be equalled by fewer than 40 'state of the art’ machines. A  
258	circuit comprising 10 pulley machines, a few benches, a few jumping boards, a few bars, a few mats, gymnastic 
259	wall-bars and a few racks can provide more clients with a larger range of exercises than 100 specialised machines- 
260	at less than 15% of the cost. Even then, the NFR machine-only facility would provide inferior multi-dimensional 
261	conditioning of the body.
262	A major advantage of sport-specific FR training devices lies in the fact that it is possible to obtain crucial 
263	visual and computerised feedback about the qualitative and quantitative characteristics of the movement, as well 
264	as to control the athlete's special strength training. All of these advantages create significant potential foe 
265	perfecting the athlete's special strength training programme. Therefore, the design, introduction of various types 
266	of FR training device becomes a very important task.
267	In using any machine, however, it is vital to note that simulation of any sporting movement against heavy 
268	loads can alter the force-time characteristics of the action significantly and disrupt the neuromuscular programmes 
269	responsible for the movement. The magnitude of the load, the pattern of movement and the principle of dynamic 
270	correspondence have to be considered carefully if one intends to use machines to simulate actual sporting 
271	movements in any way. Most important is the fact that functionality is not the automatic consequence of a 
272	specific exercise, but of the functional objectives associated with using any exercise, irrespective of its similarity 
273	to any sports action and integrating it effectively into the long-term conditioning programme.
274	4.2.7.2 Non-Functional Resistance Machines
275	Non-functional resistance (NFR) machines can play a useful supplementary role to free weight and functional 
276	machine training, but in general they are unable to provide the same degree of multi-dimensional, full range 
277	neuromuscular and musculoskeletal training as free weights and ‘functional’ machines.
278	Very often, NFR machines compel the user to sit or lie, thereby minimising the training effect on the major 
279	stabilising musclcs of the body and involving fewer of the joints in fewer degrees of freedom of movement While 
280	this may be valuable in the earlier stages of rehabilitating certain injuries, it is an incomplete way of regularly 
281	training the body for functional development. One of their major deficiencies for the competitive athlete or average 
282	person is the limitation they impose on proprioceptive processes and the kinaesthetic sense in functional 
283	strength development. Since machines usually stabilise major regions of the body and limit the number of joints 
284	which move, they diminish one's ability to exercise freely in three dimensional space and thereby do not 
285	adequately train balance, coordination and other components of proprioception. The dangers of regular 
286	supplementary circuit training as a form of'cross training' for sporting preparation should then become obvious.
287	NFR machines may be useful in concentrating more on the development of certain muscle groups for 
288	supplementing overall bodybuilding training or the primary stages of injury rehabilitation, but they are unsuitable 
289	for providing all-round conditioning of entire muscle groups, interacting agonist/antagonist muscles and motor 
290	systems. For instance, there is no single machine that can rival the training effect of a barbell squat, a barbell or 
291	dumbbell curl, a barbell bench press, a power clean, a standing press, lateral raises with dumbbells or a barbell 
292	deadlift. On the other hand, one machine, namely the 'lat pulley' machine, is generally more suitable and safer for 
293	training the latissimus dorsi than the free weights equivalent of bent-over rowing.
294	It is important to note that, if a machinc compels a user to use fewer joints and muscles than an equivalent 
295	free weights or pulley exercise, then the stress on all of those structures will be increased proportionately. For 
296	example, the free standing squat involves three joints (hip, knee and ankle), whereas the seated knee extension 
297	machinc constrains the body to use only one joint (the knee) in exercising the quadriceps, so that, in producing a 
298	comparable level of exercise over the same range of movement, this machine increases the shearing force across the 
299	knee. Moreover, the squat also offers the added advantages of exercising the thigh adductors, the spinal erectors 
300	and several other stabilising muscles, besides enhancing general balance and bone density (due to longitudinal 
301	compressive loading of the skeleton).
302	It is not often appreciated that seated exercise always imposes a greater load on the lumbar spinal discs than 
303	equivalent standing exercises. Even without an added load, sitting with the back maintaining its neutral curvatures 
304	increases the lumbar disc pressure by about 40% (Chaffin & Andersson, 1984). If the back is allowed to flex 
305	forwards, this stress can increase by as much as 90%. An ergonomically designed backrest which adequately 
306	supports the lumbar region lowers the stress, but even then the lumbar disc pressure can be some 75% greater
307	238
308	
309	
310	=== page 250 viewer 251 ===
311	SUPERTRAINING
312	than during standing. The increase in stress becomes far greater against resistance, particularly if jerky movements 
313	are used to initiate or terminate the movement. The dangers are exacerbated by sitting, because one is unable to 
314	absorb any shock loading by flexing the knees, hips or ankles, as is the case when standing.
315	In the vast majority of cases, NFR machines provide an inferior, incomplete and less efficient way of training 
316	the musculoskeletal system. This is particularly true regarding the conditioning of the neuromuscular system in 
317	rapid or explosive movements, as well as the elastic qualities of the tendons and other conncctive tissues which 
318	ire essential in all sports involving running, jumping, throwing, catching or any other ballistic actions. Isokinetic 
319	machines can be especially deficient in this regard, so that their appropriateness of use must be clearly understood 
320	if they are to prove beneficial in sport specific training (see 4.2.6). Nevertheless, some machines may be used 
321	productively as an occasional form of General Physical Training, rehabilitation or restoration.
322	4.2.7.3 Machines and the Variable Resistance Philosophy
323	As discussed elsewhere in this text, the torque produced by a muscle in a particular movement varies with joint 
324	angle. Many machine manufacturers have used this fact to justify the design of machines whose resistance varies 
325	in an attempt to match the torque curves of natural joint movement. They maintain that variable resistance 
326	machines offer superior strength training to free weights and other resistance devices. What they fail to point out 
327	is that regular training on any machine, whether variable resistance or not, provides inadequate functional 
328	proprioceptive training and thereby can reduce one's level of motor efficiency, stability and safety.
329	Their claims are based on the faulty premise that the resistance offered to the muscles by a free weight 
330	always remains the same. So, for example, if you perform a biceps curl with 50 kg, then it is implied that you are 
331	exciting a force of 50 kg weight (about 490 Newtons) from beginning to end of movement. Machinc 
332	manufacturers stress that their bicep curl machine offers some form of automatically adjusting resistance to 
333	account for the variation of strength with joint angle, apparently something that never happens with free weights.
334	A simple application of Newton's Second Law of Motion (force is proportional to the acceleration of the ob­
335	ject) reveals that the resistance offered by a free weight changes with acceleration from rest and during any other 
336	time when the trainee speeds up or slows down the movement when the weight feels lighter or heavier 
337	respectively. The force exerted by any weight which begins from and returns to rest is always varying, anyway, 
338	as can easily be demonstrated by force plate, cable tensiometer or high speed video analysis. The skilled trainee is 
339	able to rely on his proprioceptive apparatus to perceive any changes in force or pattern of movement so as to 
340	statically and dynamically vary the resistance and its direction more efficiently than any current machines.
341	4.2.7.4 The Training Safety of Machines
342	It is often claimed that the NFR machines found in most fitness centres are much safer to use than free weights. 
343	Injuries to the back and knees (on leg press, hack-squat and hip-sled machines), the shoulders and chest (on bench 
344	press and pec-deck machines), the elbow joint (bicep curl machines), the back (back extension machines) and other 
345	joints are just as common with machines as with free weights. In fact, many machines, such as the 'pec-dcck', 
346	bench-prcss, leg press, calf-raise and seated press machines force the user to commence the movement from the 
347	biomechanically least efficient and potentially most harmful position for the relevant joint. Partners to 'spot' 
348	machine users are just as necessary as spotters for free weights users. Faulty technique is equally dangerous with 
349	machines or free weights.
350	Some machines such as leg extension, lat pulley and seated bicep curl machines are certainly safer if an 
351	individual is suffering from back weakness or injury. They can be very helpful in the early stages of rehabili­
352	tation, but are not helpful in the long-term, since continual avoidance of stress to the regions involved eventually 
353	leads to their progressive weakening. There is a definite supplementary place in a gymnasium for certain NFR 
354	machines, but they should not replace free weights, pulley machines and other FR devices. A more detailed 
355	analysis of the safety of training with specific machines is covered later (Ch 8.8).
356	4.2.7.5 The Efficiency of Machine Training
357	Contrary to what the equipment manufacturers state, it takes far longer for NFR machines to provide a similar 
358	multi-faceted training effect to the equivalent free weights or FR machines. For instance, it requires at least twelve 
359	NFR machines to approximately equal the training effect of the clean-and-push press, at least four machines to 
360	rival the training effect of the free standing squat, more than three machines to equal the training effect of the 
361	standing dumbbell curl, and at least five machines to rival the effectiveness of the flexed-knee deadlift.
362	239
363	
364	
365	=== page 251 viewer 252 ===
366	SUPERTRAINING
367	In other words, more than 24 NFR machines are required to challenge the effectiveness of a circuit 
368	comprising only four free weights exercises: the clean-and-push press, the squat, deadlift, and biccps curl. In this 
369	case, the combined cost of these machines is about forty times greater than the combined cost of several sets of 
370	free weights and the necessary racks. Moreover, the maintenance cost of most NFR machines is considerably 
371	higher than that of virtually indestructible free weights and the breakdown of machines is a regular occurrence in a 
372	well-used gymnasium.
373	4.2.8 The Concept of Symmetric Training
374	Asymmetry in leg length, muscle strength, stride length and several other features of human structure and function 
375	has been blamed as one of the causes of inefficient movement and injury. Likewise, imbalances in muscle 
376	strength between agonists and antagonists, left and right limbs, and in isokinetic muscle endurance, as measured on 
377	isokinetic devices have been singled out as leading causes of muscle injury (see 4.2.6).
378	Research, however, has revealed that isokinetically-measurcd discrepancies as large as 10% between 
379	left/right leg strength and agonist/antagonist strength of the right and left legs do not statistically correlate with a 
380	major increase in muscular injuries.
381	The body and its muscles, tendons and bones are characteristically asymmetric and any attempts to produce 
382	greater anthropomorphic and kinesiological symmetry could cxaccrbate the existing problem or cause new injuries. 
383	One has to ascertain the degree of asymmetry not only by static measurements of structural features such as leg 
384	length and spinal curvature, but also by dynamic biomechanical analysis of Junctional features such as force 
385	distribution, movement patterns, ground reaction force, electrical activity of postural (tonic) and phasic muscle 
386	groups, and the timing of the different phases of movement.
387	Differences in structural characteristics including muscle and tendon length, the sites of tendon and ligament 
388	attachments to bone, and bone size and mass are quite natural in all humans. It is only when these structural 
389	differences lead to serious Junctional imbalances in movement patterns that surgical or orthotic means may have to 
390	be implemented to solve the problem. Even then, one has to ensure that the excessive functional asymmetry is 
391	due primarily to structural and not neuromuscular or central nervous processes. It may be that the centrally 
392	stored nervous patterns are producing the troublesome kinesiological imperfections, so that the answer lies in 
393	paying attention to modifying the motor skills required for the specific sport.
394	It is important to appreciate that there is no perfect way of executing any movement: everyone has an 
395	individualised version of the supposedly 'ideal' model of every skill. Some sports coaches and aerobic instructors 
396	place an unnecessarily restrictive emphasis on what they consider to be 'correct' exercise technique and allow 
397	inadequate latitude for individual interpretation (i.e. style, as opposed to skill). One simply has to examine the 
398	drastically different walking and running styles of world class athletes to realise that there is no such thing as 
399	perfect style. There is only an optimal style for each individual, where style refers to the individual expression of 
400	a motor skill. This style has to be developed on the basis of observing and experimenting with the 'ideal' model 
401	until the person produces a central nervous programme which suits his or her body.
402	Recent research by Yushkcvich (1989) supports these points. He analysed the symmetry of leg strength in 
403	sprinters and concluded that striving for full leg symmetry is inappropriate. He found that the extensors of all the 
404	joints of the push-off leg generally were significantly stronger than those of the swing-leg, whereas there was no 
405	definite difference between the flexor strengths of either leg. There were distinct differences in the patterns of 
406	asymmetry between novice. Class 3, Class 2, Class 1  and more highly qualified athletes. For instance, novices 
407	displayed greater strength of the hip flexors of the push-off leg than of the swing-leg. The knee flexors of novices, 
408	Class 3 and Class 2 were stronger in the swing-leg, whereas those of Class I, Master and other more highly 
409	qualified athletes were stronger in the push-off \cg. Dorsiflexion was stronger in the push-off leg of all athletes 
410	except novices.
411	Interestingly, leg strength asymmetry was found to increase as sprinters increase in proficiency, reaching a 
412	peak among Class 2 athletes, then diminishing again as level of sports mastery increased. Furthermore, 
413	Yushkevich found that good sprint times correlated more closely with swing-leg strength than push-off leg 
414	strength.
415	This study concluded that, not only are attempts to produce symmetrical muscle strength ill-advised, but 
416	that it can be beneficial to perform asymmetric exercises by running or jumping on sloping or inclined tracks, by 
417	running around curves in both directions, running and jumping in shoes with soles of different thickness, or 
418	running with leg weights of different mass. Yushkevich (1989) stressed this type of training thus: \Asymmetric 
419	exercises destabilise the space-time characteristics of motor acts, thereby helping athletes break speed barriers'.
420	240
421	
422	
423	=== page 252 viewer 253 ===
424	SUPERTRAINING
425	There is an ancient injunction that the weavers of Eastern carpet must include at least one flaw in their 
426	w ork to recognisc that perfection is reserved for the Divine and not for humans. The above findings imply that 
427	ijnilar asymmetry or lack of perfection may be desirable for all human physical performance and training.
428	4.2.9 The Concept of Muscle Isolation
429	Generations of muscle magazine authors have extolled the virtues of special ways of training to isolate specific 
430	muscle groups. They have advocated certain machines, ways of fixating the joints, precise placement of the limbs 
431	ud numerous other ingenious manoeuvres to ensure that one muscle is maximally recruited while others remain 
432	largely dormant.
433	EMG studies reveal that isolation of minute muscle groups is indeed possible under low intensities of 
434	loading (e.g. Basmajian, 1978). Intuitively, we are aware that low intensity actions such as eye-blinking, piano- 
435	playing or relaxed speaking are due to the precise action of specific muscle groups, a fact which the EMG clearly 
436	corroborates.
437	However, if large loads are imposed on a given muscle group by intense resistance, isolation becomcs virtu- 
438	illy impossible. Immediately the load is applied, stabilising muscles become involved to ensure that the body or 
439	specific joints remain stable, while the prime movers attempt to cope with the load. If the nervous system signals 
440	that the prime movers are inadequate to execute the desired joint action, assistant movers, shunt muscles, 
441	emergency muscles and neutralises may all be recruited to augment the action of the prime movers.
442	Physiotherapists relying on PNF techniques sometimes impose maximal loading on a joint to elicit 
443	compensatory or overflow activity of muscles other than the ‘prime movers.* This is not possible if the 
444	resistance imposed is inadequate to overload the ‘prime movers.* Similarly, the weight trainer who wishes to 
445	increase hypertrophy or strength of a given muscle selects a weight which forces it to operate at high intensity. 
446	H ie higher the intensity or the greater the duration of the exercise, the less likely is isolation of the prime mover, 
447	even if certain joints arc restrained as on an isokinetic test machine.
448	In many cases the tension developed in the stabilisers or assistant stabilisers will equal or exceed that of the 
449	pnme movers. For example, during heavy standing tricep press-downs with cable machines, the abdominal 
450	muscles, latissimus dorsi and erector spinae of the back may be as strongly contracted as the triceps, even though 
451	this is supposedly an isolation exercise for the triceps. Analysis of many seated or reclining isolation exercises on 
452	machines reveals that isolation simply docs not occur with heavy loads.
453	This is not to negate the value of so-called isolation exercises. Not only can they be useful during the early 
454	stages of injury rehabilitation, but overflow to other muscle groups may be very desirable (if the exercise is 
455	performed safely), sincc it simultaneously offers isometric and dynamic training to many other muscle groups. It 
456	tsnecessary, however, to clarify the popular misconceptions surrounding the misleading concept of muscle 
457	isolation still proliferated by numerous instructors and in many training texts.
458	4.3 Dynamic Correspondence as a Means of Strength 
459	Training
460	Devising methods of special strength training is associated firstly with the selection of the means and methods for 
461	developing muscular strength. AH sporting movement is specific and goal-directed. Therefore, the strength 
462	displayed in the execution of each movement is also specific and goal-directed. One should not refer to strength in 
463	general, but only in the context of the given task. In other words, the means and methods of strength training 
464	should provide an adequate conditioning regime for the motor system in the special exercises and thereby ensure 
465	continued improvement in sporting performance.
466	The foundation of this assertion lies in the principle of dynamic correspondence, which emphasizes that the 
467	means and methods of strength training for specific sports should be chosen to enhance the required motor 
468	qualities in terms of:
469	• The amplitude and direction of movement
470	• The accentuated region of force production
471	• The dynamics of the effort
472	• The rate and time of maximum force production
473	• The regime of muscular work
474	241
475	
476	
477	=== page 253 viewer 254 ===
478	SUPERTRAINING
479	4.3.1 The Amplitude and Direction of Movement
480	The criterion of correspondence with respect to the amplitude and direction originates from the patterns of the 
481	movement relative to the adjacent body part. It determines which muscles are involved in the work and allows for 
482	anatomical peculiarities and the external conditions of work. Thus, the movement of the shoulder girdle of a row« 
483	or shot putter is about the same in amplitude, but the direction of the working force is different (Fig 4.17). In the 
484	first case the pulling of the oars involves shoulder extension, whereas in the second case it involves shoulder 
485	flexion acting in opposition to the force of inertia of the shot.
486	The importance of the correspondence of muscular work, in terms of the relevant criteria may be illustrated 
487	by the following example. In track-and-field training, jumpers and sprinters sometimes do exercises to develop the 
488	hip flexor muscles in a standing position on a hip flexor machine which offers resistance by means of a pad 
489	pressing against the front of the thigh.
490	However, the amplitude of thigh movement in running and jumping (when moving the legs forward) ij 
491	significantly greater than the amplitude of this exercise, and begins at an angle of about 210° in the hip joint, 
492	relative to the torso. Therefore, the execution of this exercise in the standing position docs not duplicate the 
493	mcchanism of the movement in the sport specific exercise ( e.g. jumping or sprinting).
494	Figure 4.17 Working amplitude of shoulder movement of a rower and a shotputter (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
495	If the athlete’s position changes (Fig 4.18), the criterion of the correspondence is met, not only with respect to the 
496	amplitude of the movement, but also to the sporting movement, because the resistance imitates the inertial 
497	resistance of the mass of the leg rotating about the hip joint in the special exercise. By altering the load, the 
498	number of repetitions and the tempo of movement, the task of developing the strength to produce the required 
499	force and strength-endurance, will be solved. Thus, to fulfill the criteria of correspondence with respect to the 
500	amplitude and direction of movement, it is advisable to select the exact starting position and posture of the ath­
501	lete, as well as to calculate the direction of action of the forces associated with the working links of the system 
502	and the additional load.
503	The line of action of the applied external resistance and of the loaded movement as a whole must also be 
504	taken into account. For example, in middle-distancc running, skiing and skating, a knapsack full of sand ora 
505	weight belt are sometimes used as resistance. However, the muscles which bear the load are those which resist the 
506	weight of the body. This can increase the ability to cope with vertical loading and develop general strength- 
507	endurance, but docs not strengthen those muscles which propel the body horizontally.
508	Figure 4.18 Exercise for developing hip flexion strength based on consideration for the accentuated part of the working amplitude and 
509	the resistance to the force of muscle contraction (SiflF & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
510	Similarly, a skater may exccute jumps on one leg on the floor or from a bench. These exercises strengthen the leg 
511	muscles supporting the body and the static-endurance of the back muscles, but do not fully imitate the working of 
512	the muscles for the push-off, where the force is directed backward.
513	242
514
