# Seventeen Claimed Clinical and Physiological Effects of Electrostimulation, With Their Original Citations

**What it is** — The authors catalog electrostimulation's (ES) reported applications and
effects, each with cited sources: (1) increase in muscle strength, strongest in
incapacitated, unfit or weakest subjects, with ES alone at best matching or trailing
voluntary exercise, though periodised programmes combining ES with training sometimes
increased competitive athletes' strength (Francis, 1982; Kots & Chwilon, 1971; Matteson,
1984; Reding, 1973); (2) re-education of faulty muscle-action patterns, e.g. chondromalacia
patellae, tennis elbow, "frozen shoulder" (Eriksson, 1981; Godfrey et al, 1979; Johnson et
al, 1977; Nirschl & Sobel, 1981); (3) facilitation of contraction when voluntary contraction
is blocked by disuse, pain or injury, reducing tissue wasting; (4) increased muscular and
systemic endurance from prolonged sub-maximal ES, with low-frequency (under 15 Hz),
24-hour continuous stimulation shown in animal studies to shift fast-twitch fibres toward a
more aerobic, fatigue-resistant profile (Jolesz & Sreter, 1981; Pette, 1984; Pette & Vrbova,
1985; Salmons & Vrbova, 1969; Salmons & Henriksson, 1981); (5) increased speed of
contraction from long-term, higher-frequency (over 40 Hz) ES, improving reaction time and
decreasing time-to-peak-tension of fast-twitch fibres (Fleury & Lagasse, 1979; Salmons &
Vrbova, 1967, 1969); (6) increased local blood supply, with measured increases from about
20% to over 200%, greatest below roughly 30 Hz (Currier et al, 1986; Richardson, 1981;
Wakim et al, 1948; Wakim, 1953); (7) a massage-like pumping action on venous/lymphatic
return; (8) pain relief via TENS, using low-frequency (50-100 Hz) stimulation without
contraction for superficial pain, or short, high-intensity bursts (1-150 Hz) with
contraction for deeper pain; (9) reduction of protective muscle spasm and spasticity; (10)
promotion of relaxation and recuperation, attributed to central endorphin/enkephalin
release, used by Russian athletes for post-training recuperation and to aid sleep onset even
with mild thigh-only stimulation; (11) increased range of movement, used alongside PNF
mobilisation; (12) reduction of non-infectious swelling; (13) halting or slowing mild to
moderate scoliotic curvature with ES applied to specific back muscles (Axelgaard et al,
1983; Friedman et al, 1982; Kots & Chwilon, 1971; Schultz et al, 1981); (14) preferential
recruitment of the largest-diameter motor axons first, the reverse of natural recruitment
order, making them a supplementary route to axons that are hard to activate under normal
training (Enoka, 1988); (15) an acute strength increase after a single session: Alon (1985),
studying 14 subjects, found one experimental ES session produced a mean 13% increase in
quadriceps strength; (16) improved metabolic economy: Ratov & Kryazhev (1986) found
electrically stimulating the quadriceps during cycling and speed skating reduced oxygen
consumption by 10-17% and extended time-to-fatigue by 15-20%, and treadmill running with ES
reduced oxygen consumption by about 10%, or by about 5% if the stimulated muscles had just
performed the work; (17) increased contractile speed of skeletal muscle via phasic-type ES.
(PDF pp. 221-224, printed pp. 210-213, "4.2.1.3 Clinical Applications of
Electrostimulation.")

**Why it works** — The authors give a distinct proposed mechanism for each effect
(catalogued above per item) rather than one unifying mechanism; several (items 4-5, 14, 17)
are tied to fibre-type recruitment and conversion, while others (6-13) are tied to blood
flow, central neurochemistry, or mechanical pumping action. Inference: no single theory in
this passage ties all seventeen together; the authors' own attempt at unification is the
separate MACS/MICS theory (see
[[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]]).

**When to apply** — Use this as a reference catalog when deciding whether ES could serve a
specific, narrow purpose (e.g. swelling reduction, pain relief, post-training recuperation)
distinct from strength development, which the authors treat as ES's weakest and most
contested claimed benefit (see
[[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]]). Inference: for Athletic
Medicine or Applied Performance settings, items 6-13 (blood flow, pain, spasm, swelling,
recuperation, ROM) map most directly onto standard rehabilitation and recovery use cases,
while items 1-5, 14-17 (strength, endurance, speed, recruitment, metabolic economy) are the
more contested performance-training claims.

**When NOT to apply** — Each item rests on citations from roughly 1948-1988, mostly single
studies or small samples (e.g. Alon's 13% figure is from 14 subjects, one session); none are
independently re-validated within this ingest. Item 4's fibre-type conversion evidence is
from animal (cross-innervation, continuous 24-hour stimulation) studies, not directly
transferable to standard clinical ES dosing. Do not treat this list as equally strong
evidence across all seventeen items; some (blood flow, pain relief, swelling) have broader
citation support here than others (scoliosis, acute strength).

**Example** — Inference: a post-training recovery application (item 10, low-current
stimulation to aid relaxation and sleep onset) is a narrower, better-supported use case than
citing this same list to justify ES as a primary strength-training tool (item 1, contested
above); a practitioner should not conflate the two when deciding whether to add ES to a
program.

[[heuristic--nine-reasons-electrostimulation-research-conflicts]],
[[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]].

effects, each with cited sources: (1) increase in muscle strength, strongest in
incapacitated, unfit or weakest subjects, with ES alone at best matching or trailing
voluntary exercise, though periodised programmes combining ES with training sometimes
increased competitive athletes' strength (Francis, 1982; Kots & Chwilon, 1971; Matteson,
1984; Reding, 1973); (2) re-education of faulty muscle-action patterns, e.g. chondromalacia
patellae, tennis elbow, "frozen shoulder" (Eriksson, 1981; Godfrey et al, 1979; Johnson et
al, 1977; Nirschl & Sobel, 1981); (3) facilitation of contraction when voluntary contraction
is blocked by disuse, pain or injury, reducing tissue wasting; (4) increased muscular and
systemic endurance from prolonged sub-maximal ES, with low-frequency (under 15 Hz),
24-hour continuous stimulation shown in animal studies to shift fast-twitch fibres toward a
more aerobic, fatigue-resistant profile (Jolesz & Sreter, 1981; Pette, 1984; Pette & Vrbova,
1985; Salmons & Vrbova, 1969; Salmons & Henriksson, 1981); (5) increased speed of
contraction from long-term, higher-frequency (over 40 Hz) ES, improving reaction time and
decreasing time-to-peak-tension of fast-twitch fibres (Fleury & Lagasse, 1979; Salmons &
Vrbova, 1967, 1969); (6) increased local blood supply, with measured increases from about
20% to over 200%, greatest below roughly 30 Hz (Currier et al, 1986; Richardson, 1981;
Wakim et al, 1948; Wakim, 1953); (7) a massage-like pumping action on venous/lymphatic
return; (8) pain relief via TENS, using low-frequency (50-100 Hz) stimulation without
contraction for superficial pain, or short, high-intensity bursts (1-150 Hz) with
contraction for deeper pain; (9) reduction of protective muscle spasm and spasticity; (10)

release, used by Russian athletes for post-training recuperation and to aid sleep onset even

mobilisation; (12) reduction of non-infectious swelling; (13) halting or slowing mild to
moderate scoliotic curvature with ES applied to specific back muscles (Axelgaard et al,
1983; Friedman et al, 1982; Kots & Chwilon, 1971; Schultz et al, 1981); (14) preferential

order, making them a supplementary route to axons that are hard to activate under normal
training (Enoka, 1988); (15) an acute strength increase after a single session: Alon (1985),

# The Authors' MACS/MICS Theory of Electrostimulation: A Speculative Synthesis, Not a Settled Mechanism

**What it is** — Building on research showing that very low currents (as little as 10
microamps, far below the milliamp-range currents of standard faradic/TENS devices) can
match or exceed conventional electrostimulation's (ES) benefits without causing contraction,
pain blockade or heating (Matteson & Eberhardt, 1985), the authors propose an "integrated
theory": macroelectric cellular stimulation (**MACS**, currents exceeding one milliamp) acts
as a physiological stressor producing Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome-type alarm
response (citing Eriksson et al, 1981, who found traditional ES's acute effects resemble
intense voluntary exercise; and Gambke et al, 1985, who found in animal studies that
long-term MACS causes some, mainly fast-twitch, fibres to degenerate and be replaced via
satellite-cell proliferation). Applying Selye's model (see 1.16), the body would draw on
"superficial adaptation energy stores" to adapt to MACS via increased strength, endurance,
or fibre-type transformation; if the ES is too intense, prolonged or misapplied, adaptation
might fail or shift toward slow-twitch fibres and reduced strength, and "excessively
demanding MACS conceivably might cause the body to draw on its deep adaptation energy and
lead to permanent tissue damage." Microelectric cellular stimulation (**MICS**, currents
below one milliamp) is proposed not to act as a stressor at all, but to elicit biochemical
changes tied to "resonant attunement" of the stimulus to cellular/subcellular processes,
citing a chain of supporting findings: Becker and colleagues on sub-threshold modulation of
electric fields across nerve and glial cells regulating growth and communication, including
wound-healing acceleration and partial limb regeneration in animals (Becker, 1974; Becker &
Marino, 1982); Nordenstrom's proposed "closed electric circuits" in the body carrying ionic
flow via blood vessels (Nordenstrom, 1983); Pilla's (1974) electrochemical membrane-signaling
model and "cellular windows" that respond most to specific frequencies, pulse widths and
amplitudes (Pilla, 1981); Rodan et al (1978), who found 5 Hz ES stimulated DNA synthesis in
chick cartilage and rat bone by up to 27% (but not in chick skin fibroblasts or rat spleen
lymphocytes) 4-6 hours after 15 minutes of stimulation; and Cheng et al (1982), who found
50-1000 microamp currents increased rat tissue ATP concentration by 300-500% and amino-acid
transport/protein synthesis by up to 40%, while currents above one milliamp depressed ATP
and protein synthesis (traditional ES commonly exceeds 20 milliamps, at which point this
depression is "nearly 50%"). Practical implication drawn from the theory: MICS can be used
far more routinely than MACS, since it "cannot produce overtraining or injury," while MACS
should be dosed and progressed like any other training stressor. (PDF pp. 224-227, printed
pp. 213-216, "4.2.1.4 Further Research Findings" and "4.2.1.5 An Integrated Theory of
Electrostimulation.")

**Why it works** — This is the authors' own proposed synthesis, not a mechanism independently
established elsewhere in the text. It rests on two distinct evidentiary threads of very
different standing: (a) a defensible, mainstream physiological point that MACS-range ES acts
as a training/adaptation stressor subject to a dose-response and overtraining risk (the
Selye/Eriksson/Gambke citations); and (b) a set of bioelectromagnetic claims (Becker's
regeneration work, Nordenstrom's "biologically closed electric circuits," Pilla's cellular
windows) that were speculative even by 1990s standards and have not entered mainstream
sports-science or clinical practice as the general theory of cell communication the authors
present them as. The authors themselves flag some of this as still-developing: "little is
known about electrical fields at the subcellular level," and classical action-potential
theory "does not explain the mechanisms whereby electric and other fields stimulate
processes such as the repair of fractures... and reduction of thrombosis" (printed 210).

**When to apply** — Inference: the (a) thread, that macro-current ES functions as a
stressor requiring progressive dosing rather than a fixed protocol, is a reasonable,
generally-applicable caution consistent with basic training-load principles and does not
depend on accepting thread (b). Do not use this entry to justify low-current "microcurrent"
devices for performance claims (tissue repair beyond standard wound-healing use, cellular
"resonance," or Nordenstrom-style circuit theory) without independent, modern verification
outside this book.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked contested: several supporting claims in thread (b) (glial-cell
signaling as a major regulatory pathway comparable to semiconductor circuits; Nordenstrom's
"closed electric circuits"; "resonant attunement" as the operative principle of MICS) are
not mainstream, independently-replicated physiology as of this ingest, and this entry does
not attempt to verify them against current literature. The Rodan (1978) and Cheng (1982)
findings are animal/cell-culture studies (chick cartilage, rat bone, rat tissue) at specific
narrow current ranges; they do not establish that MICS produces the general "growth,
adaptation and repair" effects the authors attribute to it in human athletes. Do not treat
"MACS" and "MICS" as terms used outside this text; they appear to be the authors' own
coinage for this section.

**Example** — Inference: a practitioner who reads "10-microamp microcurrent devices are as
effective as faradic stimulators without the risks" should recognize this claim rests
primarily on thread (b) above (Becker, Nordenstrom, Pilla), not on independently replicated
modern evidence, and should treat performance or healing claims for such devices with the
same skepticism the authors themselves apply to unverified action-potential-only models.

**Related** — [[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]],
[[heuristic--electrostimulation-sequencing-dosage-and-safety-practicalities]] (the
practical dosing limits the authors draw partly from this theory).

# Ratov's Functional Electrostimulation (FES): Timing the Current to the Athlete's Own EMG Signal During the Sport Skill Itself

**What it is** — Siff writes in the first person that "little or no mention is made in the
West" of Functional Electrostimulation (FES, called FENS in the West), which in the West
refers narrowly to using ES to produce movement in spinally disabled patients who cannot
voluntarily activate their muscles. In Russia and other Eastern European countries the term
also covers a different application: applying electrostimulation to able-bodied athletes
during natural sporting movements, timed to intensify muscle tension at the most
appropriate phase of the movement itself. Professor Igor Ratov of the State Central
Institute of Sports Science in Moscow developed this from his PhD work on the interrelation
between electrical stimulation and electromyography, using EMG signals from agonist and
antagonist muscles as triggers or control mechanisms to phase electrical stimulation into
the specific phases of a functional sporting movement. Ratov applied this with fencers,
boxers, rowers, shotputters and weightlifters, and, per Siff's first-person account of
witnessing the work in Ratov's laboratory, used concurrent EMG recordings "to phase the FES
correctly into specific sporting movements, most specifically to avoid producing spurious
muscle tension or uncoordinated movement." Over time, athletes learn to contract their
muscles synchronously with the externally applied electrical field, said to produce greater
strength, power and speed; this is called "active electrostimulation" (applied to actively
contracting muscles) as distinct from "passive electrostimulation" (applied to relaxed
muscles), the latter being the method most common in physical therapy. Ratov reportedly
"stresses that this type of functional stimulation is far more consistently successful than
the passive methods attributed to Kots by his Western supporters" (see
[[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]]). (PDF pp. 226-227, printed
pp. 215-216, "4.2.1.6 The Use of Electrostimulation in Training," "Sports Functional
Electrostimulation.")

**Why it works** — The stated logic: because the electrical stimulus is phased by the
athlete's own real-time EMG signal into the correct part of the movement (rather than
applied on a fixed, movement-independent schedule as in passive/general ES), it can
intensify muscle tension precisely when and where the sport skill needs it without disrupting
the coordinated movement pattern. Inference: no data (strength gain percentages, EMG
amplitude changes, performance-test results) are reported for this method in this passage;
the claim of superiority over passive ES is Ratov's own stated position, as reported by
Siff, not a cited experimental comparison.

**When to apply** — Inference: relevant to anyone considering EMG-triggered or
movement-phased electrical stimulation for sport-specific training (as opposed to general
or isolated-muscle ES); the distinguishing feature to look for in any modern device or
protocol claiming this lineage is real-time EMG-based triggering synchronized to the
athlete's own voluntary movement, not a fixed timing schedule.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: no quantitative outcome data are reported for Ratov's
method in this passage, only a description of the approach and Siff's first-hand
observation that it was applied with named elite-sport categories (fencers, boxers, rowers,
shotputters, weightlifters). The claimed superiority over passive ES ("far more consistently
successful") is reported as Ratov's own assessment via Siff, not verified against a cited
trial. Access to this specific method also depended on specialized laboratory equipment (EMG-linked
stimulators) not generally available.

**Example** — The book's own example is Ratov's application with the named sport
categories above (fencers, boxers, rowers, shotputters, weightlifters), reported by Siff as
directly observed; no further invented example is added here.

**Related** — [[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]],
[[case-study--reding-electrostimulation-protocol-siff-account]].

the reverse order; a still larger effect came from using ES and plyometrics concurrently
with heavy resistance exercise, while the ES-plyometric combination had its smallest

adjacent (close) electrode attachment localises the contraction and keeps it fairly
superficial, while distant attachment (one electrode placed at a remote or neutral site)
produces a more extensive, deeper contraction; electrode gel or weak saline solution is
needed for comfortable conduction, and skin irritation or prickliness "invariably" results
from the gel drying out. Placing electrodes directly over major nerves increases contraction
intensity but "can be harmful," and the authors restrict this to use by experienced physical
therapists. On dosing: it is "generally not advisable to apply more than 5-10 minutes of
intense ES per major muscle group," due to associated tissue necrosis and prolonged soreness
that can follow (see [[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]] for the
macroelectric/microelectric distinction behind this limit); biofeedback TENS devices that
monitor cellular electrical characteristics and adjust parameters automatically reduce
overstimulation risk. The authors' closing recommendation is that "the untutored reader is
not encouraged to use ES," since safe, effective application "requires considerable
theoretical and practical training," and that casual users typically see only sporadic,
short-term progress before discontinuing within a few months; in several countries
(the authors name the USA), ES devices may not legally be sold to the public or used
commercially by anyone without medical or physiotherapy training. (PDF pp. 225-227, printed
pp. 214-216, "4.2.1.6 The Use of Electrostimulation in Training.")

beyond the general after-effect logic already stated for training order (see
[[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]]): ES applied first may

through tissue between the two electrode sites. For the dose limit, the mechanism given

stress on the stimulated tissue, consistent with the MACS-as-stressor framing.

# Power Output Peaks and Declines With Load in a Barbell Jump, but Falls Steadily in a Leg-Press, Because of Elastic Energy

**What it is** — As barbell load increases, work increases, but power output is not
unidirectional: for a jump with a barbell on the shoulders, power output initially
increases, then, once barbell weight exceeds about 66% of maximum, it begins to decrease
(Chikvadze, 1961). Maximum power output for this jump is achieved with weights of 30-40% of
1RM, and maximal reactivity coefficient at 30-33% of 1RM. Verified against the page image
(Fig 4.2, printed p. 217): as load rises from 14% to 86% of max strength, maximal force
(Fmax) and movement time both rise, while power and the reactivity coefficient (R) show a
non-monotonic pattern across the load range rather than rising or falling steadily
throughout. The authors attribute the rise in power and reactivity coefficient with
increasing movement time to "additional elastic energy accumulated in the muscles by
absorbing the kinetic energy of the body and apparatus during the amortisation phase." A
contrasting experiment removes that elastic-energy source: seated leg extensions from a
110-degree initial knee angle, lifting 20/40/60/80% of maximum concentrically with no
countermovement or amortisation phase. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.3, printed p.
217): here, maximal force and movement time again increase with resistance, "analogous to
jumps with a barbell," but power output decreases progressively across the whole load range
instead of peaking mid-range, "because the extra elastic energy is lacking in this case."
(PDF pp. 216-217, printed pp. 216-217, "4.2.2 Resistance and Strength Training," Figs 4.2-4.3.)

**Why it works** — The authors' stated mechanism is the presence or absence of an
amortisation (countermovement/stretch-shortening) phase that stores and releases elastic
energy: the jump-with-barbell condition includes this phase, so at moderate loads the added
elastic-energy return can boost power and reactivity even as load rises, up to the point
(about 66% of max) where added weight overwhelms that benefit; the seated leg-extension
condition has no comparable amortisation phase, so power falls steadily as soon as
resistance climbs, since only added resistance (not stored elastic energy) is changing.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution when generalising a load-power relationship from
one exercise type to another: a countermovement or stretch-shortening exercise (jump,
countermovement press) can show power peaking at a specific submaximal load band (here,
30-40% of 1RM for maximal power, 30-33% for maximal reactivity), while a purely concentric,
no-amortisation exercise (seated leg extension here) shows power declining steadily as load
rises, with no such peak. Inference: this is consistent with why "optimal power load"
testing protocols (e.g. jump squats across a load spectrum) find a load band that maximizes
power, while purely concentric single-joint machine exercises typically do not show the same
peak.

**When NOT to apply** — This is single-lab, era-specific data (Chikvadze, 1961; Siff &
Verkhoshansky, 1999 figure redraws) on unspecified subjects; the specific percentages
(66% threshold, 30-40% for max power, 30-33% for max reactivity) should be treated as
illustrative for this particular jump-with-barbell protocol, not as universal constants for
all jumping or pressing exercises. Do not assume every loaded jump variation shows peak
power at exactly 30-40% of 1RM; load-power curves are known to vary by exercise and by
population in the modern literature, which this passage does not address.

**Example** — Inference: a coach programming loaded jump squats for maximal power output
should expect the power curve to rise then fall across the load spectrum (consistent with
Fig 4.2's pattern), and should not extrapolate that same rise-then-fall shape to a
non-countermovement exercise like a seated leg press or leg extension machine, where this
entry's Fig 4.3 data show power declining steadily as load increases instead.

**Related** — [[framework--force-time-curve-adaptation-pattern-by-movement-type]],
[[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]] (a related but distinct
reactivity-coefficient formulation from a different protocol, Ch3.2.1).

# Two Ways Resistance Exercises Develop Force: Against a Load's Weight, or Against Its Inertia

**What it is** — The authors distinguish resistance exercises by two different bases: first,
by whether the working force is developed after preliminary muscular tension already equal
to the apparatus's weight (e.g. the starting position of a squat or squat jump, where the
legs and torso have already developed tension equal to the barbell's weight before the
dynamic effort begins), or whether force is developed essentially from zero without
appreciable preliminary tension (e.g. the snatch or clean-and-jerk, where the working force
accelerating the bar starts from near zero). The first group does not appreciably influence
the excitation-tension processes in the muscle and, depending on the weight used, chiefly
develops either muscular strength or speed of contraction, but not the speed of switching
from rest to active state; the second group has "simultaneous potential for developing
dynamic strength, speed of movement and especially starting strength." Second, and
separately, the authors classify exercises by which physical quantity the force is directed
against: force against the weight of a load (F = m(g+a), determined by the load's mass and
its acceleration against gravity, e.g. lifting a barbell), or force against the inertia of a
load (F = ma, dependent only on the load's inertial force at a given acceleration, e.g.
throwing, sprinting out of blocks, punching, where force acts roughly perpendicular to
gravity). In the first (overcoming weight) case, muscular force first equals the load's
weight (developed under virtually isometric conditions), then exceeds it as motion begins,
producing "a large gradient of acceleration-strength." In the second (overcoming inertia)
case, if friction and air resistance are excluded, movement begins with insignificant
propulsive force, and further force changes depend entirely on the speed of muscular
contraction, i.e. the muscle's simultaneous production of maximal strength and maximal speed
of contraction. Consequently, resisting a load's weight primarily stimulates the strength
component, while resisting a load's inertia primarily stimulates the speed of muscular
contraction. (PDF pp. 218-219, printed pp. 218-219, "4.2.2 Resistance and Strength
Training.")

**Why it works** — The mechanism is straightforward Newtonian mechanics: F = m(g+a) versus F
= ma describe two different physical situations a muscle can be asked to produce force
against, and the authors' point is that a muscle's neuromuscular demand differs between
starting from a preloaded isometric-like state (weight-bearing) and starting from
essentially unloaded rest and having to generate speed against only inertia. The "large
gradient of acceleration-strength" in the weight-bearing case follows from force already
being non-zero (equal to the load's weight) at the instant motion begins, unlike the
inertia-only case, which starts from near-zero force.

**When to apply** — Use the preliminary-tension distinction (loaded-start vs
from-zero-start) to classify which exercises best target starting strength specifically:
per this framework, exercises that begin from essentially zero muscular tension (snatch,
clean-and-jerk, and by extension sprint starts, punches, throws) uniquely combine dynamic
strength, movement speed and starting-strength development, while loaded-start exercises
(squat, squat jump) do not train the speed of switching from rest to active state in the
same way. Use the weight-versus-inertia distinction to separate exercises meant to build
raw strength capacity (heavy squats, deadlifts) from those meant to build speed of
contraction against a light or unloaded resistance (medicine-ball throws, sprint
acceleration drills, punching).

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: this is a biomechanical classification of the demand an
exercise places on the neuromuscular system, not a training-volume or periodization
prescription; the authors do not state how much of each type of exercise to program, only
that the two types target different qualities. Do not assume every "explosive" exercise
falls cleanly into one category; many sport movements (e.g. a jump shot, a football block)
mix a loaded start with subsequent inertia-dominated acceleration, and this framework
addresses the two idealized cases, not every blend.

**Example** — Inference: a back squat (loaded start, force against weight) and a standing
broad jump with no external load (unloaded start, force against inertia) place different
demands on the same lower-body musculature per this framework: the squat's preliminary
tension already equals the bar's weight before the concentric drive begins, while the broad
jump must generate all of its propulsive force from a near-zero starting tension, making
starting strength and speed of contraction the dominant qualities rather than absolute force
capacity against a heavy external weight.

**Related** — [[claim--power-output-peaks-then-declines-with-load-jump-vs-leg-press]],
[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]] (Ch1, a related point that free-weight
resistance already varies with acceleration per Newton's second law).

# Muscle Recruitment Stays Fairly Consistent at Moderate Loads but Shifts Toward Proximal Muscles as Resistance or Velocity Rises

**What it is** — Two related findings on how muscle involvement changes with load and
velocity during repetitive barbell lifting. First, the "most stable indicator" of
coordinated muscular activity in repetitive lifting is the sequential involvement of the
same specific muscles across reps: in an experiment at 60% of 1RM, the muscles taking part
in the work remained the same for 82% of the time across all athletes tested; at 80% of
1RM, consistency was lower (showing greater individuality), but higher among qualified
athletes than novices, and fatigue also disrupted coordination (Pakhomov, 1967). The
relative contribution of participating muscles can also change during repetitive work
(Lazareva, 1966; Kozlov, 1966), and the number of muscle groups involved can either decrease
(Moikin, 1964) or increase (Averyanov, 1963) as a set progresses. Second, movements executed
with little effort or low velocity involve mostly the muscles of the body's distal links
(Tochilov, 1946; Kosilov, 1948; Vinogradov, 1951); against significant resistance or at high
velocity, activity characteristically shifts to the muscles of the proximal links, "which
tend to play a more tonic or postural role." The authors draw a direct implication from this
second finding: "muscle isolation under conditions of significant resistance is impossible,"
a point developed later in the chapter (see
[[claim--muscle-isolation-is-load-dependent-mostly-illusory-under-heavy-load]]). (PDF p.
229, printed p. 218, "4.2.2 Resistance and Strength Training.")

**Why it works** — No explicit mechanism is given for why recruitment consistency at 60% of
1RM (82%) exceeds that at 80% of 1RM, only the observation that qualified athletes show
greater consistency than less qualified ones at the higher load, and that fatigue disrupts
it further. Inference: this is consistent with the general principle that skilled athletes
have more stable, better-rehearsed motor patterns, which higher loads and fatigue both stress
more than lower loads. For the proximal/distal shift, the authors give no mechanism beyond
the empirical citations; Inference: this is plausibly related to proximal muscles' larger
cross-sectional area and postural/stabilising role becoming more necessary as the system
must resist larger external forces or move faster.

**When to apply** — Use the 60%-vs-80%-of-1RM recruitment-consistency finding as a caution
when interpreting EMG or force-plate data collected across a set: consistency of which
muscles are active can itself change with load and fatigue state, independent of the
athlete's technique intent. Use the proximal/distal shift finding when auditing exercise
selection for "isolation" claims at high resistance: expect proximal, postural muscle
involvement to increase, not stay constant, as load or velocity rises. **Eric's baseline:**
this is directly relevant to interpreting force-plate strategy metrics (phase durations,
which segments contribute) that vary with load, per the department's driver/strategy metric
framework (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`hd-odsf-metrics.md`).

**When NOT to apply** — These are single-lab, era-specific findings (Pakhomov 1967;
Lazareva/Kozlov 1966; Moikin 1964; Averyanov 1963; Tochilov 1946; Kosilov 1948; Vinogradov
1951) without reported sample sizes, exercise types, or modern replication in this text; the
specific 82% figure applies to Pakhomov's particular protocol at 60% of 1RM, not a general
constant. Do not assume the direction of the number-of-muscle-groups change (increase per
Averyanov vs decrease per Moikin) is reconciled in the text; both are cited as findings
without explanation of why they differ.

**Example** — Inference: an assistant coach comparing an athlete's EMG-active muscle groups
on an early, light-effort warm-up set against a heavy top set within the same exercise
should expect to see a proximal shift in the heavy set (more trunk/hip involvement) even if
technique looks visually similar, per this claim; this is a monitoring inference, not stated
in the source.

**Related** — [[claim--muscle-isolation-is-load-dependent-mostly-illusory-under-heavy-load]]
(the chapter's own forward reference, 4.2.9, which this claim explicitly anticipates),
[[claim--irradiation-effect-raises-prime-mover-force-and-endurance]] (Ch3, a related finding
on how effort in one muscle group spreads to others).

# Inertial (Flywheel) and Elastic Resistance: Different Force Profiles From Free Weights, Each With Its Own Limitation

**What it is** — The authors note that specialised equipment for training against a load's
inertia (rather than its weight) is rarely used, despite the concept warranting more serious
attention. Two solutions are given: applying force against a horizontal wheel or a
suspended, pendulum-like load, or spinning a heavy flywheel ergometer with the arms or legs
(Fig 4.4, elbow-flexion flywheel device, Verkhoshansky 1977). A flywheel device's moment of
inertia can be varied to change the speed-of-contraction demand, and it can be used several
ways: accelerating against high inertia, using the wheel's momentum to compel a certain
movement cadence, or opposing the wheel's angular momentum via eccentric muscle action to
decelerate it, with these methods combinable in short or mixed bursts. Elastic bands are
treated as a separate special case: resistance follows Hooke's Law (F = kx, where k is the
spring constant and x is extension), so elastic force starts at zero and rises with range of
movement; the authors state plainly that "elastic materials should not be used for
developing starting-strength in ballistic movements or for developing explosive-strength,"
because those qualities need force available from the very start of the movement, which
elastics cannot supply. For strength-endurance over a selected range, however, an elastic
band's length and elasticity can be chosen so its resistance changes minimally over the
working range, a method used by swimmers to develop pulling strength-endurance (Fig 4.5,
Verkhoshansky 1977). Resistance at "sticking points" can be reduced by moving toward the
band's attachment point, or increased by moving away from it; resistance can also be varied
across the full range by accelerating free weights through a decreasing-resistance portion
of the lift (so-called Compensatory Acceleration Training, see
[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]]) or by using dedicated variable-resistance
machines. (PDF pp. 219-220, printed pp. 219-220, "4.2.2 Resistance and Strength Training,"
Figs 4.4-4.5.)

**Why it works** — For flywheel/inertial devices, the mechanism is that resistance is
determined by the load's inertia (F = ma) rather than its weight (F = m(g+a)), so the
athlete can train speed of contraction against a resistance that does not exist at rest, only
once acceleration is applied, unlike a gravity-loaded free weight. For elastic bands, the
mechanism is Hooke's Law itself: resistance is proportional to extension, so it is
inherently near-zero at the start of the range and maximal at the end, the opposite loading
curve from what ballistic and explosive-strength work typically needs (high force available
immediately).

**When to apply** — Use flywheel/inertial devices when the training goal is speed of
muscular contraction against inertia specifically (per
[[framework--two-force-regimes-overcoming-weight-vs-inertia]]), varying moment of inertia to
adjust the demand, and consider eccentric-deceleration use of the same device for eccentric
overload. Use elastic bands specifically for strength-endurance work over a selected range
(the authors' cited example: swimmers' pulling strength-endurance), choosing band length and
elasticity to minimise resistance variation across that range, and use position along the
band (closer to or farther from the attachment) to manage sticking-point loading.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use elastic-band resistance alone for developing
starting-strength or explosive-strength in ballistic movements; the authors state this
directly, since Hooke's Law resistance is lowest exactly when ballistic/explosive movements
most need force to be available. The flywheel and pendulum devices described are
purpose-built or improvised apparatus (a 1992 University of the Witwatersrand student
biomechanics project supplied the plyometric bench-press device shown nearby, Fig 4.6, a
related but separate kinetic-energy device); the authors give no standardised commercial
specification for the flywheel or pendulum devices described here.

**Example** — Inference: a swim coach building pulling strength-endurance with resistance
bands, per the authors' own cited example, should select a band whose resistance changes
little across the stroke's working range, rather than a stiffer band whose resistance would
spike sharply near full extension; a sprint or jump coach chasing starting-strength or
explosive-strength should not substitute elastic-band resistance for free weights or
inertial-device training for that specific quality.

**Related** — [[framework--two-force-regimes-overcoming-weight-vs-inertia]],
[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]].

# Stimulating Muscle by Absorbing a Fall's Kinetic Energy: The Mechanics and Five Claimed Advantages Over Weighted Resistance

**What it is** — When a training device such as a barbell falls from a height and the
athlete's task is to actively stop it, then quickly thrust it upward (Fig 4.6, a purpose-built
plyometric bench-press device from a 1992 University of the Witwatersrand student
biomechanics project), the total muscular working force developed by eccentric amortisation
followed by active concentric work can be calculated as F = m(V1^2/2S1 + g) + m(V2^2/2S2 +
g), where V1 and V2 are the barbell's velocity at displacements S1 and S2 (derived from V^2 =
u^2 + 2as). Much of the falling apparatus's kinetic energy converts, during the amortisation
phase, into elastic energy used in the subsequent concentric work; excluding losses such as
heat and viscous damping as a first approximation, this elastic energy equals the kinetic
energy at the end of the fall (KE = mgh, where h is the fall height). Muscular force at the
eccentric-to-concentric switch is greater for a shorter amortisation phase and shorter
braking time, provided the goal is to thrust the apparatus at maximum speed immediately
after stopping it. The authors state the external mechanical stimulus here is "not so much
the weight (and its force of inertia) as the energy accumulated after its free-fall,"
distinguishing this from ordinary weighted resistance (see
[[framework--two-force-regimes-overcoming-weight-vs-inertia]]). Drawing on the vertical-jump
data in Fig 4.7 (see
[[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]), the authors list five claimed
advantages of this stimulation method: (1) it develops maximal dynamic force very rapidly;
(2) the magnitude of that maximum is significantly larger than other methods produce; (3) a
large maximal force is achieved without additional resistance; (4) the eccentric-to-concentric
switch happens far more rapidly than with other methods; (5) the elastic energy accumulated
without additional resistance produces greater power and faster contraction in the thrust
phase, inferred from the greater jump height reached. (PDF pp. 220-222, printed pp. 220-221,
"4.2.3 Kinetic Energy and Strength Processes," Fig 4.6.)

**Why it works** — The authors' stated mechanism is elastic-energy storage and release during
the amortisation phase (the same mechanism underlying the shock method, see
[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]), combined with the mechanical

# Heavier Falling Loads Reduce How High They Get Thrown, but Falling From Higher Reduces It Less: The Kinetic-Energy Throw Experiment

**What it is** — A laboratory stand measured the height a subject could throw a load
upward after it had first fallen from a set height (0.5 to 3.0 metres), with load
expressed as a fraction of the subject's maximum isometric strength (Po): 3.3%, 6.6%,
9.9% and 13.3% of Po (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Verified against the page image (Fig 4.8a,
printed p. 222): as fall height (h1) increases from 0 to 3 metres, throw height (h2)
rises for every load, but the lighter loads (3.3% Po) reach a substantially greater throw
height at every fall height than the heavier loads (13.3% Po), and the heaviest load's
curve flattens and slightly declines at the greatest fall heights rather than continuing to
rise. The authors summarise: "an increase in kinetic energy caused by an increase in the
mass of the load decreases the height to which a load is thrown, but an increase in the
distance through which a load falls increases the height to which it is thrown." A similar
pattern appears for reactive ability (Fig 4.8b, reactivity coefficient plotted against the
falling load's kinetic energy in joules): verified against the page image, each load curve
(3.3%, 6.6%, 10%, 13.3% Po) is an inverted-U shape rising to a peak reactivity coefficient
then declining as kinetic energy increases further, with the peak's position and height
differing by load (the lightest, 3.3% Po, load reaches the highest peak reactivity
coefficient, around 7, at a moderate kinetic energy). The authors conclude "it is not
beneficial to increase kinetic energy by use of heavier loads," and that a better means of
increasing thrust height is needed. (PDF pp. 221-223, printed pp. 221-222, "4.2.3 Kinetic
Energy and Strength Processes," Fig 4.8.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no separate mechanism beyond the shared elastic-energy
logic already stated for this section (see
[[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]]): a heavier load
carries more kinetic energy at a given fall height (KE = mgh scales with mass), but that
extra energy appears to exceed what the muscle can productively absorb and return within a
short amortisation phase, so throw height and reactivity fall off rather than continuing to
rise with load. Inference: this is consistent with an optimal-loading phenomenon where
elastic-energy return and voluntary concentric contribution both have a productive range,
beyond which added mass mainly adds braking demand rather than usable stored energy.

**When to apply** — Use this as evidence against assuming "more kinetic energy equals more
training stimulus" when programming falling-load or catch-and-thrust exercises (e.g. weighted
plyometric throws, loaded catch-and-press devices): per this experiment, increasing the drop
height is a more productive way to raise thrust/throw height than increasing the load,
within the tested range (0.5-3.0 m fall heights, 3.3-13.3% of isometric strength as load).

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single-lab (Verkhoshansky, 1977) experimental stand using a
narrow load range expressed relative to isometric strength (Po), not a standard external
load; the specific percentages and the shape of the reactivity-coefficient curves should not
be assumed to transfer directly to other exercises, populations, or load types (e.g. a
barbell drop-catch versus this stand's specific apparatus) without direct testing. The
authors do not report the subject population or sample size for this experiment.

**Example** — The book's own example is this experimental stand and its Fig 4.8 data; no
further invented example is added here.

**Related** — [[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]],
[[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]],
[[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]] (Ch3.2.1, a related but distinct
reactivity-coefficient protocol using a fixed 0.4 m depth jump with externally added mass
rather than this section's variable fall-height, variable-load-as-%-of-Po stand).

# The Optimal Depth-Jump Drop Height Is 0.75-1.15 Metres: Maximal Power at the Low End, Maximal Force at the High End

**What it is** — Verified against the page image (Fig 4.7, printed p. 221): comparing three
vertical-jump conditions by force (in bodyweights) against time, (1) jumping from rest from
a low squat produced the lowest and latest force peak and a jump height of 0.67 m; (2) the
usual jump with a dip/amortisation phase produced a higher, earlier force peak and 0.74 m;
(3) a jump after a depth-jump from 0.4 m produced the highest and earliest force peak and
0.80 m (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Extending this to depth jumps from a range of drop heights
(Fig 4.10, printed p. 223): maximal force (Fmax) increases with drop height up to 1.15
metres, then diminishes sharply; movement time changes little at first, then increases
sharply at greater drop heights; maximum power output and maximum reactivity are both
achieved at a drop height of approximately 0.75 metres. The authors state the optimal range
of depth jumping for stimulating muscular activity is therefore 0.75-1.15 metres: "at the
lower end of this range the muscles are working at maximal power and at the upper end they
are working at maximal dynamic force." This finding underlies the training recommendations
for advanced jumpers (Verkhoshansky 1963, 1964, 1966), though the authors recommend erring
toward considerably lower drop heights for anyone unaccustomed to this training and strictly
limiting volume of this "shock" training. Beyond 1.15 metres, ground-contact (support) time
increases quickly, primarily because the eccentric-to-concentric switching phase lengthens,
while maximum dynamic force and contraction speed at take-off stabilise and stop increasing.
The take-off is described as two distinct phases: amortisation (kinetic energy absorbed,
characterised by progressively deeper knee flexion) and thrust proper (characterised by a
fairly constant speed of muscle contraction). (PDF pp. 222-223, printed pp. 221-223,
"4.2.3 Kinetic Energy and Strength Processes," Figs 4.7, 4.9, 4.10.)

**Why it works** — The authors' stated mechanism is again elastic-energy storage during
amortisation and its release in the thrust phase (see
[[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]]); at greater drop
heights, force capacity is used mainly for braking (absorbing more kinetic energy),
explaining why force keeps rising up to 1.15 m while power and reactivity peak earlier (at
0.75 m), once the added braking demand from a higher drop starts to lengthen the
amortisation phase and slow the eccentric-to-concentric switch.

**When to apply** — Use 0.75 m as a drop height when the training goal is maximal power and
reactivity, and up to about 1.15 m when the goal is maximal dynamic force, per this specific
protocol; for athletes unaccustomed to depth-jump training, start considerably lower than
this range and strictly limit training volume, per the authors' own caution. This gives a
citable historical anchor for programming depth-jump height, distinct from (and using a
different, variable-height protocol than) the fixed 0.4 m depth-jump reactivity test already
in this library (see [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]]).

**When NOT to apply** — This is single-lab, era-specific data (Verkhoshansky, 1963-1977) on
an unspecified population (the authors do not state training age, sport, or sample size for
the drop-height range experiment); the specific numbers (0.75 m, 1.15 m) should not be
applied to every athlete without accounting for training age, technical competency and
bodymass, which the authors themselves flag by recommending lower heights for the
unaccustomed athlete. Do not conflate this protocol's variable drop-height range with the
separate, fixed-0.4-m depth-jump reactivity test already documented in this library (see
Related); they are different experiments answering different questions (optimal training
drop height here, versus a reactive-ability measurement protocol there).

**Example** — The book's own example is the Fig 4.7 and Fig 4.10 data described above; no

metres, then diminishes sharply; movement time changes little at first, then increases
sharply at greater drop heights; maximum power output and maximum reactivity are both
achieved at a drop height of approximately 0.75 metres. The authors state the optimal range

# Hettinger and Muller's Original Isometric-Training Finding: About 5% Strength Gain Per Week From One Daily 6-Second Effort at Two-Thirds Maximum

**What it is** — Isometric exercises became popular in the mid-1950s in the search for
economical, effective strength methods. Hettinger and Muller (1953, 1955) established that
one daily effort at two-thirds of maximum, held for six seconds, performed for 10 weeks,
increases strength by about 5% per week. Separately, Clark et al (1954) found that static
strength continues to increase even after a four-week isometric programme has concluded.
This early success prompted considerable research comparing isometric training's
effectiveness against dynamic training, which produced "rather contradictory data" (see
review by Verkhoshansky, 1970). The authors' general conclusion from that body of research:
isometric training can be more effective than dynamic exercise specifically where the target
exercise requires a large-magnitude muscle contraction at a certain stage of a movement, or
during early-stage injury rehabilitation; if the target exercise involves high-speed
movement, sustained isometric training is less effective. The authors also note that
because isometric training's usual purpose is developing absolute strength, tension should
be increased slowly and held for a relatively long time, since prolonged tension maintenance
demands the energy expenditure that stimulates adequate neuromuscular adaptation; some
researchers found no essential difference in strength gain from varying isometric tension
intensity, from which the authors infer that tension duration, not magnitude, is the
"fundamental conditioning factor." (PDF pp. 235, printed pp. 223-224, "4.2.4 Isometric
Training.")

**Why it works** — The authors' stated reasoning: prolonged maintenance of muscular tension
requires an energy expenditure that "stimulates adequate adaptation in the neuromuscular
system, thereby determining its strength potential," and this can exceed the stimulus from
brief transient dynamic tension. Inference: no cellular or neural mechanism is given for why
duration outweighs magnitude specifically; this is an inference the authors draw from
studies not finding a strength-gain difference across tension intensities, not a stated
physiological pathway.

**When to apply** — Use the 5%-per-week figure and the two-thirds-maximum, 6-second, daily,
10-week protocol as a citable historical anchor for isometric-training dosing, and use the
authors' scoping rule (isometrics favoured for large-magnitude contraction at a specific
movement stage or early rehab; less favoured when the target skill is high-speed) to decide
when isometric work is the better tool versus dynamic resistance training.

**When NOT to apply** — This is single-era data (1950s studies, corroborated only by a 1970
review) without modern replication in this text; treat "5% per week" as specific to
Hettinger and Muller's exact protocol (two-thirds max, 6 seconds, daily, 10 weeks), not a
generalizable isometric-training growth rate. The "contradictory data" comparing isometric
to dynamic training is acknowledged by the authors themselves, so this entry's headline
finding should not be read as settling the isometric-versus-dynamic debate; it explains only
the original claim's origin and the authors' scoping conditions for it.

**Example** — The book's own example is the Hettinger and Muller protocol itself (daily,
6-second, two-thirds-maximum isometric effort for 10 weeks, yielding about 5% weekly
strength gain); no further invented example is added here.

**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]],
[[claim--isometric-regional-specificity-not-strictly-angular]].

# Isometric Contraction Is Not One Thing: Voluntary vs Reflexive, Slow vs Explosive

**What it is** — The authors argue isometric training is not simply holding a static
contraction for a set time: a true isometric contraction requires the muscle to raise
tension from rest to a maximal or sub-maximal value over a rise ("attack") time, sustain
that tension for a resistance phase, then decrease it to rest or a lower value over a decay
time. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.11, printed p. 225): the authors categorise
isometric contraction into voluntary isometrics (splitting further into slow isometrics and
voluntary explosive isometrics) and reflexive isometrics (splitting further into reflexive
explosive isometrics and oscillatory isometrics). A voluntary isometric contraction can be
produced deliberately; a reflexive one occurs involuntarily via the muscle's reflex response
between the eccentric and concentric phases of plyometric activities such as a depth jump or
the weightlifting clean-and-jerk. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.12, printed p.
225): slow isometrics show a gradual force rise, a longer resistance-phase plateau, and a
gradual decay; explosive (reflexive) isometrics show a much steeper rise phase and a
substantially shorter resistance phase before decay. The authors argue that because the
steepness of the isometric force-time curve, and the higher magnitude of maximum isometric
versus dynamic maximum force at equivalent joint angles, both support developing explosive
strength isometrically when the training accent is on speed of force development, "it is
doubtful whether it is always productive to maintain a rigid distinction between dynamic and
isometric exercise": as resistance grows very large, dynamic work becomes progressively more
isometric, so isometric work is "really the limiting case of dynamic work as the velocity of
movement tends to zero." Because reflexive isometric contraction bypasses the inhibitory
effects normally associated with voluntary muscle action, "even greater explosive force can
be displayed isometrically than dynamically." A related but separate finding on impulsive
loading: short bouts of low-frequency mechanical vibration (10-35 Hz) applied to the body
have been shown to speed recovery, modulate muscle activity, raise strength/power stable
state, lower arterial pressure and enhance oxidative processes (Kopysov, 1978; Lebedev &
Peliakov, 1991), and whole-body vibration at 26 Hz through the lower extremities has been
shown to produce marked increases in jumping power (Bosco et al, 1998); the authors note
this fuels an open debate about whether plyometric training effects are driven mainly by
elastic-energy storage/release, neural facilitation, or intrinsic muscle changes (Ingen
Schenau et al, 1997). (PDF pp. 235-236, printed pp. 224-225, "4.2.4 Isometric Training,"
Figs 4.11-4.12.)

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism for the voluntary/reflexive distinction is neural:
reflexive isometric contraction (occurring automatically between eccentric and concentric
phases) escapes voluntary inhibitory control that would otherwise limit force, permitting
higher force display than a deliberately initiated voluntary contraction can achieve.
Inference: the slow-vs-explosive distinction within each category follows from how quickly
neural drive ramps up to the target tension level, which the force-time curve shape (Fig
4.12) captures directly.

**When to apply** — Use this taxonomy when specifying what kind of isometric work a given
drill is training: a sustained maximal hold at a joint angle is a slow voluntary isometric;
a deliberately fast ramp to near-maximal tension is a voluntary explosive isometric; the
brief isometric moment at the bottom of a depth jump or clean-and-jerk catch is a reflexive
(explosive or oscillatory) isometric that the athlete does not consciously initiate. Per the
authors, distinguish "isometric training for developing absolute strength" from "isometric
training for developing explosive strength" and select the appropriate type for the goal.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors themselves flag this distinction as still needing
"detailed experimental corroboration." The vibration/whole-body-vibration findings are a
separate line of evidence (Bosco et al, 1998, and others) that the authors connect to this
discussion only by analogy (impulsive loading), not by stating vibration produces isometric
contraction in the sense defined here; treat the two topics as related but distinct.

**Example** — The book's own example is the depth-jump and clean-and-jerk catch positions
cited as sources of reflexive isometric contraction; no further invented example is added
here.

**Related** — [[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]] (Ch1, the broader
concentric/eccentric/isometric/quasi-isometric terminology this taxonomy sits within),
[[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]].

# Hettinger and Muller's Original Isometric-Training Finding: About 5% Strength Gain Per Week From One Daily 6-Second Effort at Two-Thirds Maximum

**What it is** — Isometric exercises became popular in the mid-1950s in the search for
economical, effective strength methods. Hettinger and Muller (1953, 1955) established that
one daily effort at two-thirds of maximum, held for six seconds, performed for 10 weeks,
increases strength by about 5% per week. Separately, Clark et al (1954) found that static
strength continues to increase even after a four-week isometric programme has concluded.
This early success prompted considerable research comparing isometric training's
effectiveness against dynamic training, which produced "rather contradictory data" (see
review by Verkhoshansky, 1970). The authors' general conclusion from that body of research:
isometric training can be more effective than dynamic exercise specifically where the target
exercise requires a large-magnitude muscle contraction at a certain stage of a movement, or
during early-stage injury rehabilitation; if the target exercise involves high-speed
movement, sustained isometric training is less effective. The authors also note that
because isometric training's usual purpose is developing absolute strength, tension should
be increased slowly and held for a relatively long time, since prolonged tension maintenance
demands the energy expenditure that stimulates adequate neuromuscular adaptation; some
researchers found no essential difference in strength gain from varying isometric tension
intensity, from which the authors infer that tension duration, not magnitude, is the
"fundamental conditioning factor." (PDF pp. 235, printed pp. 223-224, "4.2.4 Isometric
Training.")

**Why it works** — The authors' stated reasoning: prolonged maintenance of muscular tension
requires an energy expenditure that "stimulates adequate adaptation in the neuromuscular
system, thereby determining its strength potential," and this can exceed the stimulus from
brief transient dynamic tension. Inference: no cellular or neural mechanism is given for why
duration outweighs magnitude specifically; this is an inference the authors draw from
studies not finding a strength-gain difference across tension intensities, not a stated
physiological pathway.

**When to apply** — Use the 5%-per-week figure and the two-thirds-maximum, 6-second, daily,
10-week protocol as a citable historical anchor for isometric-training dosing, and use the
authors' scoping rule (isometrics favoured for large-magnitude contraction at a specific
movement stage or early rehab; less favoured when the target skill is high-speed) to decide
when isometric work is the better tool versus dynamic resistance training.

**When NOT to apply** — This is single-era data (1950s studies, corroborated only by a 1970
review) without modern replication in this text; treat "5% per week" as specific to
Hettinger and Muller's exact protocol (two-thirds max, 6 seconds, daily, 10 weeks), not a
generalizable isometric-training growth rate. The "contradictory data" comparing isometric
to dynamic training is acknowledged by the authors themselves, so this entry's headline
finding should not be read as settling the isometric-versus-dynamic debate; it explains only
the original claim's origin and the authors' scoping conditions for it.

**Example** — The book's own example is the Hettinger and Muller protocol itself (daily,
6-second, two-thirds-maximum isometric effort for 10 weeks, yielding about 5% weekly
strength gain); no further invented example is added here.

# Isometric Training's Six Advantages, Six Drawbacks, and the Authors' Recommended Execution Protocol

**What it is** — The authors list six advantages proponents claim for isometric training:
(1) it requires very simple apparatus; (2) it can locally exercise any muscle group at a
specific joint angle, which dynamic work can only briefly pass through, since movement
inertia usually carries the load past the angle of greatest mechanical effect; (3) it is
time-productive, since each 6-second isometric contraction is "equivalent in its effect" to
many dynamic ballistic contractions in which maximal force lasts no more than 0.1 second,
meaning 10 minutes of targeted isometric tension can replace "a fatiguing hour" of dynamic
weight training; (4) it produces an insignificant increase in muscle mass and bodymass
compared with dynamic strength work, particularly pressing exercises; (5) it costs far less
time and energy than dynamic weight training, letting an athlete preserve a high
speed-strength level during a crucial competition period; (6) it offers more potential than
dynamic exercise for using visual and kinaesthetic cues to hold a given position, an
advantage for studying and correcting technical errors. Six drawbacks are also listed:
isometrics fatigue the nervous system; may harm the cardiovascular system in some
individuals via prolonged breath-holding and elevated blood pressure; disturb coordination;
enhance muscle performance only near the specific trained joint angle; decrease speed of
movement; and diminish soft-tissue elasticity and functional range of dynamic movement.
Proper breathing, adequate rest/relaxation between exercises, and limiting contraction length
to 6 seconds (some authors recommend up to 10) can minimise these harmful after-effects. The
authors give four methods of producing isometric tension: (1) pressing against an immovable
structure or a partner's resistance, with the drawback that strength change can only be
judged subjectively without a dynamometer; (2) holding a raised load for a set period, with a
quasi-isometric variant shifting the load slowly across the range with stops at different
joint angles; (3) pushing a weight from a lower support up to press against an upper stop
(a power rack), giving a brief dynamic phase before the isometric hold and letting the
athlete lift several times between stops; (4) using a dynamometer or other resistance
device to control and display tension magnitude. For non-explosive isometrics, the authors
give a specific protocol: apply force gradually, hold maximal tension no longer than 8
seconds, perform 6 repetitions, rest 5-10 seconds between reps, limit total isometric
training to 10 minutes per session, and finish with relaxation exercises; for developing
explosive strength instead, tension should be generated at maximum speed to 70-80% of
maximum strength, and reflexive explosive isometric action from plyometric movements "can be
extremely effective" for this. (PDF pp. 236-237, printed pp. 225-226, "4.2.4 Isometric
Training.")

**Why it works** — The authors give a specific mechanism only for advantage (2), regarding
joint-angle specificity of loading, and advantage (3), the time-efficiency claim, which rests
on comparing sustained near-maximal isometric tension duration against the brief (about 0.1
second) duration of maximal force during a ballistic dynamic contraction. Inference: the
remaining advantages and drawbacks are stated as observations rather than derived from a
single unifying mechanism.

**When to apply** — Use the 8-second hold, 6-repetition, 5-10-second-rest, 10-minute-session
protocol as the authors' recommended baseline for non-explosive isometric training aimed at
absolute strength, and the 70-80%-max, maximum-speed protocol for explosive-strength-focused
isometric work. Weigh the six advantages against the six drawbacks for a given athlete and
context: the cardiovascular caution (drawback 2) is particularly relevant for athletes with
existing cardiovascular risk factors, and the coordination-disturbance and range-of-movement
drawbacks argue for pairing isometric work with dynamic training rather than using it as a
sole training means.

**When NOT to apply** — This protocol and these advantages/drawbacks are the authors' own
synthesis from an era (1950s-1970s citations) predating modern force-plate or dynamometer-based
isometric dosing research; do not treat the "equivalent to a fatiguing hour of training"
comparison (advantage 3) as a rigorously measured equivalence, since no controlled outcome
comparison is cited for that specific claim. The drawbacks (cardiovascular risk, coordination
disturbance, reduced movement speed, reduced tissue elasticity) argue against using isometric
training as an athlete's sole or dominant training means, per the authors' own framing.

**Example** — Inference: a coach using isometric mid-thigh pulls to reinforce a specific
sticking-point joint angle is applying advantage (2) directly; the same coach should still
program dynamic work elsewhere in the week to offset the coordination and movement-speed
drawbacks this entry lists.

**Related** — [[framework--isometric-contraction-categorization-voluntary-reflexive]],
[[claim--hettinger-muller-isometric-strength-gain-rate]],
[[principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting]] (Ch3,
the cardiovascular/breath-holding caution this entry's drawback 2 overlaps with).

# Isometric Strength Gains Spread Further From the Training Angle When the Muscle Trains in a Lengthened Position

**What it is** — Many studies report isometric training producing maximum strength gains at
or very close to the trained joint angle, leading some athletes to avoid isometric training
altogether; the authors argue this "angular specificity" framing needs critical revision,
citing other studies showing isometric training also produces significant strength increase
up to about 15 degrees either side of the training angle. Because every type of muscle
contraction has its own force/torque-versus-joint-angle curve (see 2.1.2), the authors argue
it is "highly unlikely" that strength gain would be confined to one precise angle and
nowhere else, and prefer the term "regional specificity" over "angular specificity" (or
muscle-length specificity). Thepault-Mathieu et al (1988) found this regional specificity is
strongest when the muscle trains in its most shortened position and weakest when it trains
most lengthened: males training isometrically for 5 weeks (5 sets of 5 reps, 5 seconds each,
3 times weekly) at 25 degrees of elbow flexion (full extension = 0 degrees) gained 54%
strength at the training angle but only about 25% averaged over the rest of the range; a
group training at 80 degrees gained 30% at the training angle and about 25% over the rest of
the range; a group training at 120 degrees gained 25% at the training angle but only about
7% over the rest of the range. The authors' summary: isometric training of a relatively
lengthened muscle can produce substantial strength increase "not only near the region of
training, but also throughout the range of movement." They caution this finding should not
be read as meaning isometric training can replace other strength-training forms, since a
specific type of static or dynamic strength depends on the neuromuscular factors governing
how force is exerted in a given situation. (PDF pp. 237-238, printed pp. 226-227, "4.2.4
Isometric Training," "Isometric Training and Angular Specificity.")

**Why it works** — The authors give the biomechanical basis (a distinct force/torque-vs-angle
curve exists for every contraction type) for why strict single-angle specificity is
implausible, but they do not give a mechanism for why the Thepault-Mathieu et al (1988)
lengthened-position condition specifically produced the broadest transfer across the range
(54%/25 degrees training angle giving about 25% elsewhere, versus 120 degrees training angle

# Isometric Endurance Collapses Above 10-15% of Maximal Tension, and Recovers in Three Distinct Phases

**What it is** — Isometric endurance at resistance exceeding 10-15% of a muscle's maximal
strength is very short compared with dynamic exercise, because of metabolic demand and
impaired blood flow to the exercising muscle under sustained contraction (Petrofsky &
Phillips, 1986); below that threshold, contractions are considered non-fatiguing, since
intramuscular pressure stays low and is readily exceeded by rising mean arterial pressure in
the capillaries. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.13, printed p. 227, cat soleus and
gastrocnemius, electrically stimulated, based on Petrofsky & Hendershot, 1984): intramuscular
pressure rises roughly linearly with muscle tension, from near 0 kPa at rest to over 20 kPa
at 100% of maximal strength. As tension rises, intramuscular pressure rises with it and
metabolism cannot keep pace, producing a hyperbolic drop in performance and marked fatigue
increase (the Rohmert curve, first derived by Monod and Sherrer 1967, later by Rohmert
1968). Verified against the page image (Fig 4.14, printed p. 227, finger flexors, based on
Petrofsky 1980): endurance time falls hyperbolically as %MVC (maximum voluntary contraction)
rises, and females sustain the same tension level for longer than males at every tension
level tested, a difference the authors say "has not been adequately explained yet." Muscle
temperature also affects isometric endurance: hot packs reduce it and pre-exercise icing
increases it, with an optimum core muscle temperature (later work places it around 27-28
Celsius, Petrofsky & Phillips, 1986) above and below which endurance drops; higher bodyfat
percentage, associated with higher resting muscle temperature, is linked to lower isometric
endurance in most situations. Unlike dynamic exercise (which is more efficient at higher
temperatures, likely due to reduced tissue viscosity), isometric contraction involves no
fibre movement, so viscosity plays an "insignificant role compared with that of muscle
metabolism." Recovery from isometric contraction proceeds in three phases (Petrofsky &
Phillips, 1986): a rapid recovery of about 50% of endurance in the first 3 minutes; a slower
recovery lasting about 20 minutes, reaching about 90% of initial endurance; and complete
recovery within at least 24 hours; recovery from low-tension isometric contraction is
"interestingly" slower during the initial recovery phases. (PDF pp. 236-239, printed pp.
226-228, "4.2.4 Isometric Training," "Isometric Endurance," "Recovery after Isometric
Activity," Figs 4.13-4.14.)

**Why it works** — The authors' stated mechanism is a mechanical-metabolic one: rising muscle
tension raises intramuscular pressure, which above roughly 10-15% of maximal strength begins
to exceed the arterial pressure available to perfuse the muscle, choking off the blood flow
that metabolism needs to sustain the contraction, producing the hyperbolic Rohmert-curve
drop in endurance. No mechanism is given for the sex difference in endurance or for the
27-28 Celsius optimum temperature beyond citing the studies that measured them.

**When to apply** — Use the 10-15%-of-maximal-strength threshold as a practical dividing line
between "non-fatiguing" and rapidly fatiguing isometric holds when designing isometric
protocols (e.g. low-level postural holds versus near-maximal strength holds). Use the
three-phase recovery timeline (about 50% back in 3 minutes, about 90% back in 20 minutes,
full recovery by 24 hours) when spacing repeated maximal isometric efforts within and between
sessions.

**When NOT to apply** — The intramuscular-pressure data (Fig 4.13) are from electrically
stimulated cat soleus and gastrocnemius (Petrofsky & Hendershot, 1984), not human voluntary
contraction; treat the specific kPa values as animal-model data illustrating the
tension-pressure relationship, not human norms. The Rohmert-curve endurance data (Fig 4.14)
are specifically finger-flexor endurance (Petrofsky, 1980), a small, distal muscle group;
the shape of the curve (hyperbolic decline, female advantage) should not be assumed to hold
identically for large, proximal muscle groups without separate verification. The 27-28
Celsius optimum-temperature finding and the bodyfat-endurance link are each from single
cited sources without reported effect sizes.

**Example** — Inference: a coach prescribing a sustained postural isometric hold (e.g. a
plank or wall-sit at low relative intensity) can expect it to be comparatively non-fatiguing
per the 10-15%-of-maximum threshold, while a near-maximal isometric mid-thigh pull hold will
fatigue rapidly and require the multi-minute recovery windows this entry describes before a
comparable maximal effort can be repeated.

**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-training-execution-protocol-and-advantages-drawbacks]],
[[principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting]] (Ch3,
a related discussion of intramuscular/intrathoracic pressure during sustained maximal
effort).
